# Breton Civil War, 1341–1343

The **Breton Civil War, 1341–1343** was a succession conflict in the Duchy of Brittany that erupted following the death of Duke John III in April 1341. Two rival claimants competed for control of the duchy: Joan of Penthièvre, niece of the deceased duke, whose claim was backed by her husband Charles of Blois and the French crown; and John of Montfort, half-brother of John III, who was supported by John's wife, Joanna of Flanders, and eventually by King Edward III of England. The conflict formed an integral part of the early Hundred Years' War due to the involvement of France and England in supporting their respective claimants. The war, which would ultimately last until 1365, saw dramatic military campaigns featuring the celebrated defense of Hennebont by Joanna of Flanders and the first significant Anglo-French land battle at Morlaix in 1342.

### Background and Succession Dispute

In the early 14th century, the Duchy of Brittany occupied a unique position within the Kingdom of France. Although the dukes were nominally vassals of the French crown, they governed their territory with considerable autonomy. When Duke John III died childless on 30 April 1341, he left a contested succession dispute that would escalate into a broader European conflict.

John III had married three times but produced no direct heirs. By his first marriage to Mary of Limoges, he had two brothers: one was his heir as John III, and another was Guy, Count of Penthièvre. By his father Arthur II's second marriage to Yolande of Dreux, John had a half-brother named John of Montfort. John III spent much of his reign attempting to exclude his half-siblings from the succession, even seeking an annulment of his father's second marriage to bastardize them.

At John III's death, two principal claimants emerged. Joan of Penthièvre, the niece of the late duke and daughter of Guy of Penthièvre, asserted her claim through her marriage to Charles of Blois, a nephew of King Philip VI of France. The alternative claim came from John of Montfort, the half-brother of John III. The succession question became intertwined with the concept of semi-Salic law, which governed Brittany. Under this system, male succession was strongly preferred, but if no male heir of the previous duke existed, inheritance could pass through a female to her male relatives. John of Montfort's supporters emphasized that Brittany's status as a duchy-peerage ("duchy-peerage") of the French crown should be subject to strict male succession principles, while the Blois faction argued for a more flexible interpretation that would allow a woman to inherit if married to a capable male heir.

The French king, Philip VI, naturally favored his nephew Charles of Blois and the Blois claim, viewing this as an opportunity to bring the semi-autonomous Duchy of Brittany under more direct royal control. The situation became further complicated by the fact that both claimants' patrons—Edward III of England and Philip VI of France—were locked in the Hundred Years' War, a conflict that had begun in 1337.

### Initial Campaign of 1341

Upon John III's death, John of Montfort acted with remarkable speed. By August 1341, he and his wife Joanna of Flanders had secured control of most of the major fortified towns and cities in Brittany, including Rennes, Vannes, Auray, Hennebont, Quimper, Brest, and Nantes. An assembly of citizens and minor nobility in Nantes formally acknowledged John as duke, giving his claim a veneer of local legitimacy. This early maneuvering secured the Montfort faction's position and demonstrated that John of Montfort had considerable support among the Breton nobility and merchant classes.

However, Philip VI of France grew concerned when reports of John's negotiations with English emissaries reached him. On 7 September 1341, the French king officially declared Charles of Blois the rightful heir to the duchy and resolved to enforce this claim militarily. Philip dispatched a substantial French army to Brittany under the command of Charles and Jean, Duke of Normandy (the future King John II of France), to compel the Montfort faction to submit.

The result was swift and dramatic. Under overwhelming military pressure, the French forces besieged John of Montfort in the city of Nantes. After a siege lasting approximately three weeks, John surrendered on 21 November 1341 and was taken prisoner. He was subsequently transferred to Paris and imprisoned in the Louvre, where he would remain for several years. With the male leader of the Montfort cause captured, many observers assumed the conflict had been resolved in favor of Charles of Blois and the French crown.

### The Role of Joanna of Flanders

The conflict, however, was far from settled. Joanna of Flanders, John of Montfort's wife, now took the unprecedented step of assuming military and political leadership of the Montfort faction. This decision proved transformative for the character of the war. Rather than accept her husband's captivity and her family's apparent defeat, Joanna acted with strategic vision and considerable courage. She secured the ducal treasury and transferred it westward to the stronghold of Brest, beyond the reach of the French forces. She captured the town of Redon and then established herself at Hennebont, a fortified port town in southern Brittany with strong defensive walls.

Most significantly, Joanna declared her two-year-old son, John (the future John IV), as the legitimate heir and figurehead of the Montfort faction. By elevating a child to nominal leadership, she maintained the continuity of the Montfort claim and provided a rallying point for supporters who might otherwise have accepted the loss of John of Montfort's cause. She then sent emissaries to England to appeal directly to King Edward III for military assistance, leveraging the fact that Edward had strategic reasons to support any force that could weaken French authority in Brittany.

Edward III, engaged in his own conflict with France and seeking to establish English influence in Brittany as a springboard for operations against France, agreed to provide military support. However, the practical difficulties of transporting troops across the English Channel—limited shipping capacity, unfavorable weather, and competing military priorities—meant that English reinforcements were delayed and limited in scale throughout 1342.

### Siege of Hennebont and Joanna's Defense

In late May 1342, Charles of Blois launched a siege of Hennebont, where Joanna had positioned herself and the bulk of the Montfort faction's remaining forces. This siege became one of the most celebrated episodes of the conflict and established Joanna's reputation for military prowess and leadership.

According to contemporary chronicles, Joanna personally participated in the defense of the town. During the initial assault, when French forces attacked the gates in disarray, Joanna rallied the defenders and inflicted a sharp defeat on the attackers, with many French casualties. Most dramatically, she reportedly organized a daring sortie of approximately 300 mounted men-at-arms. Under her leadership, these troops rode out of the fortified town, set fire to the French siege camp, destroyed supplies and siege equipment, and inflicted significant casualties before withdrawing. This bold action and the resulting destruction of the French encampment earned Joanna the epithet "Jeanne la Flamme," or "Fiery Joan."

After this initial repulse, Charles attempted a more systematic siege, bringing up siege engines and establishing a closer blockade. By late May or early June 1342, the situation appeared dire for the defenders, and there was discussion of surrender. However, Joanna held firm, expressing confidence that English reinforcements would arrive within three days. Her faith proved justified. In June 1342, a small English relief force arrived by sea, having penetrated the harbor of Hennebont. This modest English reinforcement was sufficient to encourage the defenders and to prompt Charles to withdraw his besieging forces temporarily. Joanna and her remaining troops evacuated the town and moved further west, continuing the struggle in the extreme western portions of Brittany.

### English Military Intervention and Battle of Morlaix

The arrival of English forces marked a significant escalation in the Breton conflict. In August 1342, an English fleet of approximately 260 ships commanded by William of Northampton arrived off the coast of Brittany with approximately 1,350 fighting men. This modest force caused a dramatic reversal of the military situation through a combination of shock effect and psychological impact. When Charles of Blois, who was besieging the port of Brest, saw the large English fleet crowded with what he assumed were vast numbers of troops, he dramatically overestimated the size of the landing force and withdrew his siege forces, retreating northward along the coast to Guingamp, a distance of approximately 120 kilometers.

Northampton, reinforced and moving inland from Brest, soon engaged Charles's army at Morlaix on 30 September 1342 in what became the first significant land battle of the Hundred Years' War fought in France. At Morlaix, the English employed defensive tactics and superior use of longbowmen, elements that would characterize English military success throughout the Hundred Years' War. The English force, numbering approximately 1,500 men, was heavily outnumbered by Charles's army of roughly 3,000 men. However, Northampton positioned his troops on rising ground and had his men dig concealed pits and ditches to impede the French cavalry charge. When the French attacked in successive waves, the English longbowmen, armed with powerful yew bows capable of penetrating armor, inflicted devastating casualties on the charging horsemen. The French could not overcome the English defensive position, and after repeated failed assaults, Charles withdrew from the field, leaving the English victorious.

### Edward III's Campaign

Following the English success at Morlaix, King Edward III himself arrived in Brittany in October 1342 with additional reinforcements, though not in the numbers he had hoped for due to difficulties in assembling sufficient shipping. Edward proceeded to besiege the important town of Vannes, seeking to consolidate English and Montfort control over southern Brittany. However, the siege proved inconclusive, and the English advance was soon checked.

The numerical advantage shifted dramatically against the English when Philip VI raised a much larger French army and marched it into Brittany. This large French force, commanded by royal princes and numbering in the thousands, advanced toward Edward's position near Vannes and came to a halt at Malestroit, approximately 18 miles (29 kilometers) from the English camp. With Edward's forces facing a massive French army and the supply situation becoming critical due to inability to send sufficient provisions and reinforcements from England, both monarchs agreed to negotiate.

### Truce of Malestroit

On 19 January 1343, the Truce of Malestroit was sealed between Edward III and Philip VI at the town of Malestroit. This truce was mediated by papal emissaries and was intended to pause the Hundred Years' War for approximately three and a half years, lasting until 29 September 1346. The truce provided that both monarchs would send delegations to Avignon, then the seat of the Papacy, where Pope Clement VI would mediate negotiations aimed at achieving a permanent peace settlement between England and France.

The Truce of Malestroit formally suspended major military operations between the English and French crowns, though the underlying conflict remained fundamentally unresolved. Both Edward and Philip viewed the truce as a temporary respite rather than as a genuine peace agreement, and neither side engaged in good-faith negotiations during the subsequent peace conference in Avignon. The truce also raised questions about the status of the Breton conflict, as it suspended the active military engagement between the French and English armies that had characterized the conflict since 1342.

### Aftermath

Although the Truce of Malestroit brought large-scale military operations to an end in 1343, the Breton Civil War itself continued, albeit at reduced intensity and often at the periphery of larger Franco-English military operations. The Montfort faction retained control of western and northern Brittany, while the Blois faction controlled the east and south. The fundamental question of the duchy's succession remained unresolved through the 1340s and 1350s. The conflict would eventually continue with renewed intensity following the expiration and renewal of various truces between England and France, culminating in the definitive English-supported victory of John of Montfort (John IV) at the Battle of Auray in 1364, which resulted in the death of Charles of Blois and the end of active hostilities in 1365.

died 1309)​ * [Isabella of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_Castile,_Queen_of_Aragon "Isabella of Castile, Queen of Aragon") ​ ​ (m. 1310; died 1328)​ * [Joan of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Savoy "Joan of Savoy") ​ (m. 1329)​ | | [House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynasty "Dynasty") | [Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Dreux "House of Dreux") | | Father | [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany") | | Mother | [Marie, Viscountess of Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie,_Viscountess_of_Limoges&action=edit&redlink=1 "Marie, Viscountess of Limoges (page does not exist)") | **John III _the Good_** (in [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language "Breton language") _Yann III_, in [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") _Jean III_; 8 March 1286 – 30 April 1341) was [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Brittany "Duke of Brittany"), from 1312 to his death and 5th [Earl of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Richmond "Earl of Richmond") from 1334 to his death. He was the son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany"), and his first wife Marie, Viscountess of Limoges.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-1) John was strongly opposed to his father's second marriage to [Yolande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_of_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scotland") and attempted to contest its legality. In 1297, John married Isabella of Valois,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988210-2) eldest child of [Charles, Count of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Valois "Charles of Valois") and his first wife [Margaret of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_of_Naples "Margaret of Naples"). At the time of their marriage John was eleven years old and his bride five. She died childless in 1309. In 1310, John married his second wife, [Isabella of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_Castile,_Duchess_of_Brittany "Isabella of Castile, Duchess of Brittany").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-1) She died childless in 1328. In 1329, John married his third wife [Joan of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Savoy "Joan of Savoy").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-1) He predeceased his third wife by three years and died childless. He was unwilling to cede the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") to his half-brother [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), son of his hated step-mother Yolande. He wished to leave the duchy to the French [King Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), but his nobles objected. The marriage of his niece [Joanna of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joanna_of_Dreux "Joanna of Dreux") to [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois") gave Charles a plausible claim to the duchy, but the matter was unresolved at John's death. After his death, John of Montfort claimed his rights as duke of Brittany, but King Philip VI supported the Blois faction, and the [Breton War of Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") (1341–1364) was triggered. The Breton Civil War was fought between the [House of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blois "House of Blois") and the [House of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfort_of_Brittany "Montfort of Brittany"). It became part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), as England supported the Montfort faction, which won, against the House of Blois, which was supported by France. Brittany was a province of [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France"), but although the dukes of Brittany were [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the French kings they governed the duchy as independent rulers. When Duke [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") (r. 1312–1341) died childless on 30 April 1341, title to the duchy was claimed by both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his younger half-brother, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). Joan's claim was exercised through her husband, [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), a nephew of the king of France, [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") (r. 1328–1350). A complicating factor was the ongoing [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between France and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") that had broken out in 1337. A truce was in place which was due to expire in June 1341 but was extended to June 1342. It was generally assumed that Joan's claim would prevail and that Charles would become the new duke, but John acted quickly and installed friendly garrisons in most of the towns and castles of Brittany by August. He discussed the possibility of a military treaty with English emissaries but made no move towards effecting one. Rumours of these discussions reached Philip, causing him to turn against John and in September Charles was recognised as the new duke. John refused to give way and Philip sent an army to Brittany to impose Charles. Within a month John had been defeated and was a prisoner. His wife, [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), sent the ducal treasury west to [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"), took command of her husband's field army, stormed the town of [Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon,_Ille-et-Vilaine "Redon, Ille-et-Vilaine") and moved to the small but strongly walled town of [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"). She despatched a senior counsellor to encourage English military intervention, set up her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy, and waited on events. The war lasted 24 years, frequently as a part of the Hundred Years' War. [![Image 3: A pen and ink drawing of the head and shoulders of a bearded man in early modern style](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/CarlosIdebritania.jpg/240px-CarlosIdebritania.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CarlosIdebritania.jpg) Charles of Blois as envisaged in 1621 In the 14th century, [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") was a province of France, but although the dukes of Brittany were [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the French kings they governed the duchy as independent rulers.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199017,_34%E2%80%9335-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006b62-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19888-3) Nevertheless, when the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") broke out in 1337 between France and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") the Duke of Brittany, [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") (r. 1312–1341), fought alongside his feudal lord the [King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_of_France "Kings of France"), [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") (r. 1328–1350). John III died on 30 April 1341, leaving a disputed succession; both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his younger half brother, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), claimed the dukedom. Joan was the only child of John III's dead younger brother Guy, and was married to [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"), a well-connected and militarily oriented French nobleman who was also a nephew of the King of France. Complicating the legal situation – which was unprecedented in Breton law – John III seems to have on separate occasions formally promised the succession to both John of Montfort and Charles of Blois.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199966%E2%80%9367-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202037%E2%80%9338,_47%E2%80%9349-6) John had the stronger legal claim but the [aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocracy "Aristocracy") and [clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy "Clergy") knew little about him and mostly preferred Charles' claim. What support John had came largely from the lower levels of society, especially in the towns. It was widely accepted in Brittany that Charles would inherit.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990371,_374-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007202-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006a60-9) John, encouraged by his wife, [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), took 200 men and seized [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes"), the most important town in Brittany, shortly after John III's funeral. He then took control of the Breton treasury and unsuccessfully wooed the great men of Brittany. In early June 1341 John moved on to an alternative plan: to take control of as much of Brittany as he could, and so encourage Philip to confirm him as the new duke to avoid possible conflict. John left Nantes to secure [Champtoceaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champtoceaux "Champtoceaux"), a large ducal castle about 30 kilometres (19 mi) to the north east on the south bank of the [River Loire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loire "Loire"). It protected Nantes from enemies approaching from central or northern France and John garrisoned it with mercenaries.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371,_374%E2%80%93377,_387-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007202%E2%80%93203-11) John continued on to [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes"), the second-largest town in Brittany and its capital. It had strong walls and a large garrison, but after a brief and fumbled defence the town surrendered. [Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier "Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier"), a strong fortification defending the approach to Rennes from [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), followed suit, as did the walled town of [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan"). Having subdued most of eastern Brittany – the richest and most populous part of the duchy – John returned to Nantes, then during July and early August overran most of the towns of southern and western Brittany. Few were well-fortified or stoutly defended and there was only fighting at [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"). By mid-August, John had all but made good his claim to the duchy. Philip disregarded the situation, ignoring requests for assistance from Charles of Blois. John's loyalty at this point was unquestioned and so expelling him by force when he had a strong legal case was politically unappealing, and ran the risk of driving him into an alliance with the English. Philip passed the question of who should succeed John III to the [Parlement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement_of_Paris "Parlement of Paris") – a judicial rather than legislative body – where deliberations were liable to be long drawn out.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-12) English intervention -------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: English intervention")\] A map of Brittany, with modern administrative boundaries, showing the locations of some of the places mentioned in the text While these events were taking place, the [Truce of Espléchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was in force between France and England. Ostensibly halting all fighting, in practice it prevented either country from deploying their main field armies, but was otherwise ill observed. The truce was originally due to expire on 24 June 1341, but was extended on 9 June to 29 August, and on 10 August to 14 September. Fighting on a large scale continued in south-west France and at sea as both sides prepared to mobilise major forces once the truce expired.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006c122%E2%80%93123-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990358%E2%80%93359,_379%E2%80%93380,_383-14) [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") sent an emissary to John of Montfort, who held discussions with him on 10 July regarding John recognising Edward as king of France in exchange for Edward's recognising John's claim to Brittany and providing military support. John equivocated: he wished to have support for his claim in the event of Philip's deciding in favour of Charles of Blois, but was not ready to cause a break with Philip if it could be avoided.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990383%E2%80%93385-15) Rumours of these negotiations reached Philip VI, causing him to come down firmly in favour of Charles of Blois as the new duke of Brittany,[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200236-16) but he did not announce it. Instead he planned for an armed seizure of Brittany and accelerated the hearing of the case by the Parlement of Paris. John was summoned to Paris as a witness, arriving in late August.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990384-17) While attending on Philip VI it became clear that he had lost the French King's confidence. In early September John fled from Paris for Nantes. On 7 September the Parlement formally decided that Charles of Blois was the legitimate successor to John III.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-18) Once the issue was definitively decided in favour of Charles, his nephew, the idea of bringing the traditionally semi-autonomous province more firmly under royal control was attractive to Philip; he was willing to commit considerable military resources, which were available due to the truce with England.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-19) [![Image 4: A Medieval image of Philip VI seated, wearing a blue robe](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Philippe_VI_de_Valois_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Philippe_VI_de_Valois_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Philippe_VI_de_Valois_/(cropped/).jpg) By late August 1341 Edward III had decided against an early renewal of the war. In particular the lack of a response from John and the knowledge that he had left Brittany for Paris seemed to rule out an otherwise potentially inviting opportunity. Accordingly, on 12 September 1341 the Truce of Espléchin was extended again, this time for nine months, to 24 June 1342. Edward and his [council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_England "Privy Council of England") agreed that the English army would be disbanded for the winter and the fleet paid off; while this was taking place representatives arrived from John announcing that he had broken with Philip VI and that as soon as military support arrived in Brittany he would swear [fealty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fealty "Fealty") to Edward III as his [liege lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liege_lord "Liege lord") and the rightful king of France. Edward saw great possibilities in the situation and in early October agreed a formal alliance with John, allocated £10,000 for military expenditure,[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-21) gave orders to attempt to reassemble the recently disbanded fleet, and allocated a small force of men to sail in it, hopefully – if optimistically – by early November.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990385%E2%80%93386-22)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-18) This was the start of Edward's "provincial strategy", by which he sided with French vassals of Philip in their disagreements with him: this promoted Edward's claim to be the rightful king of France and potentially created military allies.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-23) Strategically Edward had the opportunity to set up a ruler in Brittany at least partially under his control, which would provide access to Breton ports, greatly aiding England's naval war and giving ready entry to France for English armies.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-19) [![Image 5: A colourful Medieval image of a castle under siege in a romantic style](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Si%C3%A8ge_de_Champtoceaux_%281420%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Si%C3%A8ge_de_Champtoceaux_%281420%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Si%C3%A8ge_de_Champtoceaux_/(1420/)_/(cropped/).jpg) A fifteenth-century impression of Champtoceaux under siege In late September the French gathered a 7,000-strong army together with a strong force of [siege artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engine "Siege engine") at [Angers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angers "Angers"), 80 kilometres (50 mi) east of the Brittany border, to enforce Charles's claim. This was commanded by Philip's eldest son, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") (future King John II), although Philip, nervous and half-hearted about resorting to armed force, allocated minders to oversee him and issued strict instructions. John of Montfort in turn garrisoned the Breton towns and fortifications he controlled. In early October Charles of Blois led the [advance guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanguard "Vanguard") of the French army along the Loire valley as far as Champtoceaux and laid siege to it, starting the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"). The rest of the army followed a few days later. John was heavily outnumbered but boldly advanced with a small force to a fortified outpost at L'Humeau, 5 kilometres (3 mi) west of Champtoceaux. Unknown to John, L'Humeau had already fallen to the French and Charles of Blois was there. When John arrived he almost captured Charles, who escaped with most of the garrison to a fortified tower and barricaded himself in. After two days of fierce fighting, with many casualties on each side, John was driven off by the much larger French force and the tower relieved. By the end of the month Champtoceaux had capitulated to the French.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990386%E2%80%93387-24) John of Montfort retreated to Nantes and within a few days the French army was encamped outside the walls. The French were unable to besiege or even effectively [blockade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade "Blockade") the town. Instead they stormed the outlying castles loyal to John and executed the prisoners taken in sight of the town walls to terrorise the populace. The speed of the French advance cut off John from his main field force, which was concentrated around [Saint-Renan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Renan "Saint-Renan") in the far west of Brittany waiting for English reinforcements. John repeatedly led sorties against the besiegers, using the small force he had with him and the town militia. These met with little success and suffered heavy casualties. Less than a week after the French arrived, and after one such attack led to the deaths of many of a large force of townsmen who had accompanied John, a town assembly insisted that he open negotiations for a [capitulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitulation_/(surrender/) "Capitulation (surrender)"). John personally surrendered to John of Normandy on 2 November, and Charles of Blois entered Nantes, to be celebrated as the rightful duke.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990388%E2%80%93389-25)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006a59-26) When news of the fall of Nantes arrived Joanna of Flanders was in Rennes with her children, the duchy's treasury and a strong garrison. Modern historians consider her to have been an energetic and effective leader, and she acted decisively and aggressively. She sent the treasury west to Brest, recalled the field army and took command herself.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390,_409-27)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-28)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199967-29)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433%E2%80%9334-30) Joining it with some of the troops from Rennes she stormed the town of [Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon,_Ille-et-Vilaine "Redon, Ille-et-Vilaine") and then moved on to [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"). This was a small but strongly walled town with access to the sea and from there Joanna took control of what forces were still lending their allegiance to her husband's cause, setting up her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy. She despatched her senior counsellor, [Amaury of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_de_Clisson "Amaury de Clisson"), to Edward III to encourage English intervention and waited on events.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-31)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-28) When John surrendered he agreed to give up all of his Breton possessions and abide by King Philip's ruling regarding the inheritance of the Duchy of Brittany, and had been promised a [safe conduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_conduct "Safe conduct") to Paris and back. He travelled to Paris at the end of 1341, escorted by John of Normandy. Philip proposed to John that he repudiate all claim to Brittany and his possessions there in favour of Charles of Blois, receiving an [annuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annuity "Annuity") and land in France in exchange. John declined, at which Philip withdrew his son's promised safe conduct and had him imprisoned. As this was happening, the military commanders of many of the towns and castles held for John were negotiating handovers to Charles of Blois in exchange for pardons. In eastern Brittany only Rennes held out for the Montfort cause by the end of February 1342. The west remained mostly under Joanna's control.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990388%E2%80%93391-32) A small English force reinforced Joanna in May 1342, which was sufficient to keep the Montfort cause alive. [Edward III landed in Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign "Edward III's Breton campaign") with a larger force in late October, only to agree a [truce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit") the following January.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1980174-33)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-34) John of Montfort died in 1345,[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-35) but the Breton Civil War continued as a disjointed and inconclusive series of sieges, skirmishes and truces, frequently as part of the Hundred Years' War, until Charles of Blois was killed in 1364 at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") and his army decisively defeated. The next year Joan of Penthièvre, Charles' widow, signed the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"), recognising John's son as Duke of Brittany, which ended the war.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1980174-33)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-34)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1999106-36)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006a92%E2%80%9393-37) **John of Montfort** ([Middle Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Breton_language "Middle Breton language"): _Yann Moñforzh_, [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Jean de Montfort_) (1295 – 26 September 1345),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-1) sometimes known as **John IV**,[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-2) was [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Brittany "Duke of Brittany") and [Earl of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Richmond "Earl of Richmond") from 1341 to 1345 in dispute with his niece [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") and her husband [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"). He was also [Count of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Montfort-l%27Amaury "Count of Montfort-l'Amaury") from 1322. He was the son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany"), and his second wife, [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_de_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande de Dreux, Queen of Scotland"). His contesting of the inheritance of the Duchy of Brittany with his niece Joan led to the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"), which in turn evolved into being part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France. John's patron in his quest was King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrevit%C3%A9-Orton1978877-3) He died in 1345, 19 years before the end of the war, and the victory of his son [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), over Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois.

[![Image 2: Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg/250px-Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg "Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.")

Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.

John of Montfort was born in 1295, the only son to Arthur II of Brittany and his second wife Yolande of Dreux.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) In 1322 he inherited from his mother the title of count of Montfort-l'Amaury,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-5) and in 1329 he married [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") in [Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres "Chartres").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) Joanna was the daughter of [Louis I, Count of Nevers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I,_Count_of_Nevers "Louis I, Count of Nevers"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) and [Joan, Countess of Rethel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan,_Countess_of_Rethel "Joan, Countess of Rethel"). They had:

*   [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") (1339–1399), married (1) [Mary of Waltham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_of_Waltham "Mary of Waltham") (1344–1362), daughter of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), in 1361 in Oxfordshire;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (2) [Joan Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Holland,_Duchess_of_Brittany "Joan Holland, Duchess of Brittany") (1350–1384) in 1366 in London;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (3) [Joan of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Navarre,_Queen_of_England "Joan of Navarre, Queen of England") (1370–1437), daughter of King [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), in 1386 in Saillé-près-Guérande.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988123-6)
*   [Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Brittany,_Baroness_of_Drayton "Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton") (1341–1402), married before 21 October 1385 to [Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Basset,_3rd_Baron_Basset_of_Drayton "Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChibnall1965130-7)

Succession to Duke John III
---------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Succession to Duke John III")\]

On 30 April 1341, [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), died without a male heir. His half-brother, John of Montfort, was a candidate for the succession, which was also claimed by Joan of Penthièvre, niece of John III and wife of Charles of Blois, himself a nephew of the [Philip VI, King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). The King was, of course, favourable to his nephew.

The Duchy of Brittany historically had a "semi-Salic" mode of inheritance; male primogeniture was followed unless no direct male descendants remained. At that point the closest female descendant inherited as duchess, with her husband serving as duke by "right of representation". The position of John of Montfort was legally founded on the belief that a brother (even a half-brother) was a closer heir than a beneficiary niece, and that the Salic form of inheritance adopted by the Kingdom of France should be followed. This argument was based on the fact that since 1297 Brittany had been a _duché-pairie_ ("member and part of the crown"), and that the legislation of the suzerain kingdom should therefore be applied.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin198299-8) Challenges to the [Salic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salic_law "Salic law") of the Franks had historically been rejected for the Kingdom of France, allowing Philip V to gain the throne in 1316, and Philip VI most recently. This made Philip VI's support of Joan of Penthièvre quite ironic, in that the argument for Philip VI to inherit the Kingdom of France was based on the opposing philosophy that the crown should not be able to descend through the female line to Edward III.

A civil war, termed the War of the Breton Succession, then began and lasted 23 years. This conflict was also called _La guerre de deux Jeanne_, after the French names of the two duchesses in competition: Jeanne de Penthièvre and Jeanne de Flanders, wife of John of Montfort.

Early stages of the War (1341)
------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early stages of the War (1341)")\]

After the funeral of John III, Charles of Blois returned to the Court of France and John of Montfort returned to his Breton estate in [Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gu%C3%A9rande "Guérande"). Then, incited by his wife (according to tradition), he went with a small army to [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") where he was well received by the inhabitants who swore their loyalty. John then went to [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges") where he managed to obtain the ducal treasury. John returned to Nantes and was recognised as Duke in May 1341 by an assembly composed of members of the towns and minor nobles, but shunned by the major vassals with the exception of Hervé VII, Count of Léon. Thanks to the ducal treasury, he recruited mercenaries which allowed him to perform in June and July a 'great ride in Brittany' (as described by Arthur de la Borderie) and take control of the duchy. John first gained [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes"), then [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes") and the places surrounding the [Château de Suscinio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Suscinio "Château de Suscinio"), [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray"), [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), and then [Quimperlé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimperl%C3%A9 "Quimperlé"). Having failed to take the domains of [Rohan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Rohan "House of Rohan"), he submitted [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper "Quimper") and [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France") before descending to [Carhaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carhaix "Carhaix"), and then went back northward and captured [Saint-Brieuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Brieuc "Saint-Brieuc"), [Lamballe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamballe "Lamballe"), [Jugon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jugon-les-Lacs_/(delegated_commune/) "Jugon-les-Lacs (delegated commune)"), [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan"), [Dol-de-Bretagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne "Dol-de-Bretagne"), and returned to Nantes via [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel").

Always accompanied by Hervé VII of Léon, John obtained the submission, if not the support, of some of the major nobles who possessed several of these strongholds and had been loyal to Charles of Blois. However it would probably require getting [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin"), or the support of the high secular clergy and great lords, or more, to control the domains of the Penthièvres and the House of Rohan, which represented about two-thirds of Brittany.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975425%E2%80%93429-9) John also went to England and met with Edward III of England in Windsor, who promised him military assistance and invested him with the [Honour of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honour_of_Richmond "Honour of Richmond").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin1982100-10)

Charles of Blois then made an appeal to Philip VI, who summoned John of Montfort to a Court of Peers session in Conflans in September 1341. In this context by the judgment of Conflans, the Duchy of Brittany was attributed to Charles of Blois. Philip VI agreed to receive _l'hommage lige_ of Charles of Blois on behalf of his wife, and confiscated from John of Montfort the French lands of the County of Montfort-l'Amaury, as well as the Viscounty of Limoges that he held more unduly.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975430%E2%80%93432-11)

In October 1341, Charles of Blois and [John II, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") (later King of France), put together an army and penetrated into Brittany. They managed to retrieve a number of strongholds which had been lost, including Nantes, which relented on 21 November 1341 after three weeks of siege. John of Montfort was captured and imprisoned in the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre") in Paris. Despite the change of camp of Hervé VII de Leon (due to criticisms from John regarding his handling of the siege of Nantes), Joanna, the wife of John of Montfort, continued the armed struggle supported by his allies.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975441%E2%80%93449-12)

Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)
----------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)")\]

After a winter break that ended on 15 April 1342, Charles of Blois resumed the fight and regained a large part of Brittany between May and September 1342. King Edward III of England decided to intervene on behalf of the House of Montfort. Charles de Blois failed to take Hennebont, which was defended by [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), while [Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois") was mortally wounded besieging Vannes in vain leading an English contingent. In January 1343, through [Pope Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), a truce was signed at [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit") to bring peace and the liberation of John of Montfort. The latter was released in September 1343 and retired to England 27 March 1345. His return to the struggle with reinforcements provided by King Edward III of England put an end to the truce. John of Montfort unsuccessfully laid siege to Quimper, then fell ill and died in Hennebont on 26 September 1345.

Tomb of John of Montfort
------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tomb of John of Montfort")\]

He was buried in the convent of the Dominicans of Quimperlé[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-13) where his tomb, which had already been desecrated, was found again in December 1883.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Villemarqu%C3%A91884278%E2%80%93297-14) His remains are now in the Church of Sainte-Croix de Quimperlé.

*   [Dukes of Brittany family tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Brittany_family_tree "Dukes of Brittany family tree")
*   [List of works of the two Folgoët ateliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_works_of_the_two_Folgo%C3%ABt_ateliers "List of works of the two Folgoët ateliers")

1.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_ref-2)** Until recently, most English historians designated him as John IV, since the English king recognised his claim. However, [French historians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_historians "French historians") have never recognised him as Duke of Brittany, but rather as a pretender, a position that most historians now accept.
