| Salic law | | --- | | [![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Jugement_de_Childebert_III_accordant_%C3%A0_l%27abbaye_de_Saint-Denis_la_terre_de_Hodenc-l%27Ev%C3%AAque_dans_l%27Oise.jpg/330px-Jugement_de_Childebert_III_accordant_%C3%A0_l%27abbaye_de_Saint-Denis_la_terre_de_Hodenc-l%27Ev%C3%AAque_dans_l%27Oise.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jugement_de_Childebert_III_accordant_%C3%A0_l%27abbaye_de_Saint-Denis_la_terre_de_Hodenc-l%27Ev%C3%AAque_dans_l%27Oise.jpg)Record of a judgement by [Childebert III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Childebert_III "Childebert III"), who reigned from 694 to 711 AD | | Created | c. 500 AD | | Commissioned by | King [Clovis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I "Clovis I") | | Subject | Law, justice | | Purpose | [Civil law code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_/(legal_system/) "Civil law (legal system)") | | Full text | | ![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/20px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png) [The Salic Law](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Salic_Law "wikisource:The Salic Law") at [Wikisource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikisource "Wikisource") | The **Salic law** ( or ; [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _Lex salica_), also called the **Salian law**, was a Frankish [civil law code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_/(legal_system/) "Civil law (legal system)") compiled around 500 AD by [Clovis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I "Clovis I"), the first [Frankish king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankish_king "Frankish king"). The name may refer to the Salii, or "[Salian Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salian_Franks "Salian Franks")", but this is debated. The written text is in [Late Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Latin "Late Latin"),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-1) and contains some of the earliest known instances of [Old Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch "Old Dutch").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-2) It remained the basis of Frankish law throughout the [early medieval period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_medieval_period "Early medieval period"), and influenced future [European legal systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Western_law "History of Western law"). The best-known tenet of the old law is the principle of exclusion of women from inheritance of thrones, fiefs, and other property. The Salic laws were arbitrated by a committee appointed by the [Frankish king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_the_Franks "King of the Franks"). Dozens of manuscripts dating from the 6th to 8th centuries and three emendations as late as the 9th century have survived.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-3) Salic law provided written codification of both civil law, such as the statutes governing [inheritance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inheritance "Inheritance"), and [criminal law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_law "Criminal law"), such as the punishment for [murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder "Murder"). Although it was originally intended as the law of the [Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franks "Franks"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-4) it has had a formative influence on the tradition of [statute law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_law "Statute law") that extended to [modern history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_history "Modern history") in much of Europe, especially in the [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") states and [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary") in [Central Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Europe "Central Europe"), the [Low Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries") in [Western Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe"), [Balkan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans") kingdoms in [Southeastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Europe "Southeastern Europe"), and parts of [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_historic_states_of_Italy "List of historic states of Italy") and [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Aragon "Crown of Aragon") in [Southern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Europe "Southern Europe"). Its use of [agnatic succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnatic_succession "Agnatic succession") governed the succession of kings in kingdoms such as [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy_/(Holy_Roman_Empire/) "Kingdom of Italy (Holy Roman Empire)"). [![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Salic_Law.png/250px-Salic_Law.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Salic_Law.png) [King Clovis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I "Clovis I") dictates the _Lex Salica_ surrounded by his military chiefs. [![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Frankish_Foederatus.png/250px-Frankish_Foederatus.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frankish_Foederatus.png) Salian settlement in [Toxandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxandria "Toxandria"), where they had recently settled or been settled in 358, when [Julian the Apostate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_the_Apostate "Julian the Apostate") made them _[dediticii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dediticii "Dediticii")_ The original edition of the code was commissioned by the first king of all the Franks, [Clovis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I "Clovis I") (c. 466–511), and published sometime between 507 and 511.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-5) He appointed four commissioners[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-6) to research customary law that, until the publication of the Salic law, had been recorded only in the minds of designated elders, who would meet in council when their knowledge was required. Transmission was entirely oral. Salic law, therefore, reflects ancient usages and practices.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-7) To govern more effectively, having a written code was desirable for monarchs and their administrations. For the next 300 years, the code was copied by hand, and was amended as required to add newly enacted laws, revise laws that had been amended, and delete laws that had been repealed. In contrast with printing, hand copying is an individual act by an individual copyist with ideas and a style of his own. Each of the several dozen surviving manuscripts features a unique set of errors, corrections, content, and organization. The laws are called "titles", as each one has its own name, generally preceded by _de_, "of", "concerning". Different sections of titles acquired individual names, which revealed something about their provenances. Some of these dozens of names have been adopted for specific reference, often given the same designation as the overall work, _lex_.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The [recension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recension "Recension") of [Hendrik Kern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Hendrik_Caspar_Kern "Johan Hendrik Caspar Kern") organizes all of the manuscripts into five families according to similarity and relative chronological sequence, judged by content and dateable material in the text.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-8) Family I is the oldest, containing four manuscripts dated to the eighth and ninth centuries, but containing 65 titles believed to be copies of originals published in the sixth century.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-9) In addition, they feature the _Malbergse Glossen_, "[Malberg Glosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Malberg_Glosses&action=edit&redlink=1 "Malberg Glosses (page does not exist)")", marginal [glosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloss_/(annotation/) "Gloss (annotation)") stating the native court word for some Latin words. These are named from native\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] _malbergo_, "language of the court".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-10) Kern's Family II, represented by two manuscripts, is the same\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] as Family I, except that it contains "interpolations or numerous additions, which point to a later period".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-11) Family III is split into two divisions. The first, comprising three manuscripts, dated to the eighth–ninth centuries, presents an expanded text of 99 or 100 titles. The Malberg Glosses are retained. The second division, with four manuscripts, not only drops the glosses, but also "bears traces of attempts to make the language more concise".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-Kernxvii-12) A statement gives the provenance: "in the 13th year of the reign of our most glorious king of the Franks, Pipin".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-Kernxvii-12) Some of the internal documents were composed after the reign of [Pepin the Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepin_the_Short "Pepin the Short"), but it is considered to be an emendation initiated by Pepin, so is termed the _Pipina Recensio_. Family IV also has two divisions – the first comprised 33 manuscripts; the second, one manuscript. They are characterized by the internal assignment of Latin names to various sections of different provenances. Two of the sections are dated to 768 and 778, but the emendation is believed to be dated to 798, late in the reign of [Charlemagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlemagne "Charlemagne"). This edition calls itself the _Lex Salica Emendata_, or the _Lex Reformata_, or the _Lex Emendata_, and is clearly the result of a law code reform by Charlemagne.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-Kernxvii-12) By that time, Charlemagne's [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") comprised most of Western Europe. He added laws of choice (free will) taken from the earlier law codes of Germanic peoples not originally part of Francia. These are numbered into the laws that were there, but they have their own, quasisectional title. All the Franks of Francia were subject to the same law code, which retained the overall title of _Lex Salica_. These integrated sections borrowed from other Germanic codes are the _[Lex Ribuariorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Ripuaria "Lex Ripuaria")_, later _Lex Ribuaria_, laws adopted from the [Ripuarian Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripuarian_Franks "Ripuarian Franks"), who, before Clovis, had been independent. The _[Lex Alamannorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Alamannorum "Lex Alamannorum")_ took laws from the [Alamanni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alamanni "Alamanni"), then subject to the Franks. Under the Franks, they were governed by Frankish law, not their own. The inclusion of some of their law as part of the Salic law must have served as a palliative.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Charlemagne goes back even earlier to the _Lex Suauorum_, the ancient code of the [Suebi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suebi "Suebi") preceding the Alemanni. The Salic law code contains the _Malberg glosses_, which, despite the name, are not technically [glosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloss_/(annotation/) "Gloss (annotation)") in the traditional sense, but rather Germanic terms interspersed through the Latin legal docoment.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-Hoff-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-14) These Germanic words and several short sentences are, though heavily corrupted by subsequent copyists unfamiliar with the original language, have been used to [reconstruct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_reconstruction "Linguistic reconstruction") the earliest stage of the Dutch language, [Old Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch "Old Dutch"),[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-Seebold-15)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-Hoff-13)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-16) containing what is likely the earliest surviving full sentence in the language:[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-17)
Malberg glossmalthothi*afriolito**
(Modern) Dutchik meld,joubevrijd ik,laat
EnglishI tell you:I am setting you free,serve
\* Old Dutch and Early Modern and earlier versions of English used the second-person singular pronouns, such as _thou_ and _thee_. \*\* A _lito_ was a form of [serf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serfdom "Serfdom") in the [feudal system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_system "Feudal system"), a half-free farmer, connected to the lord's land, but not owned by that lord. In contrast, a slave was fully owned by the lord. This sentence is also given as the following:[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-18)
Malberg glossmaltho:thiafrio,letu!
translationI declare judicially:I let you free,half-free (farmer)!
Some tenets of the law ---------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Salic_law&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Some tenets of the law")\] These laws and their interpretations give an insight into Frankish society. The criminal laws established damages to be paid and fines levied in recompense for injuries to persons and damage to goods, [theft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theft "Theft"), and unprovoked insults. One-third of the fine paid court costs. Judicial interpretation was by a [jury of peers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jury_of_peers "Jury of peers"). The civil law establishes that an individual person is legally unprotected if he or she does not belong to a [family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family "Family"). The rights of family members were defined; for example, the equal division of land among all living male heirs, in contrast to [primogeniture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primogeniture "Primogeniture"). One tenet of the civil law is [agnatic succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrilineality#Agnatic_succession "Patrilineality"), explicitly excluding females from the inheritance of a throne or [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief"). Indeed, "Salic law" has often been used simply as a [synonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym "Synonym") for agnatic succession, but the importance of Salic law extends beyond the rules of inheritance, as it is a direct ancestor of the systems of law in use in many parts of continental Europe today.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Salic law regulates succession according to sex. "Agnatic succession" means succession to the throne or fief going to an agnate of the predecessor – for example, a brother, a son, or nearest male relative through the male line, including collateral agnate branches, for example very distant cousins. Chief forms are [agnatic seniority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnatic_seniority "Agnatic seniority") and [agnatic primogeniture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnatic_primogeniture "Agnatic primogeniture"). The latter, which has been the most usual, means succession going to the eldest son of the monarch; if the monarch had no sons, the throne would pass to the nearest male relative in the male line. Concerning the inheritance of land, Salic law said: > But of Salic land no portion of the inheritance shall come to a woman: but the whole inheritance of the land shall come to the male sex.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-19) or, another transcript: > \[C\]oncerning terra Salica, no portion or inheritance is for a woman, but all the land belongs to members of the male sex who are brothers. The law merely prohibited women from inheriting ancestral "Salic land"; this prohibition did not apply to other property (such as [personal property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_property "Personal property")); and under [Chilperic I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilperic_I "Chilperic I") sometime around the year 570, the law was actually amended to permit inheritance of land by a daughter if a man had no surviving sons (This amendment, depending on how it is applied and interpreted, offers the basis for either Semi-Salic succession or male-preferred [primogeniture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primogeniture "Primogeniture"), or both). The wording of the law, as well as common usage in those days and centuries afterwards, seems to support an interpretation that inheritance is divided between brothers, and if it is intended to govern succession, it can be interpreted to mandate agnatic seniority, not direct primogeniture. In its use by continental hereditary monarchies since the 15th century, aiming at agnatic succession, the Salic law is regarded as excluding all females from the succession, and prohibiting the transfer of succession rights through any woman. At least two systems of hereditary succession are direct and full applications of the Salic Law: [agnatic seniority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnatic_seniority "Agnatic seniority") and [agnatic primogeniture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnatic_primogeniture "Agnatic primogeniture"). The **Semi-Salic** version of succession order stipulates that firstly all-male descendance is applied, including all collateral male lines, but if all such lines are extinct, then the closest female agnate (such as a daughter) of the last male holder of the property inherits, and after her, her own male heirs according to the Salic order. In other words, the female closest to the last incumbent is "regarded as a male" for the purposes of inheritance and succession. This has the effect of following the closest extant blood line (at least in the first instance) and not involving any more distant relatives. The closest female relative might be a child of a relatively junior branch of the whole dynasty, but still inherits due to her position in the male line, due to the longevity of her own branch;\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] any existing senior\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] female lines come behind that of the closest female. From the Middle Ages, another system of succession, known as cognatic male primogeniture, actually fulfills apparent stipulations of the original Salic law; succession is allowed also through female lines, but excludes the females themselves in favour of their sons. For example, a grandfather, without sons, is succeeded by a son of his daughter, when the daughter in question is still alive. Or an uncle, with no children of his own, is succeeded by a son of his sister, when the sister in question is still alive. This fulfils the Salic condition of "no land comes to a woman, but the land comes to the male sex". This can be called a "quasi-Salic" system of succession and it should be classified as primogenitural, cognatic, and male-preferred. A title in the Salic law code required the unanimous consent of a village for any newcomer wishing to move and settle there, with the disapproval of just a single resident being sufficient to deny settlement rights. A migrant's tenure in a settlement would only become secure if no objections were received within 12 months of arrival.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-20) Applications of the succession and inheritance laws --------------------------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Salic_law&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Applications of the succession and inheritance laws")\] The Merovingian kings divided their realm equally among all living sons, leading to much conflict and fratricide among the rival heirs. The Carolingians did likewise, but they also possessed the imperial dignity, which was indivisible and passed to only one person at a time. Primogeniture, or the preference for the eldest line in the transmission of inheritance, eventually emerged in France, under the Capetian kings. The early Capetians had only one heir, the eldest son, whom they [crowned during their lifetimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_of_the_French_monarch#Coronation_of_the_heir "Coronation of the French monarch"). Instead of an equal portion of the inheritance, the younger sons of the Capetian kings received an [appanage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appanage "Appanage"), which is a feudal territory under the suzerainty of the king. Feudal law allowed the transmission of fiefs to daughters in default of sons, which was also the case for the early appanages. Whether feudal law also applied to the French throne, no one knew, until 1316. #### The succession in 1316 \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Salic_law&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: The succession in 1316")\] For a remarkably long period, from the inception of the Capetian dynasty in 987 until the death of [Louis X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_X_of_France "Louis X of France") in 1316, the eldest living son of the King of France succeeded to the throne upon his demise. No prior occasion existed to demonstrate whether or not females were excluded from the succession to the crown. Louis X died without a son, but left his wife pregnant. The king's brother, [Philip, Count of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_France "Philip V of France"), became regent. Philip prepared for the contingencies with [Odo IV, Duke of Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odo_IV,_Duke_of_Burgundy "Odo IV, Duke of Burgundy"), maternal uncle of Louis X's daughter and prospective heiress, [Joan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_II_of_Navarre "Joan II of Navarre"). If the unborn child were male, he would succeed to the French throne as king; if female, Philip would maintain the regency until the daughters of Louis X reached their majority. The opportunity remained for either daughter to succeed to the French throne. The unborn child proved to be male, [John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_France "John I of France"), to the relief of the kingdom, but the infant lived for only a few days. Philip saw his chance and broke the agreement with the Duke of Burgundy by having himself anointed at Reims in January 1317 as [Philip V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_France "Philip V of France"). [Agnes of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_of_France,_Duchess_of_Burgundy "Agnes of France, Duchess of Burgundy"), daughter of [Louis IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_IX_of_France "Louis IX of France"), mother of the Duke of Burgundy, and maternal grandmother of the Princess Joan, considered it a usurpation and demanded an assembly of the peers, which Philip V accepted. An assembly of prelates, lords, the bourgeois of Paris, and doctors of the university, known as the [Estates-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates_General_/(France/) "Estates General (France)") of 1317, gathered in February. Philip V asked them to write an argument justifying his right to the throne of France. These "general statements" agreed in declaring that "Women do not succeed in the kingdom of France", formalizing Philip's usurpation and the impossibility for a woman to ascend the throne of France, a principle that remains in force to this day. The Salic law, at the time, was not yet invoked; the arguments put forward in favor of Philip V relied only on the degree of proximity of Philip V with Louis X. Philip had the support of the nobility and had the resources for his ambitions. Philip won over the Duke of Burgundy by giving him his daughter, also named [Joan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_III,_Countess_of_Burgundy "Joan III, Countess of Burgundy"), in marriage, with the counties of [Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Artois "County of Artois") and [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Burgundy "County of Burgundy") as her eventual inheritance. On March 27, 1317, a treaty was signed at [Laon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laon "Laon") between the Duke of Burgundy and Philip V, wherein Joan renounced her right to the throne of France. #### The succession in 1328 \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Salic_law&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: The succession in 1328")\] Philip, too, died without a son, and his brother Charles succeeded him as [Charles IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IV_of_France "Charles IV of France") unopposed. Charles, too, died without a son, but also left his wife pregnant. It was another succession crisis, the same as that in 1316; it was necessary both to prepare for a possible regency (and choose a regent) and prepare for a possible succession to the throne. At this point, it had been accepted that women could not claim the crown of France (without any written rule stipulating it yet). Under the application of the agnatic principle, the following were excluded: * The daughters of Louis X, Philip V and Charles IV, including the possible unborn daughter of the pregnant Queen [Jeanne d'Évreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_d%27%C3%89vreux "Jeanne d'Évreux") * [Isabella of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_France "Isabella of France"), sister of Louis X, Philip V, and Charles IV, wife of King [Edward II of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_II_of_England "Edward II of England") The widow of Charles IV gave birth to a daughter. [Isabella of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_France "Isabella of France"), sister of Charles IV, claimed the throne for her son, [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"). The French rejected the claim, noting that "Women cannot transmit a right which they do not possess", a corollary to the succession principle in 1316. The regent, Philip of Valois, became [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") in 1328. Philip became king without serious opposition, until his attempt to confiscate [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") in 1337 made Edward III press his claim to the French throne. #### Emergence of the Salic law \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Salic_law&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Emergence of the Salic law")\] As far as can be ascertained, Salic law was not explicitly mentioned either in 1316 or 1328. It had been forgotten in the feudal era, and the assertion that the French crown can only be transmitted to and through males made it unique and exalted in the eyes of the French. In 1358 the monk Richard Lescot invoked it to dispute the claim of [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre") to the French crown, an argument that would later be echoed by other jurists in defence of the Valois dynasty.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-21) In its origin, therefore, the agnatic principle was limited to the succession to the crown of France. Prior to the [Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Valois "House of Valois") succession, Capetian kings granted appanages to their younger sons and brothers, which could pass to male and female heirs. The appanages given to the Valois princes, though, in imitation of the succession law of the monarchy that gave them, limited their transmission to males. Another Capetian lineage, the [Montfort of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfort_of_Brittany "Montfort of Brittany"), claimed male succession in the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"). In this they were supported by the King of England, while their rivals who claimed the traditional female succession in Brittany were supported by the King of France. The Montforts eventually won the duchy by warfare, but had to recognize the suzerainty of the King of France. This law was by no means intended to cover all matters of inheritance – for example, not the inheritance of movables — only to lands considered "Salic" – and debate remains as to the legal definition of this word, although it is generally accepted to refer to lands in the royal [fisc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisc "Fisc"). Only several hundred years later, under the [direct Capetian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Capet "House of Capet") kings of France and their English contemporaries who held lands in France, did Salic law become a rationale for enforcing or debating succession. Shakespeare says that [Charles VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VI_of_France "Charles VI of France") rejected [Henry V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England")'s claim to the French throne on the basis of Salic law's inheritance rules, leading to the [Battle of Agincourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt "Battle of Agincourt"). In fact, the conflict between Salic and English law was a justification for [many overlapping claims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne") between the French and English monarchs over the French throne. More than a century later, during the [French wars of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion "French Wars of Religion"), [Philip II of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain "Philip II of Spain") attempted to claim the French crown for his daughter [Isabella Clara Eugenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_Clara_Eugenia "Isabella Clara Eugenia"), born of his third wife, [Elisabeth of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_of_Valois "Elisabeth of Valois") in order to prevent the [Huguenot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenots "Huguenots") candidate [Henry of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_France "Henry IV of France") from becoming king. Philip's agents were instructed to "insinuate cleverly" that the Salic law was a "pure invention". Even if the "Salic law" did not really apply to the throne of France, though, the very principle of agnatic succession had become a cornerstone of the French royal succession; they had upheld it in the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") with the English, and it had produced their kings for more than two centuries. The eventual recognition of Henry of Navarre as King Henry IV of France following his conversion to Catholicism, the first of the [Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Bourbon "House of Bourbon") kings, further solidified the agnatic principle in France. Although no reference was made to the Salic law, the imperial constitutions of the [Bonapartist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonapartist "Bonapartist") [First French Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_French_Empire "First French Empire") and [Second French Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_French_Empire "Second French Empire") continued to exclude women from the succession to the throne. In the lands that [Napoleon Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_Bonaparte "Napoleon Bonaparte") conquered, Salic law was adopted, including the [Kingdom of Westphalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Westphalia "Kingdom of Westphalia"), the [Kingdom of Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Holland "Kingdom of Holland"), and under Napoleonic influence, [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden") under the [House of Bernadotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Bernadotte "House of Bernadotte"). ### Other European applications \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Salic_law&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Other European applications")\] [![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Ernest_Augustus_I_of_Hanover.PNG/250px-Ernest_Augustus_I_of_Hanover.PNG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ernest_Augustus_I_of_Hanover.PNG) _[Portrait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_the_Duke_of_Cumberland "Portrait of the Duke of Cumberland") of the [Duke of Cumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Augustus,_King_of_Hanover "Ernest Augustus, King of Hanover")_ [George Dawe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Dawe "George Dawe"). In 1837 Cumberland became [King of Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Hanover "King of Hanover") ahead of his niece [Queen Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria "Queen Victoria"). Several military conflicts in European history have stemmed from the application of, or disregard for, Salic law. The [Carlist Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlist_Wars "Carlist Wars") occurred in [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") over the question of whether the heir to the throne should be a female or a male relative. The [War of the Austrian Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Austrian_Succession "War of the Austrian Succession") was triggered by the [Pragmatic Sanction of 1713](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pragmatic_Sanction_of_1713 "Pragmatic Sanction of 1713"), in which [Charles VI of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VI_of_Austria "Charles VI of Austria"), who himself had inherited the [Austrian patrimony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archduchy_of_Austria "Archduchy of Austria") over his nieces as a result of Salic law, attempted to ensure the inheritance directly to his own daughter [Maria Theresa of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Theresa_of_Austria "Maria Theresa of Austria"), which was an example of an operation of quasi-Salic law. In the modern [Kingdom of Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy"), under the [House of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Savoy "House of Savoy"), succession to the throne was regulated by Salic law. The [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland") and the [Hanoverian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hanover "Kingdom of Hanover") thrones separated after the death of King [William IV of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_IV_of_the_United_Kingdom "William IV of the United Kingdom") and of Hanover in 1837 because Hanover practiced quasi-Salic law, unlike Britain. King William's niece, [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria "Queen Victoria"), ascended to the British throne, but the Hanover throne went to William's brother [Ernest, Duke of Cumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Augustus,_King_of_Hanover "Ernest Augustus, King of Hanover"). Salic law was also an important issue in the [Schleswig-Holstein Question](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schleswig-Holstein_Question "Schleswig-Holstein Question") and played a day-to-day role in the inheritance and marriage decisions of common princedoms of the [German states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_historic_states_of_Germany "List of historic states of Germany"), such as [Saxe-Weimar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxe-Weimar "Saxe-Weimar"), to cite a representative example. European nobility would have confronted Salic issues at every turn in the practice of diplomacy, particularly when they negotiated marriages, since the entire male line had to be extinguished for a land title to pass (by marriage) "to a female's husband". Women rulers were anathema in the German states well into the modern era. In a similar way, the thrones of the [Kingdom of the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_the_Netherlands "Kingdom of the Netherlands") and the [Grand Duchy of Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxembourg "Luxembourg") were separated in 1890, with the succession of [Princess Wilhelmina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelmina_of_the_Netherlands "Wilhelmina of the Netherlands") as the first [Queen regnant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_regnant "Queen regnant") of the Netherlands. As a remnant of Salic law, the office of the reigning [monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarch "Monarch") of the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") is always formally known as "King", though her title may be "Queen". Luxembourg passed to the [House of Orange-Nassau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Orange-Nassau "House of Orange-Nassau")'s distantly related agnates, the [House of Nassau-Weilburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Nassau-Weilburg "House of Nassau-Weilburg"), but that house also faced extinction in the male line less than two decades later. With no other male-line agnates in the remaining branches of the House of Nassau, [Grand Duke William IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_IV,_Grand_Duke_of_Luxembourg "William IV, Grand Duke of Luxembourg") adopted a quasi-Salic law of succession to allow him to be succeeded by his daughters. Literary references ------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Salic_law&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Literary references")\] * [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") uses the Salic law as a plot device in _[Henry V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_/(play/) "Henry V (play)")_, saying it was upheld by the French to bar Henry V's claiming the French throne. _Henry V_ begins with the [Archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury") being asked if the claim might be upheld despite the Salic law. The archbishop replies, "That the _land Salique_ is in Germany, between the floods of [Sala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saale "Saale") and of [Elbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbe "Elbe")", implying that the law is German, not French. The archbishop's justification for Henry's claim, which Shakespeare intentionally renders obtuse and verbose (for comedic, as well as politically expedient reasons) is also erroneous, as the [Salian Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salian_Franks "Salian Franks") settled along the lower [Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine "Rhine") and [Scheldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheldt "Scheldt"), which today is for the most part in the [Flemish Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_Region "Flemish Region"). * The concept of Salic law figures heavily into the story of French author [Maurice Druon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Druon "Maurice Druon")'s historical fiction novel series, _[The Accursed Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Accursed_Kings "The Accursed Kings") (_known as _Les Rois maudits_ in French). The series, which revolves around the Capetian succession crisis in the early-to-mid 14th century after Philip IV's sons all three die without a male heir, contains seven books which were published between the 1950s-1970s. In the fourth book (_The Royal Succession_), Philip V uses his position as regent while his sister-in-law is pregnant to get his lawyers to come up with a plan to use Salic law to get his niece [Joan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_II_of_Navarre "Joan II of Navarre") out of the line of succession. He becomes king after his nephew [John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_France "John I of France") (who'd been swapped with another baby) is ostensibly poisoned by Philip's mother-in-law [Mahaut, Countess of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahaut,_Countess_of_Artois "Mahaut, Countess of Artois"). [John I of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_France "John I of France") during his christening. In reality, it is widely believed that John died of natural causes and Giannino Baglioni, the man who claimed to be him, was a [Pretender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretender "Pretender").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-22) During the fifth and sixth books, Queen Isabella begins to press her son Edward III's claim to the French throne as the last-living grandson of Philip IV. However, the French nobility are more inclined to bypass her claim under Salic Law in lieu of that of her cousin, Philip VI, the next male-line descendant. The relationship between the two men begins to sour once Edward III reaches his majority and begins to rule on his own, eventually ending with [Robert of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_I,_Count_of_Artois "Robert I, Count of Artois") (who's also fallen out with Philip) convincing him to stake his claim once and for all at the end of the sixth book. The seventh book, _A King Without a Kingdom,_ skips ahead significantly in time to the lead-up to the devastating defeat of the French at [The Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers"), which ends with the capture of Philip VI's son [John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") at the hand of Edward III's son [Edward the Black Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_the_Black_Prince "Edward the Black Prince"). * In the novel _[Royal Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Flash "Royal Flash")_, by [George MacDonald Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_MacDonald_Fraser "George MacDonald Fraser"), the hero, [Harry Flashman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Flashman "Harry Flashman"), on his marriage, is presented with the royal consort's portion of the crown jewels, and "The Duchess did rather better"; the character, feeling hard done-by, thinks, "It struck me then, and it strikes me now, that the Salic law was a damned sound idea".[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_note-23) * In his novel _[Waverley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waverley_/(novel/) "Waverley (novel)")_, [Sir Walter Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Walter_Scott "Sir Walter Scott") quotes "Salique Law" when discussing the protagonist's prior requests for a horse and guide to take him to Edinburgh. > The hostess, a civil, quiet, laborious drudge, came to take his orders for dinner, but declined to make answer on the subject of the horse and guide; for the Salique Law, it seems, extended to the stables of the Golden Candlestick. — Chapter XX1X * [Agnatic descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnatic_descent "Agnatic descent") * [Early Germanic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Germanic_law "Early Germanic law") * [Paris, BN, lat. 4404](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris,_BN,_lat._4404 "Paris, BN, lat. 4404") 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Salica#cite_ref-1)** Hessels, Jan Hendrik; Date1341 – 12 April 1365[1]
Location

Brittany

ResultTreaty of Guérande

* [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") * [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") * [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth") [**†**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killed_in_action "Killed in action") | [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany") [**†**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killed_in_action "Killed in action") [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") | [![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png/500px-Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png) Funeral of [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), depicted in the Chronicles of [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart") The **War of the Breton Succession** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre de Succession de Bretagne_; [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language "Breton language"): _Brezel hêrezh dugelezh Breizh_) or **Breton Civil War** was a conflict between the [Counts of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_of_Blois "Counts of Blois") and the [Montforts of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfort_of_Brittany "Montfort of Brittany") for control of the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"), then a [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of the [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France"). It was fought between 1341 and 12 April 1365.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-FritzeRobison2002-1) It is also known as the **War of the Two Joans** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre des deux Jeannes_) due to the involvement of two rival duchesses of that name, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") and [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-2) The war formed an integral part of the early [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") due to the proxy involvement of the French and English monarchs in the conflict; the French supported the Blois (female heir) whilst the English backed the Montforts (male heir). The rival kings supported the duke of the principle opposite to their own claims to the French throne—the [Plantagenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Plantagenet "House of Plantagenet") having claimed it by female succession, and the [Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Valois "House of Valois") by male succession. Montfort was ultimately successful following the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") in 1364 but, in a surprising turn of events, pledged his loyalty to the king of France and not to the Plantagenet king of England who had supported him. The Breton dukes had both a historical and ancestral connection to Britain and were also [earls of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earls_of_Richmond "Earls of Richmond") in [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"). Duke [Arthur II of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany") married twice, first to Mary of Limoges (1275–1291), then to [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_of_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scotland") (1263–1322), countess of Montfort and widow of King [Alexander III of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_III_of_Scotland "Alexander III of Scotland"). From his first marriage, he had three sons, including his heir [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") and Guy, [count of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_and_dukes_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Counts and dukes of Penthièvre") (d. 1331). From Yolande, Arthur had another son, also named John, who became Count of Montfort. (See [Dukes of Brittany family tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Brittany_family_tree "Dukes of Brittany family tree").) John III strongly disliked the children of his father's second marriage. He spent the first years of his reign attempting to have this marriage annulled and his half-siblings bastardized. When this failed, he tried to ensure that [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort") would never inherit the duchy. Since John III was childless, his heir of choice became [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), _la Boiteuse_, daughter of his younger brother Guy. In 1337 she married [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), the second son of a powerful French noble house whose mother's brother was King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). But in 1340, John III reconciled himself with his half-brother, and made a will that appointed John of Montfort the heir of Brittany. On 30 April 1341, John III died. His last words on the succession, uttered on his deathbed, were, "For God's sake leave me alone and do not trouble my spirit with such things". First stage of the war ---------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: First stage of the war")\] Most of the nobility supported Charles of Blois, so if John of Montfort was to have any chance, it was dependent upon swift action before organized resistance could be made. John quickly took possession of the [ducal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke "Duke") capital [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") and then seized the Ducal treasury at [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges"). By the middle of August, John of Montfort was in possession of most of the Duchy, the three principal cities of Nantes, [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") and [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"). Up to this point, the succession crisis had been a purely internal affair. But to complicate things further, the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France had broken out four years earlier, in 1337. In 1341, there was a truce between the two countries, but there was little doubt that hostilities would be renewed when the truce ended in June 1342. Thus, when rumours reached [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") that John of Montfort had received English agents, the French Crown naturally took a more direct interest in their small neighbors situation. Charles of Blois became the official French candidate. Whatever had been his original intentions, John of Montfort was now forced to support [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") as King of France. Edward III was bound by the truce not to take any offensive action in France. Nothing in it, however, hindered France from subduing rebellious vassals. In November, after a short siege and defeat at the [Battle of Champtoceaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux "Battle of Champtoceaux"), John of Montfort was forced to surrender at [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") by the citizens. He was offered safe conduct to negotiate a settlement with Charles of Blois, but when this led nowhere he was thrown in prison. It now fell upon John's wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), to lead the Montfortist cause. Deeming her possessions in the east indefensible, she set up headquarters at [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont") in western Brittany but was driven into Brest and besieged, the siege being broken by the arrival of an English army under the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") at the [naval battle of Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Brest_/(1342/) "Battle of Brest (1342)") on 18 August 1342. Northampton then made his way inland and besieged Morlaix after an unsuccessful initial attack. The siege was lifted after the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix") on 30 September. In Paris it was feared that Edward III would land at [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais") once the truce ran out. The major part of the French army was therefore withdrawn, and Charles of Blois was left to pursue his claim on his own. Charles soon proved himself to be an able soldier: Rennes and Vannes were taken and many of the Montfortist captains defected. In late November, [Edward III arrived with his army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign,_1342%E2%80%931343 "Edward III's Breton campaign, 1342–1343") at [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"). He almost at once marched against Vannes. [The siege dragged on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieges_of_Vannes_/(1342/) "Sieges of Vannes (1342)") and a French army was assembled to meet him, but on 19 January 1343, before any major engagements could be fought, the two kings agreed the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"). Vannes was taken into papal custody. With John of Montfort in prison, his son an infant, and his wife recently gone mad, the places under Montfortist control were in practice administered from London, with a large permanent English garrison at Brest. The truce was to last until 29 September 1346 with the hopes that in the meantime the disputes between the two kingdoms could be permanently settled, but in Brittany it made little difference. The truce bound the two kings and their followers, but Charles of Blois claimed to be fighting his own separate war and was therefore not bound by any truce. The brutal small-scale fighting continued at the same pace. In Paris, John of Montfort was released from prison on 1 September 1343 in return for a huge bond and a promise to stay on his estates in the east. The English coastal garrisons held firm, but the Montfortist party continued to crumble. They had some successes, such as the expulsion of the papal custodians from Vannes, but with no unifying leadership, mostly they were reduced to pleading for men and money from London. To hamper communication between Brest and Vannes, Charles of Blois laid siege to [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper,_Finist%C3%A8re "Quimper, Finistère") in early March 1344. The city fell by assault on 1 May and, as usual at that time, this meant the slaughter of civilians in huge numbers, estimated between 1,400 and 2,000. The English prisoners were held for ransom, but the Breton and Norman captives were dispatched to Paris where they were executed for treason. During the summer and autumn, the Montfortist party fell apart. Even those who had been John of Montfort's staunchest allies now considered it futile to continue the struggle. It, therefore, mattered little that in March 1345 John finally managed to escape to England. With no adherents of note of his own, he was now little more than a figurehead for English ambitions in Brittany. Edward III decided to repudiate the truce in summer 1345, a year before it was due to run out. As part of his larger strategy, a force was dispatched to Brittany under the joint leadership of the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") and John of Montfort. Within a week of their landing in June, the English had their first victory when Sir [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth"), one of Northampton's lieutenants, raided central Brittany and defeated Charles of Blois at Cadoret near [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin"). The follow-up was less impressive. Further operations were delayed until July when Montfort attempted the recapture of Quimper. However, news had reached the French government that Edward's main campaign had been canceled and they were able to send reinforcements from Normandy. With his strengthened army, Charles of Blois broke the siege. Routed, Montfort fled back to Hennebont where he fell ill and died on 16 September. The heir to the Montfortist cause was his five-year-old son, [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). During the winter, Northampton fought a long and hard campaign with the apparent objective of seizing a harbour on the north side of the peninsula. Edward III had probably planned to land here with his main force during summer 1346. However, the English achieved very little for their efforts. Northern Brittany was Joan of Penthièvre's home region and resistance there was stiff. In the end, Edward decided upon Normandy as the landing spot for his 1346 campaign. Northampton was recalled and Thomas Dagworth was appointed as deputy lieutenant. It was during a tour through the English strongholds on 9 June that Dagworth and his escort were trapped by Charles of Blois and his army near [Saint-Pol-de-Léon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Pol-de-L%C3%A9on "Saint-Pol-de-Léon"). They dug in on a hilltop and fought off all attacks until nightfall when Charles was forced to retreat leaving many of his wounded behind. Tide turns against Charles -------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Tide turns against Charles")\] [![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg/250px-Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg) Capture of Charles of Blois At this point events outside Brittany started to have an effect on the war. The French suffered a major defeat at the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") in 1346, and at Calais in 1347. Without French support, Charles of Blois gradually began to lose ground to the English captains. The memory of the massacre at Quimper increased his unpopularity, and Breton traders had an economic interest in strengthening links with England due to Brittany's strategic position between the Atlantic and English Channel. At the [Battle of La Roche-Derrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_La_Roche-Derrien "Battle of La Roche-Derrien") in 1347, Charles was taken prisoner as he tried to recapture the town, which had just been taken by the English. He was jailed for five years in the Tower of London. The English now controlled Brest, Quimper, and Vannes. Under pressure from [Pope Innocent VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Innocent_VI "Pope Innocent VI"), the English, French, and Bretons negotiated a peace, while both factions maintained an uneasy balance of power within the duchy. It was during this period that the [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") took place, a famous episode in medieval chivalry. Conflicts between the French and English strongholds of [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin") and [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel") were resolved in a duel between thirty Montfortist knights led by [Robert Bemborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bemborough "Robert Bemborough"), and thirty supporters of Charles de Blois led by [Jean de Beaumanoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_de_Beaumanoir "Jean de Beaumanoir"). The combat took place midway between the two towns on 26 March 1351. By nightfall the Anglo-Breton Montfortists had lost nine dead against six of the pro-French knights; the surviving Montfortists were forced to surrender. Though renowned at the time, and later highly romanticised, the combat had no effect on the outcome of the war. [![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg/250px-Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Le_Combat_des_Trente_/(1857/).jpg) A 19th-century painting depicting the _[The Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Combat_of_the_Thirty "The Combat of the Thirty")_ ([Octave Penguilly L'Haridon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Penguilly_L%27Haridon "Octave Penguilly L'Haridon"), 1857) Edward III signed the Treaty of Westminster on 1 March 1353, accepting Charles of Blois as Duke of Brittany if the latter undertook to pay a ransom of 300,000 crowns, and that Brittany signed a treaty of alliance "in perpetuity" with England; this alliance was to be sealed by the marriage of the Montfortist claimant John of Montfort (son of the earlier John of Montfort) with Edward's daughter Mary. The marriage required the approval of the King of France and a papal dispensation. [Charles de la Cerda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_la_Cerda "Charles de la Cerda"), the [Constable of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constable_of_France "Constable of France"), negotiated the deal, but [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), who needed to continue the war between England and France to maintain his own power, decided to intervene by assassinating the Constable. He then switched his support to France in exchange for territory. The treaty was negated, but Charles of Blois had been freed, and returned to Brittany as Duke. [![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg/250px-Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg) The Battle of Auray, 1364 The situation remained in stalemate for some time, with Charles of Blois as _de facto_ Duke, but with significant territory still controlled by the Montfortists. Outside events again began to have an effect on the conflict. A plague struck France and the King himself was captured by the English at the [Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") in 1356. The French state was virtually paralysed. In 1362, when the younger John de Montfort reached 22 years of age, King Edward permitted him to return to Brittany. His return was conditioned by a covenant not to marry without permission, given in pledge of several fortresses. On arrival, John attempted to reach agreement with Charles of Blois to make peace and share Brittany, but Charles's wife Joan urged him to resist and crush John. The war resumed in 1363 when Charles de Blois, assisted by [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin"), had some successes, but when Bertrand left to take control of strongholds in Navarre and Normandy, Charles's advance halted at the unsuccessful siege of Bécherel. Another opportunity to negotiate an agreement arose, but again Joan blocked negotiations. John de Montfort moved to besiege [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray") with renowned English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles of Blois and Bertrand du Guesclin came to the rescue of the besieged city, but they were decisively defeated at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") on 29 September 1364. This battle marked the end of this long conflict: Charles of Blois was killed and Joan of Penthièvre, finding herself a widow, saw her cause collapse. Du Guesclin was captured and [ransomed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom "Ransom") by Charles V for 100,000 [francs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franc "Franc"). Peace was concluded on 12 April 1365 by the [First Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)") which established John of Montfort as Duke of Brittany. He did not reject completely the claims of the Penthièvre family, and established the following law of succession in Brittany: * The Duchy would be transmitted from male to male in the family of Montfort. * In the absence of male offspring, it would switch to males of the family of Penthièvre. * Joan retained the prerogative of Penthièvre and the Viscouncy of Limoges. * She would also receive 10,000 livres of annual rent taken from the French territories of the enemy. King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") did not oppose the elevation of John, fearing that he might declare homage to Edward of England, his protector and former father-in-law (Mary having died in 1361). In addition, France was clearly depleted in the context of the Hundred Years' War. He therefore recognized John as Duke. By this action, he won the friendship of the Breton nobility. In December 1366, he received the oath of the new duke who surprisingly did not pledge allegiance to Edward, recognizing Charles as his sovereign instead. The provisions of the treaty were later repudiated by the Montfortists when a later duke, [John V, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V,_Duke_of_Brittany "John V, Duke of Brittany") was kidnapped by the Penthièvres in 1420, in violation of the treaty. The Montfortists declared that the treaty had been broken, and as such were no longer required to accept its succession provisions. This became significant when [Francis II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Francis II, Duke of Brittany") failed to produce a male heir, allowing the duchy to pass to his daughter [Anne of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Brittany "Anne of Brittany") in 1488. * **30 April 1341**: John III dies without heirs. Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois became Duchess and Duke of Brittany. John of Montfort refuses to accept and calls for the help of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"). * **1343**: John of Montfort is taken prisoner, but is released shortly afterwards. Charles tries to take advantage and attacks Hennebont, but the city is defended with success by [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), wife of Montfort. An English army relieves the siege and forces the Blois to a truce, broken shortly afterwards. * **1344**: Charles takes Quimper with the help of a French army, courtesy of King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), and slaughters 2000 civilians. * **1345**: John of Montfort fails to recover Quimper and dies. His ambitions over Brittany are inherited by his son [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). His mother, Joan of Flanders, becomes the political and military commander of the Montfort faction. * **Between 1346 and 1364**, several minor battles are won and lost by both parts, several truces are signed and broken. Joan of Flanders becomes mentally ill and is institutionalized in a convent. * **27 March 1351**: [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") * **29 September 1364**: [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray"). [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin") and Charles of Blois are heavily defeated by John IV and the English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles is killed in action, ending the Blois pretensions in Brittany. * **1365**: John IV is recognized as Duke of Brittany and Joan of Penthièvre gives up any claim to the duchy in the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"). Surprisingly, the new duke declares himself as a vassal, not to the English king who helped him, but to King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France"). * [List of rulers of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_rulers_of_Brittany "List of rulers of Brittany") * [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") * [List of wars of succession in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wars_of_succession_in_Europe "List of wars of succession in Europe") * [War of the Two Pedros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Two_Pedros "War of the Two Pedros") 1. ^ [_**a**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_ref-FritzeRobison2002_1-0) [_**b**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_ref-FritzeRobison2002_1-1) Ronald H.
