**Joan of Flanders**[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-5) (c. 1295 – September 1374) was [duchess of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_consorts_of_Brittany "List of consorts of Brittany") by her marriage to [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). Much of her life was taken up in defense of the rights of her husband to the duchy, and, later, her son's rights to the duchy, which was challenged by the [House of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blois "House of Blois") during the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"). Known for her fiery personality, Joan led Montfort's cause after her husband had been captured by [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), and began the fight back. There, she displayed considerable skill as a military leader and gained the respect of her people. Shortly after taking refuge in England, she was confined to [Tickhill Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tickhill_Castle "Tickhill Castle") by order of [King Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward_III "King Edward III").

Joan was highly praised by the chronicler [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart") for her courage and energy. She may have been an inspiration to [Joan of Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc "Joan of Arc") and was a role model to Victorian feminists. Because of her feats of leadership, historian [David Hume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume "David Hume") described her as "the most extraordinary woman of the age".

Joan was the daughter of Count Louis I of Nevers and Countess Joan of Rethel.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009n2-6) Her brother, [Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I,_Count_of_Flanders "Louis I, Count of Flanders"), became the count of Flanders, Nevers, and Rethel. She married John of Monfort in March 1329. John of Monfort claimed the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"), although his claim was contested by his niece [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") and her husband, [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"). Joan of Flanders and John had two children:

*   [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") (1339–1399)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009n2-6) with his life marred by the War of Breton Succession, John was taken into the household of [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III "Edward III") before he returned to reinforce his claim as the duke of Brittany.
*   [Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Brittany,_Baroness_of_Drayton "Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton") (1341 – aft. 20 October 1399), born at the onset of the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"). When her brother returned to defend his claim as the duke of Brittany, Joan of Brittany stayed in England. She was married before 21 October 1385 to [Ralph Basset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Basset,_3rd_Baron_Basset_of_Drayton "Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton"), Baron [Basset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basset_family "Basset family") de [Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drayton_House "Drayton House")[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009n2-6)

### Question of succession

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Question of succession")\]

When Duke [John III of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III_of_Brittany "John III of Brittany") died childless in 1341, he left behind a contentious succession dispute. For many years he tried to find means to ensure that the children of his stepmother, [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_of_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scotland") would not inherit the duchy, including trying to have her marriage to his father annulled. At this time, he declared his heir to be his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre").

Shortly before dying, Duke John III reconciled with his estranged half-brother, John of Montfort, with Duke John naming Montfort as his heir. Once John III died, a succession crisis became imminent as two rival factions formed:

*   The [House of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Montfort-Brittany "House of Montfort-Brittany"), headed by John of Montfort and Joan of Flanders. Their legitimacy came from Duke John III's reconciliation with John shortly before his death. This claim was backed by the king of England, Edward III, who would benefit from the House of Montfort taking control of Brittany.
*   The [House of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blois "House of Blois"), the house of [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois") and his wife, Joan of Penthièvre. Their legitimacy came from the Duke's previous declaration that his heir would be Joan. Only shortly before the duke's death did he change who his successor would be, which raised questions of legitimacy directed at the House of Montfort. This claim was backed by the king of France, [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), who benefited from his nephew Charles and the House of Blois controlling Brittany.

In an attempt to resolve this question of succession, John of Montfort, Joan's husband, reached out to King Philip VI. Philip, the uncle of Charles of Blois. Due to the association of the House of Montfort with the English, and the House of Blois' association to the French, historians understand that John was working to avoid starting a conflict between the English and French. Philip promised John safe conduct and invited him to Paris to be heard. Once in Paris, John was quickly imprisoned and the French courts declared Joan of Penthièvre and her husband Charles of Blois to be the heirs of Brittany. This move spurred Joan's vengeance.

With her husband locked away, Joan announced her son—still an infant at the time—the rightful heir and leader of her faction. Mustering an army, she led her soldiers into the start of the War of Breton Succession.

### War of Breton Succession

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: War of Breton Succession")\]

Beginning the war with a march on [Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon,_Ille-et-Vilaine "Redon, Ille-et-Vilaine"), Charles of Blois arrived in 1342 and besieged the town [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), where Joan was residing for the time being. At the same time, her enemy Charles of Blois besieged Joan and the House of Montfort. She responded by sending Amaury de Clisson to ask King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") for aid. Edward, in dire need to become allies with Brittany, found this opportunity impossible to ignore, and sent supplies to Joan to help relieve the siege.

Edward was eager to render aid, as he had been claiming the French crown for himself, and was therefore at odds with Philip. If he could get [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") as an ally, it would be of great advantage for future campaigns. He prepared ships under the command of [Sir Walter Manny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_de_Manny,_1st_Baron_Manny "Walter de Manny, 1st Baron Manny") to relieve the siege.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-pie-7)

In the siege of Hennebont, she took up arms and, dressed in armor, conducted the defense of the town, encouraging the people to fight, and urging the women to "cut their skirts and take their safety in their own hands". When she looked from a tower and saw that the enemy camp was almost unguarded, she led three hundred men on a charge, burned down Charles' supplies and destroyed his tents. After this she became known as "**Jeanne la Flamme**". When the Blois faction realized what was happening, they cut off her retreat to the town, but she and her knights rode to [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Brest "Château de Brest"), drawing a portion of the Blois force with them. Having secured Brest, she gathered together extra supporters and secretly returned to Hennebont, evading the Blois forces and re-entering the town with her reinforcements.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-pie-7)

Charles of Blois tried to starve the people in Hennebont. During a long meeting the bishop of Leon tried to persuade Joan to surrender, but from the window she saw Walter Manny's fleet from England sailing up. Hennebont was strengthened with the English forces and held out.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-8) Charles was forced to retreat, but tried to isolate Joan by taking other towns in Brittany. On his return he again failed to capture Hennebont.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-pie-7)

Joan began to move away from her sieges and began to focus more onto her fleet. Her focus on naval warfare gave her a newfound title: [pirate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_piracy "Women in piracy").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-9)

Joan sailed to England to seek further reinforcements from King Edward, which he provided, but the English fleet was intercepted on its way to Brittany by Charles of Blois' ally, [Louis of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_de_la_Cerda "Luis de la Cerda"). In a hard-fought battle, the sailors and knights grappled in hand-to-hand combat as Louis' men attempted to board Joan's ship. According to Froissart, Joan fought in person "with the heart of a lion, and in her hand she wielded a sharp [glaive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaive "Glaive"), wherewith she fought fiercely".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-pie-7) Eventually the English forces beat off Louis's ships and made harbor near Vannes. Her forces then captured Vannes, besieged Rennes and sought to break the siege of Hennebont.

Joan of Flanders slowly started stepping further back away from the war front, which would have been expected for women of her position. English warlords slowly began taking more and more leadership and acted in her place: a duchess avenging her husband. With neither side able to achieve a decisive victory, by the truce of Malestroit in 1343, her husband John was released and hostilities ceased for a period. He was later imprisoned once again, but escaped and resumed the conflict. In the wake of her husband's death, Joan stepped up once more and became the leader of the Montfort house once more to protect the title for her son from the House of Blois. In 1347, English forces acting on her behalf captured Charles of Blois in battle.

By this time Joan and her son were living in England. After being initially welcomed with honor, she was later confined by order of King Edward III and spent the rest of her life under house arrest at [Tickhill Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tickhill_Castle "Tickhill Castle") and elsewhere. Edward entrusted her to the care of Sir William Frank (until 1346), Thomas Haukeston (1346–57), John Delves (d. 1370) and finally to his widow Isabella and Godfrei Foljambe. Arthur de la Borderie attributed her confinement to mental illness, but more recent research finds no evidence to support this.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-10) Notably, it seems unlikely that "Warmer" (Warnier?) de Giston, assisted by his yeoman, would have risked gravely compromising himself by taking her out of the castle in 1347 and attempting to flee with her if she were mentally ill.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-11)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-12) It is likely that Edward imprisoned her in order to increase his own power in Brittany.

She lived long enough to see the final victory of her son [John IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") over the House of Blois in 1364, but she never returned to the duchy. The last mention made of the duchess and her guardian is 14 February 1374, thus she may have died in that year.

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Joanna-of-Flanders-History-of-France-Guizot-1869.jpg/250px-Joanna-of-Flanders-History-of-France-Guizot-1869.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joanna-of-Flanders-History-of-France-Guizot-1869.jpg)

Joanna of Flanders spots the English fleet arriving to relieve Hennebont, 1342  
Illus. from [François Guizot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Guizot "François Guizot")'s, _History of France_, 1869

Joan became known as a prototype of the martial woman in [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"), and may have been an inspiration for [Joan of Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc "Joan of Arc").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-13) [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart") said she "had the courage of a man and the heart of a lion".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-pie-7) [David Hume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume "David Hume") described her as "the most extraordinary woman of the age".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-pie-7) Victorian feminists also cited her as a role-model. [Harriet Taylor Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Taylor_Mill "Harriet Taylor Mill") mentions her as one of the "heroic chatelaines" of the Middle Ages in her essay "The Enfranchisement of Women".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-14) [Amelia Bloomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amelia_Bloomer "Amelia Bloomer") also cites her as one of the "heroic women" of the era.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-15)

Pierce Butler said that she is "known to us, through the enthusiastic record of Froissart, as an amazon, but hardly known at all as a woman". He concluded,

> In those qualities admired by chivalry she was unquestionably an extraordinary woman: courageous and personally valiant, with a head to plan daring exploits and a heart to conduct her through the thick of the danger; impulsive and generous, a free-handed ruler and an admirer of those deeds of chivalrous daring in others which she was so willing to share in herself ... One cannot read her story without enthusiasm, yet one would like to know more of the woman before bestowing unreserved praise on the countess "who was worth a man in a fight" and "who had the heart of a lion".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort#cite_note-pie-7)

Joan was later celebrated for her fiery exploits in Breton folklore, in particular in a ballad collected in [Barzaz Breiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barzaz_Breiz "Barzaz Breiz"), which relates her attack on the camp at Hennebont. In [Jeanne Coroller-Danio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Coroller-Danio "Jeanne Coroller-Danio")'s [Breton nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_nationalist "Breton nationalist") book _Histoire de Notre Bretagne_ (1922), Joan is depicted as a heroine of Breton resistance to French occupation.

| | Belligerents | | [Kingdom of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") [House of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords,_counts_and_dukes_of_Montfort-l%27Amaury "Lords, counts and dukes of Montfort-l'Amaury") | [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") [House of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blois "House of Blois") | | Commanders and leaders | | [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") | *  • [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany") *  • [Geoffrey of Charny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffroi_de_Charny "Geoffroi de Charny") | | Strength | | 3,000–5,000 | 10,000–15,000 | | Casualties and losses | | Light | Heavy | | [![Image 2: Battle of Morlaix is located in France](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/France_location_map-Regions_and_departements-2016.svg/250px-France_location_map-Regions_and_departements-2016.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:France_location_map-Regions_and_departements-2016.svg "Battle of Morlaix is located in France") ![Image 3: Battle of Morlaix](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Big_battle_symbol.svg/20px-Big_battle_symbol.svg.png) Battle of Morlaix [class=notpageimage|](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:France_location_map-Regions_and_departements-2016.svg "File:France location map-Regions and departements-2016.svg") Location of the battle within modern France | | | | | The **battle of Morlaix** was fought near the village of [Lanmeur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanmeur "Lanmeur") in [Brittany, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany,_France "Brittany, France"), on 30 September 1342 between an Anglo-Breton army and a much larger Franco-Breton force. [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"), at war with [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") since 1337 in the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), had sided with [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort")'s faction in the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") shortly after it broke out in 1341. The French were supporting [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"), a nephew of the French king. A small Anglo-Breton army under [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton"), besieged the Breton port of [Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morlaix "Morlaix"). Charles led a force several times larger than Northampton's from the town of [Guingamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guingamp "Guingamp") to relieve Morlaix. Warned of this, the English carried out a night march and prepared a defensive position just outside Lanmeur. When they sighted the English position, the French deployed into three divisions, one behind the other. The first of these, probably made up of Breton [levies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_levies "Feudal levies"), advanced and was shot to pieces by the English archers using [longbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbow "Longbow"), halting their advance; the attackers then broke without making contact. The second division, of French and Breton [men-at-arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men-at-arms "Men-at-arms"), attacked but their charge was halted when they fell into a camouflaged ditch in front of the English position. Presented with a large, close-range target the English archers inflicted many casualties. About 200 French cavalry made their way over the ditch and came to grips with the English men-at-arms, who were fighting on foot. This band was cut off by the English and all were killed or captured. Northampton was concerned that the English archers were running low on arrows and that the ditch was so full of dead and wounded men and horses as to be ineffective as an obstacle. Therefore, when the third French division was seen to be preparing to attack the English withdrew into a wood to their rear. The French were unable to force their way in, so they surrounded it and besieged the English, possibly for several days. Northampton broke out with a night attack and returned to Morlaix. Charles gave up his attempt to relieve the town and retreated. This was the first major land battle of the Hundred Years' War and the tactics used foreshadowed those of both the French and the English for the rest of the 1340s. [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") was a province of France, but though the dukes of Brittany were [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the French kings they governed the duchy as independent rulers.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199017,_34%E2%80%9335-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200662-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19888%E2%80%9311-3) Nevertheless, when the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") broke out in 1337 between France and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") the Duke of Brittany, [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") (r. 1312–1341), fought alongside his [feudal lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_lordship "Feudal lordship") the [King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_of_France "Kings of France"), [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") (r. 1328–1350). John died on 30 April 1341, leaving a disputed succession: both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his younger half-brother, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), claimed the dukedom; Joan was married to [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"), a well-connected and militarily oriented French nobleman who was also a nephew of the King of France.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199966%E2%80%9367-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202047%E2%80%9349-6) John had the stronger legal claim, but the [aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocracy "Aristocracy") and [clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy "Clergy") knew little about him and mostly preferred Charles' claim. What support John had came largely from the lower levels of society, especially in the towns.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990371,_374-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007202-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660-9) Starting in early June 1341 John seized almost all of the fortified places in Brittany and by mid-August had all but made good his claim to the duchy. Philip initially disregarded the situation, ignoring requests for assistance from Charles of Blois. Correctly suspecting that John was negotiating with the English, the French declared Charles the rightful heir on 7 September. Philip found the idea of having a relative as the duke attractive as it would bring the traditionally semi-autonomous province more firmly under royal control. He was willing to commit considerable military resources to achieve this and despatched an army to support Charles.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-12) This army overran all of eastern Brittany, apart from [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes"), in the six months from September 1341 and captured John.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389-13)[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-16) John's wife, [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), was in Rennes with her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), and the ducal treasury when news of John's capture arrived. Modern historians consider her to have been an energetic and effective leader, and she acted decisively and aggressively. She recalled the field army from western Brittany, took command and moved to [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"). This was a small but strongly walled town with access to the sea and from there Joanna retained control of most of western Brittany, setting up her son as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy. She despatched her senior counsellor, [Amaury of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_de_Clisson "Amaury de Clisson"), to [Edward III in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") with a large sum in cash to encourage English military intervention and waited on events.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390,_409-17)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-18)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199967-19)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433%E2%80%9334-20) By the end of 1341 the Montfortist cause was being supported by Edward III as an extension of the war with France.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-21) English intervention -------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Morlaix&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: English intervention")\] [![Image 4: Colour photograph of a small medieval-era single-masted sailing ship](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_/(cropped/).jpg) In 1962 a well-preserved wreck of a [cog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cog_/(ship/) "Cog (ship)") dated to 1380 was found near Bremen, Germany. This is a full-size reproduction. Merchant vessels such as these formed the bulk of the English fleet.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004120-22)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERose200716-23) English reinforcements took a long time to arrive.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-18) A small English force, 234 men, arrived under Sir [Walter Mauny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Manny,_1st_Baron_Manny "Walter Manny, 1st Baron Manny") in May 1342 and relieved the siege of Hennebont.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990393-24) The flow of events went against the Montfortists in the face of the huge military superiority of the French. By July Joanna had been forced back to the far west of Brittany and was besieged in the port of [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"), the only remaining fortified place held by her faction.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004101-25) Charles of Blois and a large army had invested the town[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26) and fourteen mercenary [galleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley "Galley"), hired from [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), [blockaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade "Blockade") it from the sea.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011112-27) Brest was on the brink of surrender when the English arrived on 18 August. Their fleet of 260 ships, including an unknown number of [galleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley "Galley"), took the Genoese by surprise. The Genoese fled and 11 of their ships were burnt.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004100-28)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-29) A map of Brittany, with modern administrative boundaries, showing the locations of some of the places mentioned in the text The English ships carried 1,350 men,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004100-28) a force far smaller than that of the French besieging Brest. But, seeing so many English ships crowded into the [Brest Roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roadstead_of_Brest "Roadstead of Brest") and the English [vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanguard "Vanguard") disembarking onto the beach, the French anticipated an attack by a vast host. Charles promptly broke off the siege and withdrew, abandoning western Brittany, where the populace strongly favoured the Montfort cause.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990399%E2%80%93400-30) Part of the French force retreated along the south coast of Brittany, but the bulk of the army accompanied him to [Guingamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guingamp "Guingamp").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-31) Here he concentrated his forces and called up local [levies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_levies "Feudal levies").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26) The English were commanded by [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") who was reinforced by 800 men under [Robert of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois") a few days after landing. He also absorbed several small English forces and an unknown number of John of Montfort's Breton partisans. Edward III was planning to follow on with a substantial force and so Northampton's first mission was to secure a port on the north coast of Brittany.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-31) [Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morlaix "Morlaix") is approximately halfway between Brest and Guingamp. It was a town with strong fortifications and a secure harbour 50 kilometres (30 mi) from Brest.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-31) Charles left it well provisioned and well garrisoned before withdrawing a further 60 kilometres (40 mi) along the north coast road. Northampton marched on Morlaix,[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26) taking over the territory to the west of it.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998141-32) Arriving on 3 September and finding the garrison well-prepared to stand a siege he assaulted the town. This lasted most of the day, was pressed hard, and was eventually repulsed with the English suffering many casualties. They then settled down for a regular siege.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401-33) It is possible Northampton was anticipating further reinforcement by Montfortist Bretons.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998141-32) Charles was now aware that his force greatly outnumbered the English, although not by as much as Charles had hoped. Edward's contingent was still in England waiting for shipping to be assembled and the French mistakenly believed it would be used in northern France, probably disembarking in [Picardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picardy "Picardy"). An army was gathered to confront this imagined threat, including many men transferred from Brittany.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401-33) Northampton's 1,350 men are described by the historian [Jonathan Sumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Sumption,_Lord_Sumption "Jonathan Sumption, Lord Sumption") as being half men-at-arms and half archers; [Kelly DeVries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_DeVries "Kelly DeVries") says most were archers. They were joined by the survivors of the 234-strong advance party which had arrived three months earlier – of whom 34 were men-at-arms and 200 archers – and at least one other group of English troops of 110 men. A few days after arriving they were reinforced by a further 800 men from England, whose composition is not known.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-34)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990392,_397,_399-35)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998143%E2%80%93144-36)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton1999258-37) The historian Andrew Ayton concludes like Sumption that the English consisted of about the same number of archers as men-at arms.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton1999261-38) The balance of the English army was made up of Bretons with variable levels of equipment, training and commitment.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400,_406-39) The total under Northampton's command has been estimated to be between 3,000 and 5,000.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139_n._13-40) It is unclear how many of this force took part in the subsequent battle, as a detachment of unknown size was left to contain the garrison of Morlaix.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) Ayton suggests a lower figure of 1,100 English and "an indeterminate number of Bretons".[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton1999261-38) [![Image 5: A colourful Medieval image of a man in armour on a horse](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Aix_Robert_d%27Anjou_miniature.jpg/250px-Aix_Robert_d%27Anjou_miniature.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aix_Robert_d%27Anjou_miniature.jpg) A contemporary image of a mounted man-at-arms: note the lack of armour on the horse. There is disagreement among modern historians on the size of the French army. Three contemporary chroniclers give 20,000; 3,000 cavalry, 1,500 mercenary infantry, and levy infantry "without number" (very many); and just "a huge army".[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998141-32) The historian [Alfred Burne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Burne "Alfred Burne") says it "attained prodigious numbers" and mentions 15,000 while dismissing earlier estimates of 30,000.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199971-42) DeVries writes "perhaps ... as many as 15,000", footnoting this to Burne and mentioning other estimates. He accepts that the English were heavily outnumbered, "perhaps by as many as four to one".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-29) Marilyn Livingstone and [Morgen Witzel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgen_Witzel "Morgen Witzel") suggest a total of between 10,000 and 15,000.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200413-43) Sumption states that Charles of Blois had 3,000 cavalry, 1,500 professional infantry and an unspecified number of Breton levy infantry, describing the last as "a motley force".[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401%E2%80%93402-44) [Matthew Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Bennett_/(historian/) "Matthew Bennett (historian)") has suggested "perhaps 3,000 men-at-arms and 1,500 Genoese mercenaries" as Charles' total force, which he opines was considerably more men than in the English army; a little later he also mentions lightly armoured Breton infantry leading the French attack.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45) The French army was "several times larger" than the English according to John Wagner.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46) The men-at-arms of both armies wore a quilted [gambeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambeson "Gambeson") under [mail armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail_/(armour/) "Mail (armour)") which covered the body and limbs. This was supplemented by varying amounts of [plate armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_armour "Plate armour") on the body and limbs, more so for wealthier and more experienced men. Heads were protected by [bascinets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bascinet "Bascinet"): open-faced iron or steel helmets, with mail attached to the lower edge of the helmet to protect the throat, neck and shoulders. A moveable visor (face guard) protected the face. [Heater shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heater_shield "Heater shield"), typically made from thin wood overlaid with leather, were carried. The English men-at-arms were all dismounted. The weapons they used are not recorded, but in similar battles they used their lances as pikes, cut them down to use as short spears, or fought with swords and battle axes.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdgePaddock198868%E2%80%9383-47)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007155-48)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200890%E2%80%9391-49)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMallett197437-50)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton200730,_n._128-51) They were mounted on entirely unarmoured horses and carried wooden lances, usually ash, tipped with iron and approximately 4 metres (13 ft) long.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdgePaddock198888-52) [![Image 6: A photograph of an iron arrowhead](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Bodkin1.jpg/250px-Bodkin1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bodkin1.jpg) The [longbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbow "Longbow"), which all of the English archers used,[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-54) was unique to them; it took up to 10 years to master and an experienced archer could discharge up to ten arrows per minute well over 300 metres (980 ft).[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-56) Computer analysis by [Warsaw University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_University_of_Technology "Warsaw University of Technology") in 2017 demonstrated that heavy [bodkin point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodkin_point "Bodkin point") arrows could penetrate typical plate armour of the time at 225 metres (738 ft). The depth of penetration would be slight at that range, but would have increased as the range closed or against armour of less than the best quality available at the time.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMagierNowakTomaszZochowski201773,_77,_81,_84-57)[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-59) Contemporary sources speak of arrows frequently piercing armour.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1998239-60) Archers carried one [quiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiver "Quiver") of 24 arrows as standard. It was common for them to each be issued with one or two extra quivers when a battle was expected, for a maximum total of 72 arrows per man. Even this was only sufficient for perhaps fifteen minutes of continuous shooting, although as the battle wore on the rate of fire would slow. Regular resupply of ammunition would be required from the wagons to the rear; the archers would also venture forward during pauses in the fighting to retrieve arrows.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973%E2%80%9374-61)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStricklandHardy201131,_278%E2%80%93279-62)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWallerWaller2010169%E2%80%93170-63) The weapons used by either the mercenary infantry or the Breton levies deployed by the French are not known. Livingstone and Witzel contend that the French "did not have any archers";[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200464-64) Alfred Burne takes at least some and possibly all of their mercenary infantry to be [crossbowmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbow "Crossbow").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199974-65) Bennett also mentions the presence of Genoese crossbowmen in the French army.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45)[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-68) A trained crossbowman could shoot his weapon approximately twice a minute[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMagierNowakTomaszZochowski201770-69) to a shorter effective range than a longbowman[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1998238-70) of about 200 metres (660 ft).[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachrachBachrach2017236-71) Charles, now more accurately informed about the size of Northampton's force, decided to relieve Morlaix and his army marched back to the west.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998141-32) Not wishing to become pinned between Charles and the garrison of Morlaix, Northampton took most of his troops on a night march on 29/30 September. The large village of [Lanmeur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanmeur "Lanmeur") was 11 kilometres (7 mi) north east of Morlaix and a little before reaching it the English found a suitable defensive position and dug in.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199971-42) They positioned themselves in a line across the road with a gentle slope down to a stream which bent to cover their right flank.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199972-72) A wood 100 metres (330 ft) behind them was too dense for cavalry to penetrate readily and so positioned their [baggage train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baggage_train "Baggage train") there – it would act as a rallying point if the battle went against them.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199974-65) Northampton decided to fight defensively and on foot,[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTETout1904714-73) and so the horses were also left in the wood.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45) A ditch and pit traps were dug a little in front of the line and camouflaged with branches and grass.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton2007c337-74)[\[note 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-77) The English deployed in what had become their standard formation, with the dismounted men-at-arms in the centre flanked on each side by archers.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199972-72) [![Image 7: Diagrammatic map of the battle of Morlaix](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Battle_of_Morlaix.png/500px-Battle_of_Morlaix.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Morlaix.png) Approximate troop movements at the battle of Morlaix, 30 September 1342 Charles of Blois' army was advancing west along the coast road and it is possible his cavalry spent the night in the village of Lanmeur with the infantry bivouacked further east. Once the English position just to the south west was identified on the morning of 30 September Charles spent some time organising his army into battle formation. He divided it into three divisions, or [battles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_/(formation/) "Battle (formation)"), one behind the other, with wide gaps between. Several accounts state that the foremost division consisted largely of Breton levy infantry, the need to pass them through the cavalry in the village explains why the French did not start their attack until about 3:00 pm.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199972%E2%80%9373-78) The first French division advanced against the English. Modern historians differ as to its composition. The majority state that it was made up of Breton levy infantry,[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-79)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45) but Sumption writes that it was predominately Franco-Breton mounted men-at-arms,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) and DeVries that it was a mix.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998142-80) The attackers crossed a brook parallel to the English line and made their way up a gentle slope. The English archers loosed their arrows once this massed target was within long range and the advance dissolved into chaos. None of the attackers got as far as the concealed trench in front of the English line before fleeing back towards Lanmeur.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-79)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46) [![Image 8: a woman holding a partly drawn longbow](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Longbow_Archer.jpg/250px-Longbow_Archer.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Longbow_Archer.jpg) A modern reenactor demonstrating a longbow draw There was a pause, and possibly some consultation among Charles' command group, then the second division advanced. This was made up entirely of mounted men-at-arms. They launched a determined but disordered charge at the English,[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998142%E2%80%93143-81) which collapsed as the leading horses fell into the concealed ditch and the following horses and riders stumbled over them. The English archers plied a deliberately aimed hail of arrows into this large, stationary, close-range target to great effect.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46) Sumption writes that "there were appalling casualties",[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) Wagner of "terrible execution".[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46) A small group of French cavalry, perhaps 200 men, made their way over this obstacle and pressed home their charge. They closed with the English dismounted men-at-arms and broke into their position, but were so few and so disordered that they were cut off, surrounded and all either killed or captured. The prisoners were sent back to the [baggage laager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagon_fort "Wagon fort").[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-79) There was another pause in the fighting, longer than the previous one, as Charles and his colleagues contemplated the situation. The remaining French division outnumbered the English army on its own; like the second division it consisted entirely of mounted men-at-arms. Eventually it was committed to a third attack. This may be attributable to the [chivalric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivalry "Chivalry") ideals held by knights of the time: nobles may have preferred to die in battle, rather than dishonourably decline to fight, especially against an outnumbered enemy.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton200725%E2%80%9326-82) Northampton was concerned that the English archers were running low on arrows and that the ditch was less of an obstacle, both because it was no longer a surprise and because it was bridged in many places by the dead and wounded bodies of men and horses. As a result, when he saw the French massing for a further assault he ordered a withdrawal into the wood to the rear. There the English took up a defensive position just inside the wood and facing in all directions.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-79)[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222%E2%80%93223-83) As the English had anticipated, the French mounted men-at-arms had difficulty forcing their way through the forested area and many were shot by English archers, despite their shortage of ammunition.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200413-43) Confounded, the French pulled back, ringed the wood with outposts and besieged the English army.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) Bennett and Burne both comment that this part of the battle was made more difficult for the French because their mercenary crossbowmen had deserted.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45) [![Image 9: A cartoon-like coloured image of a person in medieval armour leaning on a shield](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/49/Geoffroi_de_Charny.png/187px-Geoffroi_de_Charny.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Geoffroi_de_Charny.png) Geoffrey of Charny as depicted in the 14th century The English were trapped in the wood with little food, possibly for several days. Eventually they broke out at night and made their way back to Morlaix, where they continued the siege.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19996-75)[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975-84) They took with them 150 captured French knights,[\[note 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-86) one of whom was [Geoffrey of Charny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffroi_de_Charny "Geoffroi de Charny"), who had led the first mounted division to attack.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998142-80)[\[note 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-89) The number killed or wounded on each side is not known, although total French losses were heavy,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46) with one modern historian stating that thousands were killed.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007205-90) English casualties were light; there is mention of one named man-at-arms being killed and one badly wounded.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton2007b208,_211-91)[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAytonPreston2007376_n._76-92) The garrison of Morlaix held out and when [Edward III arrived at Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign "Edward III's Breton campaign") on 26 October the siege was abandoned and Northampton marched to join him.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402%E2%80%93404-93) Charles and the French survivors withdrew east after the battle.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975-84) Campaigning in Brittany was interrupted by the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"), agreed on 19 January 1343. Hostilities did not recommence until June 1345.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-94) The eastern and southern parts of Brittany were mostly held by Charles of Blois, who continued to be strongly supported by the French, while western and northern Brittany continued to be largely Montfort or English controlled.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-34) Northampton went on to have an outstanding military and diplomatic career. He campaigned with Edward III in 1359–1360 and was one of the negotiators of the [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny") in 1360 which ended the [Edwardian phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War,_1337%E2%80%931360 "Hundred Years' War, 1337–1360") of the war with a stunning English victory.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1999445-95)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200655,_60-96)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2014421-97) Charles of Blois continued to fight for control of Brittany. He was captured by the English in 1347, released in 1356 and killed in 1364 at the [battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray"). The [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)") ended the Breton Civil War the following year with a Montfortist victory.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200692%E2%80%9393-98) Morlaix established a strong English presence in Brittany and restarted the Breton Civil War when it was thought nearly over.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660,_223-99) It was the first major land battle of the Hundred Years' War[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-34)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990483-100) and the first time the English tactic of deploying their men-at-arms on foot with massed longbowmen on either flank was seen outside Britain.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTETout1904711%E2%80%93712-101) It was also the first time this approach had been used against mounted opponents, rather than infantry, and it was clear that when used correctly it was capable of defeating them.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200464-64) Livingstone and Witzel suggest it is difficult to take lessons from the battle as "Charles ... was a military incompetent".[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200464-64) Sumption states that the French behaved in the same wrong-headed way they usually did in battles of the 1340s.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) Some historians see the battle of Morlaix as part of the development of English tactics during the first half of the 14th century. They suggest that pitched battles against the Scots during the previous 30 years had enabled the English to develop an effective combination of their different troop types and agree on the devastating effectiveness of English bowmen and men-at-arms when properly coordinated. Wagner describes this as "the great tactical innovation of the war".[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200617%E2%80%9318,_291-102)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975%E2%80%9376,_171%E2%80%93172-103) Historians agree that the tactics used at Morlaix were those which won the great English victories of [Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") in 1346 and [Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") in 1356, and that Northampton's victory was the start of a military ascendancy for the English which lasted for 20 years.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19996-75)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975%E2%80%9376,_112%E2%80%93113-104)[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222,_291-105) Notes, citations and sources ---------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Morlaix&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Notes, citations and sources")\] 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_ref-16)** John surrendered on the granting of a [safe conduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_conduct "Safe conduct") to Paris and back by [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John,_Duke_of_Normandy "John, Duke of Normandy"), King Philip's oldest son, who escorted him.
