**Edward III** (13 November 1312 – 21 June 1377), also known as **Edward of Windsor** before his accession, was [King of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_England "King of England") from January 1327 until his death in 1377. He is noted for his military success and for restoring royal authority after the disastrous and unorthodox reign of his father, [Edward II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_II "Edward II"). Edward III transformed the [Kingdom of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") into one of the most formidable military powers in Europe. His fifty-year reign is [one of the longest in English history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_monarchs_in_Britain_by_length_of_reign#Ten_longest-reigning_British_monarchs "List of monarchs in Britain by length of reign"), and saw vital developments in legislation and government, in particular the evolution of the [English Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Parliament "English Parliament"), as well as the ravages of the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death"). He outlived his eldest son, [Edward the Black Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_the_Black_Prince "Edward the Black Prince"), and was succeeded by his grandson, [Richard II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_II "Richard II").

Edward was crowned at age fourteen after his father was deposed by his mother, [Isabella of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_France "Isabella of France"), and her lover, [Roger Mortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Mortimer,_1st_Earl_of_March "Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March"). At the age of seventeen, he led a successful [coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d%27%C3%A9tat "Coup d'état") against Mortimer, the _[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto "De facto")_ ruler of England, and began his personal reign. After a [successful campaign in Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_War_of_Scottish_Independence#English_invasion_of_Scotland,_1333 "Second War of Scottish Independence"), he declared himself [rightful heir to the French throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claim_to_the_French_throne "English claim to the French throne"),[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-2) starting the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") (1337–1453). Following some initial setbacks, this [first phase of the war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War,_1337%E2%80%931360 "Hundred Years' War, 1337–1360") went exceptionally well for England and would become known as the Edwardian War. Victories at [Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") and [Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") led to the highly favourable [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny") (1360), in which England made territorial gains, and Edward renounced his claim to the French throne. Edward's later years were marked by foreign policy failure and domestic strife, largely as a result of his decreasing activity and poor health. The [second phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War,_1369%E2%80%931389 "Hundred Years' War, 1369–1389") of the Hundred Years' War began in 1369, leading to the loss of most of Edward's conquests, save for the [Pale of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pale_of_Calais "Pale of Calais"), by 1375.[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-3)

Edward was temperamental and thought himself capable of feats such as healing by the [royal touch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_touch "Royal touch"), as some prior English kings did. He was also capable of unusual clemency. He was in many ways a conventional [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") king whose main interest was warfare, but he also had a broad range of non-military interests. Admired in his own time, and for centuries after, he was later denounced as an irresponsible adventurer by [Whig historians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_historians "Whig historians"), but modern historians credit him with significant achievements.

Edward's father, King [Edward II of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_II_of_England "Edward II of England") had court favourites who were unpopular with his nobility, such as [Piers Gaveston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piers_Gaveston "Piers Gaveston") and [Hugh Despenser the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Despenser_the_Younger "Hugh Despenser the Younger"). Gaveston was killed during a noble rebellion against Edward II in 1312, while Despenser was hated by the English nobility.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Baker201211-4) Edward II was also unpopular with the common people due to his repeated demands that they provide unpaid military service in Scotland.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPowicke1956114-5) None of his campaigns there were successful,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich198070-6) and this led to a further decline in his popularity, particularly with the nobility. His image was damaged again in 1322 when he executed his cousin [Thomas, Earl of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas,_Earl_of_Lancaster "Thomas, Earl of Lancaster"), and confiscated the Lancaster estates.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiven-Wilson1994553-7) Historian [Chris Given-Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Given-Wilson "Chris Given-Wilson") wrote that, by 1325, the nobility believed that "no landholder could feel safe" under the regime.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiven-Wilson1994571-8) This distrust of Edward II was shared by his wife, [Isabella of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_France "Isabella of France"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2014196-9)[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-12) who believed Despenser responsible for poisoning the King's mind against her.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiven-WilsonBrandPhillipsOrmrod2005-13) In September 1324 Queen Isabella was publicly humiliated when the government declared her an enemy alien,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod201232-14) and the King [repossessed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repossession "Repossession") her estates,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod201232-14) probably at the urging of Despenser.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParsons2004-15) Edward II also disbanded her retinue.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTELord200245_n.5-16) Edward II had already been threatened with deposition on two previous occasions (in 1310 and 1321).[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiven-WilsonBrandPhillipsOrmrod2005-13) Historians agree that hostility towards the king was universal. W. H. Dunham and C. T. Wood ascribed this to Edward II's "cruelty and personal faults",[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunhamWood1976739-17) suggesting that "very few, not even his half-brothers or his son, seemed to care about the wretched man"[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunhamWood1976739-17) and that none would fight for him.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunhamWood1976739-17) A contemporary chronicler described Edward II as _rex inutilis_, or a "useless king".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeters1970217-18)

Early life (1312–1327)
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_III_of_England&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life (1312–1327)")\]

Edward was born at [Windsor Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor_Castle "Windsor Castle") on 13 November 1312, and was described in a contemporary prophecy as "the boar that would come out of Windsor".[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer200621-19) The reign of his father, Edward II, was a particularly problematic period of English history.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChaplais19945-20)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaines200336%E2%80%9339-21)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips20119-22)[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-23) The King had alienated several [English nobles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_peerage "English peerage") and Scottish allies by abandoning [his father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I_of_England "Edward I of England")'s [war with Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_War_of_Scottish_Independence "First War of Scottish Independence") soon after his accession, and continued to lose battles against the Scots intermittently.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck198552-24)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips201117%E2%80%9319-25) Also controversial was the King's [patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") of a small group of royal [favourites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Favourite "Favourite") rather than his nobility generally. This, says the historian [Michael Prestwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Prestwich "Michael Prestwich"), "unbalanced the whole system of royal patronage".[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich198080-26) However, the birth of a male heir in 1312 – the future Edward III – soon improved Edward II's relations with the French, and a moderate element within the nobility temporarily quelled baronial opposition.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005189-27) The young prince was created [Earl of Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Chester "Earl of Chester") at only twelve days old, and by January the following year had been provided with an entire household.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer200623-28) An early influence on Prince Edward was the [Bishop of Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Durham "Bishop of Durham"), [Richard de Bury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_de_Bury "Richard de Bury"), one of the century's major [bibliophiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibliophile "Bibliophile"). Originally a tutor, he appears to have become a mentor to the King. Under Bury's tutelage, Edward learned to write and to read French and Latin. He would have had access to famous contemporary works, such as [Vegetius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetius "Vegetius")'s _[De Re Militari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Re_Militari "De Re Militari")_, which had been translated into [Anglo-Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Norman_language "Anglo-Norman language"), as well as the _[Mirror for Princes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_for_Princes "Mirror for Princes")_ and various [psalters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalters "Psalters") and religious texts.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurcell201732-29)

Since the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest") had united the [Duchy of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Normandy "Duchy of Normandy") and its French estates with those of the Crown and the land of England, English kings had held several territories, including [Poitou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poitou "Poitou"), [Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquitaine "Aquitaine"), [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy "Normandy"), [Anjou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Anjou "Duchy of Anjou") and [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_/(province/) "Maine (province)"), and these holdings – at one point covering more of France than that held by the French king – had frequently led to conflict.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry20031%E2%80%932-30) In 1325, Edward II was faced with a demand from his brother-in-law [Charles IV of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IV_of_France "Charles IV of France") to perform [homage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homage_/(feudal/) "Homage (feudal)") for the English [Duchy of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Aquitaine "Duchy of Aquitaine").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck198588-31) The King was reluctant to leave the country, as discontent was once again brewing domestically, particularly over his relationship with the favourite [Hugh Despenser the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Despenser_the_Younger "Hugh Despenser the Younger").[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-32) Instead, he had his son Edward created [Duke of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Aquitaine "Duke of Aquitaine") in his place and sent him to France to perform the homage.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer200639-33) The young Edward was accompanied by his mother Isabella, who was King Charles's sister and was meant to negotiate a peace treaty with the French.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005213-34) While in France, Isabella conspired with the exiled [Roger Mortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Mortimer,_1st_Earl_of_March "Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March") to have Edward II deposed.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005216-35) To build up diplomatic and military support for the venture, Isabella had her son engaged to the twelve-year-old [Philippa of Hainault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa_of_Hainault "Philippa of Hainault").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer200646-36) An [invasion of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_England_/(1326/) "Invasion of England (1326)") was launched and Edward II's forces deserted him completely. Isabella and Mortimer summoned [a parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_1327 "Parliament of 1327"), and the King was forced to relinquish the throne to his son, who was proclaimed king in London on 25 January 1327. The new king was crowned as Edward III at [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey") on 1 February at the age of 14.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer200654-37)[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-38)

Early reign (1327–1337)
-----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_III_of_England&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early reign (1327–1337)")\]

### Mortimer's rule and fall

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_III_of_England&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mortimer's rule and fall")\]

One of Edward's first acts – _de facto_ Mortimer's – was to lead another campaign to Scotland in July 1327.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson196526%E2%80%9327-39) It was not long before the new reign also met with other problems caused by the central position of Mortimer at court, who was now the de facto ruler of England. Mortimer used his position to acquire noble estates and titles, and his unpopularity grew with the humiliating defeat by the Scots at the [Battle of Stanhope Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stanhope_Park "Battle of Stanhope Park") in the [county of Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Durham "County of Durham"), and the ensuing [Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Edinburgh%E2%80%93Northampton "Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton"), agreed with the Scots in 1328.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack195998%E2%80%93100-40) The young king also came into conflict with his guardian. Mortimer knew his position in relation to the King was precarious and subjected Edward to disrespect. The King married Philippa of Hainault at [York Minster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Minster "York Minster") on 24 January 1328, and the birth of their first child, [Edward of Woodstock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_of_Woodstock "Edward of Woodstock"), on 15 June 1330 only increased tension with Mortimer.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer200667,_81-41) Eventually, the King decided to take direct action against Mortimer.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005223%E2%80%93224-42) Although up until now Edward had kept a low profile, it is likely that he increasingly suspected that Mortimer's behaviour could endanger Edward's own life, as the former's position became more unpopular. This was exacerbated by his execution of Edward's uncle [Edmund, Earl of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_of_Woodstock,_1st_Earl_of_Kent "Edmund of Woodstock, 1st Earl of Kent"). Contemporary chroniclers suspected, too, that Mortimer had designs on the throne, and it is likely that it was these rumours that encouraged Edward to act against him and his mother, who supposedly maintained a close relationship with Mortimer.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell200883%E2%80%9384-43)

Aided by his close companion [William Montagu, 3rd Baron Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Montagu,_3rd_Baron_Montagu "William Montagu, 3rd Baron Montagu"), and a small number of other trusted men, Edward took Mortimer by surprise and captured him at [Nottingham Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottingham_Castle "Nottingham Castle") on 19 October 1330. Mortimer was executed and Edward's personal reign began.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005223%E2%80%93224-42) The historian [Mark Ormrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Ormrod_/(historian/) "Mark Ormrod (historian)") argued that at this point Edward had had "little instruction in the art of kingship",[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200047-44) and although he had received several books on the subject on his betrothal to Philippa, "it is extremely doubtful that he read or comprehended these works".[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200047-44) His reign, continues Ormrod, was to be guided by his practical, rather than theoretical, experience.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200047-44)

Edward III was not content with the peace agreement made in his name, but the renewal of the war with Scotland originated in private, rather than royal initiative.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005244-45) A group of English [magnates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnate "Magnate") known as The Disinherited, who had lost land in Scotland by the peace accord,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson196557%E2%80%9358-46) staged an [invasion of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_War_of_Scottish_Independence#The_repelled_invasion_of_Edward_Balliol_-_1332 "Second War of Scottish Independence") and won a great victory at the [Battle of Dupplin Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dupplin_Moor "Battle of Dupplin Moor") in 1332.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005244-45) They attempted to install [Edward Balliol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Balliol "Edward Balliol") as king of Scotland in place of the infant [David II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_II_of_Scotland "David II of Scotland"), but Balliol was soon expelled and was forced to seek the help of Edward III. The English king responded by [laying siege to](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Berwick_/(1333/) "Capture of Berwick (1333)") the important border town of [Berwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berwick-upon-Tweed "Berwick-upon-Tweed") and defeated a large relieving army at the [Battle of Halidon Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Halidon_Hill "Battle of Halidon Hill"),[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1996114%E2%80%93115-47) even while under threat from foreign raids.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson1965122-48) However, Berwick was taken after the besieged Scots set fire to the town, forcing them to [treat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercy "Mercy");[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson1965123-49) at one point Edward's queen was under siege in [Bamburgh Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamburgh_Castle "Bamburgh Castle"), but this was too late to save the Scots' campaign.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson1965125%E2%80%93127-50) He reinstated Balliol on the throne and received a substantial amount of land in southern Scotland.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005244%E2%80%93245-51) These victories proved hard to sustain, as forces loyal to David II gradually regained control of the country.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200018-52) A Scottish uprising in 1334 required the raising of another army and a supporting navy. Edward, having repaired [Roxburgh Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxburgh_Castle "Roxburgh Castle"),[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson1965182-53)[\[g\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-55) launched a number of ineffective strikes against the Scots.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson1965187%E2%80%93188-56) In 1338, Edward agreed a truce with the Scots.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200018-52)

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Artist%2C_maker_unknown%2C_English_-_Heraldic_panel_with_the_Coat_of_Arms_of_Edward_III%2C_King_of_England_%28reigned_1327%E2%80%9377%29_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/250px-Artist%2C_maker_unknown%2C_English_-_Heraldic_panel_with_the_Coat_of_Arms_of_Edward_III%2C_King_of_England_%28reigned_1327%E2%80%9377%29_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Artist,_maker_unknown,_English_-_Heraldic_panel_with_the_Coat_of_Arms_of_Edward_III,_King_of_England_/(reigned_1327%E2%80%9377/)_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)

To mark his claim to the French crown, Edward III quartered the arms of France, placing them in the first and fourth quarters. English [stained glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass"), c. 1350 – 1377.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTELoudaMaclagan1981-57)

One reason for the change of strategy towards Scotland was a growing concern for the relationship between England and France. As long as Scotland and France were in [an alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auld_Alliance "Auld Alliance"), the English were faced with the prospect of fighting a war on two fronts.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959117%E2%80%93119-58) The French carried out raids on English coastal towns, leading to rumours in England of a full-scale French invasion.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200018%E2%80%9319-59)

### Creating a new nobility

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_III_of_England&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Creating a new nobility")\]

When Edward took power, he found his family in "complete disarray",[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987400-60) says Ormrod. His nobility was divided into factions after the troublesome reign of his father and was weakened by line failure among many families.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFarlane1973xxiii,_15,_55-61) While the lesser baronage was less affected by political misadventure than their seniors, they were also weaker due to their rights being more insubstantive. Edward had to pacify two noble parties: one which had been against his father from the beginning, and another which had opposed Mortimer's and Isabella's minority regime.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell19971111-62) James Bothwell argues that, while he managed to reconcile the sides bloodlessly and with minimum acrimony, it was insufficient to leave him secure on his own: he lanced the opposition but had not turned them into a loyalist cadre.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell19971111%E2%80%931112-63) Only the [Earls of Arundel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Fitzalan,_3rd_Earl_of_Arundel "Richard Fitzalan, 3rd Earl of Arundel"), [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_de_Vere,_7th_Earl_of_Oxford "John de Vere, 7th Earl of Oxford") and [Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Beauchamp,_11th_Earl_of_Warwick "Thomas Beauchamp, 11th Earl of Warwick") could be counted on as loyalists.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERaven2021498-64)

To counter the limited loyalty among the aristocrats, following the March 1337 Parliament[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERaven2021498-64) Edward created six new [earls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl "Earl"). He also summoned 61 new men to the lords with lesser titles, usually by [writ of summons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writ_of_summons "Writ of summons"), over the rest of his reign.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell19971112-65) These creations – although expensive – received very little ill will among the extant aristocracy, including the royal family.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell19971126-66) The 1337 creations were [Hugh de Audley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_de_Audley,_1st_Earl_of_Gloucester "Hugh de Audley, 1st Earl of Gloucester") to the [Earldom of Gloucester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earldom_of_Gloucester "Earldom of Gloucester"), [William de Bohun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") to that of [Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Northampton "Earl of Northampton"), [William de Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Clinton "William de Clinton") to [Huntingdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Huntingdon "Earl of Huntingdon"), [Henry of Grosmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Grosmont "Henry of Grosmont") to [Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Derby "Earl of Derby"), [William de Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Salisbury "William Montagu, 1st Earl of Salisbury") to [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Salisbury "Earl of Salisbury") and [Robert de Ufford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Ufford,_1st_Earl_of_Suffolk "Robert Ufford, 1st Earl of Suffolk") to [Suffolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Suffolk "Earl of Suffolk").[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERaven2021498-64) Of these, Bohun, Clinton, Montagu and Ufford had played leading roles in Edward's coup against Mortimer; they were likewise the greatest beneficiaries in terms of grants and estates.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell200140-67) Another common denominator was that most of them had also been trusted companions of Edward before the coup; Ufford, for example, jousted with him and attended him in his homage before [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"),[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell200423-68) while Montagu had been his "closest supporter",[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell200423-68) and had run secret diplomatic missions to the Pope for him before the coup.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell200884-69)

James Bothwell has noted that, while these men may have been less well off before they were promoted, they were not less experienced,[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell200422-70) either politically or militarily.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERaven2021499-71) These promotions were especially important to Edward because it had been from among the earls that his father had created so many bitter enemies, and therefore that was the demography that Edward wanted to reorganise in his favour.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell200419,_22-72) These promotions reinforced his own and the Crown's position and, with war approaching, he created six new recruitment conduits from the regions directly to the royal army.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERaven2021499-71) For the earls themselves, the prospect was not so positive: due to the parlous state of the royal finances, most of them did not receive a minimum of 1000 [marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_/(currency/) "Mark (currency)")[\[h\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-74) a year that was promised to them to uphold their new estate. All except Gloucester[\[i\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-76) had to be satisfied with irregular grants of land to boost their incomes, but these would often not be available until the incumbent died and they [escheated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escheat "Escheat") to the King.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERaven2021501%E2%80%93502-77)

Mid-reign (1337–1360)
---------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_III_of_England&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Mid-reign (1337–1360)")\]

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Edward_III_becomes_Vicar_to_the_Emperor_Ludwig_V.jpg/250px-Edward_III_becomes_Vicar_to_the_Emperor_Ludwig_V.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_III_becomes_Vicar_to_the_Emperor_Ludwig_V.jpg)

Portrayal of Edward's appointment as Vicar-General of the Holy Roman Empire by Emperor Louis IV in the late fourteenth-century [Chronicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Froissart%27s_Chronicles "Froissart's Chronicles") of [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart")

In 1337, [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") confiscated the English king's [Duchy of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Aquitaine "Duchy of Aquitaine") and the [county of Ponthieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Ponthieu "Count of Ponthieu"). Instead of seeking a peaceful resolution to the conflict by paying homage to the French king, as his father had done, Edward responded by [laying claim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne") to the French crown as the grandson of [Philip IV of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_IV_of_France "Philip IV of France").[\[j\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-79) The French rejected this based on the precedents for [agnatic succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrilineality "Patrilineality") set in 1316 and 1322 and upheld the rights of Philip IV's nephew Philip VI, leading to tensions that caused the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War").[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1999106-80) In the early stages of the war, Edward's strategy was to build alliances with other Continental rulers. In 1338, [Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor"), named Edward [Vicar general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicar_general "Vicar general") of the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") and promised his support.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2000155-81) As late as 1373, the [Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1373](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Portuguese_Treaty_of_1373 "Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1373") established an [Anglo-Portuguese Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Portuguese_Alliance "Anglo-Portuguese Alliance"). These measures produced few results.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959128%E2%80%93129-82)

The only major military victory during this phase of the war was the English naval victory at [Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sluys "Battle of Sluys") on 24 June 1340, which secured control of the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel").[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959128%E2%80%93129-82) This victory decimated a superior French fleet and lowered the threat of a French invasion of England, which increased English desires to attack France. This situation lasted less than a year. Edward was unlikely to have been happy with this victory due to his continuing financial problems.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand198813-78) The English also captured 166 French merchantmen; they had been raiding the south coast of England for several years and were unpopular amongst English sailors. Up to 16,000 French sailors were killed and French captain, [Nicolas Béhuchet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_B%C3%A9huchet "Nicolas Béhuchet") – who could otherwise have expected to be [ransomed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom "Ransom") – was hanged from his own [yardarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yard_/(sailing/) "Yard (sailing)").[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway201198-83) Edward saw God's hand in his victory and a triumphal coin was struck in commemoration – showing Edward in a ship, probably meant to be Béhuchet's own – and the King gained a reputation as a naval warrior.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway201199-84)[\[k\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-86)

Meanwhile, the fiscal pressure on the kingdom caused by Edward's expensive alliances led to discontent at home. The regency council at home was frustrated by the mounting national debt, while the King and his commanders on the Continent were angered by the failure of the government in England to provide sufficient funds.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005273%E2%80%93275-87) To deal with the situation, Edward himself returned to England, arriving in London unannounced on 30 November 1340.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959168-88)[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones2013385%E2%80%93390-89) Finding the affairs of the realm in disorder, he purged the royal administration of a great number of ministers and judges.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFryde1975149%E2%80%93161-90) These measures did not bring domestic stability, and a stand-off ensued between the King and [John de Stratford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_de_Stratford "John de Stratford"), [Archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury"), during which Stratford's relatives [Robert Stratford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stratford "Robert Stratford"), [Bishop of Chichester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Chichester "Bishop of Chichester"), and [Henry de Stratford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_de_Stratford "Henry de Stratford") were temporarily stripped of title and imprisoned respectively.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMyers195369-91) Stratford claimed that Edward had violated the laws of the land by arresting royal officers.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005275%E2%80%93276-92) A certain level of conciliation was reached at the Parliament of April 1341. Here Edward was forced to accept severe limitations to his financial and administrative freedom, in return for a grant of taxation.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959174%E2%80%93175-93) Yet in October the same year, Edward repudiated this statute and Archbishop Stratford was politically ostracised. The extraordinary circumstances of the April Parliament had forced the King into submission, but under normal circumstances, the powers of the king in medieval England were virtually unlimited, a fact that Edward was able to exploit.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200023%E2%80%9325-94)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Edward_III_Groat.jpg/250px-Edward_III_Groat.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_III_Groat.jpg)

[Groat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groat_/(coin/) "Groat (coin)") featuring Edward III

Historian [Nicholas Rodger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Rodger "Nicholas Rodger") called Edward III's claim to be the "Sovereign of the Seas" into question, arguing there was hardly any [royal navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Royal_Navy "History of the Royal Navy") before the reign of [Henry V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England") (1413–1422). Despite Rodger's view, [King John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John,_King_of_England "John, King of England") had already developed a royal fleet of [galleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley "Galley") and had attempted to establish an administration for these ships and others which were arrested (privately owned ships pulled into royal/national service). [Henry III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_III_of_England "Henry III of England"), his successor, continued this work. Notwithstanding the fact that he, along with his predecessor, had hoped to develop a strong and efficient naval administration, their endeavours produced one that was informal and mostly ad hoc. A formal naval administration emerged during Edward's reign, comprising lay administrators and led by William de Clewre, Matthew de Torksey and John de Haytfield successively bearing the title of _Clerk of the King's Ships_. [Robert de Crull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_de_Crull "Robert de Crull") was the last to fill this position during Edward III's reign[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERose19827-95) and would have the longest tenure in this position.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherborne199432-96) It was during his tenure that Edward's naval administration would become a base for what evolved during the reigns of successors such as [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII")'s _Council of Marine_ and _Navy Board_ and [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England")'s _Board of Admiralty_. Rodger also argues that for much of the fourteenth century, the French had the upper hand, apart from Sluys in 1340 and, perhaps, off [Winchelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Winchelsea "Battle of Winchelsea") in 1350.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger199799-97) Yet, the French never invaded England and King [John II of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") died in captivity in England. There was a need for an English navy to play a role in this and to handle other matters, such as the insurrection of the Anglo-Irish lords and acts of piracy.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959509-98)

Edward's military command structure began with himself at the centre, and then members of the court acted as his generals. This included the King's family, and Edward utilised the martial capabilities of his sons, particularly his eldest son, Edward the Black Prince. This was not only pragmatic, in that they were all good warriors, but had the added propaganda value of demonstrating the hereditary nature of Edward's claim to the French throne.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand198870-99)[\[l\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-100) However, command was not always the prerogative of the nobility. [Knights Banneret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_Banneret "Knights Banneret") – knights able to lead other knights[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHefferan2021115-101) – were also favoured as leaders of armies or divisions,[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand198870-99) as they were also already close to the king, being part of his household and bodyguard. They bore particular responsibilities during King Edward's _[chevauchées](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevauch%C3%A9e "Chevauchée")_, which often required the main army to split into smaller forces, each requiring its own captain.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHefferan2021115-101) This sometimes led to dissension. For example, in the 1369 [Loire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loire "Loire") campaign, the [Earl of Pembroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hastings,_2nd_Earl_of_Pembroke "John Hastings, 2nd Earl of Pembroke") shared command with [Sir John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_John_Chandos "Sir John Chandos"); although the latter was appointed [seneschal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneschal "Seneschal") of France by the Black Prince, Pembroke refused to work beneath him on account of his superior social status.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarber2004a-102)[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJack2004-103) Ultimately, though, the task of raising the armies that they would lead fell to both: the aristocracy could raise the largest number of tenants and [retainers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affinity_/(medieval/) "Affinity (medieval)") after the King, but it was the lower men who acted as recruiting sergeants in the regions.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand198870%E2%80%9371-104) Unlike during his father's or great-grandfather's campaigns in Scotland, the [feudal levy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_levy "Feudal levy") ― whereby military service was provided for free in exchange for land rights ― by the outbreak of the Hundred Years' War it had become the norm for men of all ranks to be paid for their service from the King. In return, the crown shouldered the responsibility for paying for the bulk of equipment. The military historian Andrew Ayton has described this transition as amounting to a "military revolution", and one spearheaded by the King himself.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton199496-105)

By the early 1340s, it was clear that Edward's policy of alliances was too costly, and yielded too few results. The following years saw more direct involvement by English armies, including in the [Breton War of Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession"), but these interventions also proved fruitless at first.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2006205-106)[\[m\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-108) Edward defaulted on large scale [Florentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence") loans, and partly as a result the lenders declared bankruptcy.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005501-109)

A change came in July 1346, when Edward staged a major offensive, sailing for [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy "Normandy") with a force of 15,000 men.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959132-110) His army [sacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Caen_/(1346/) "Battle of Caen (1346)") the city of [Caen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caen "Caen"), and marched across northern France, to meet up with [Flemish forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people") in [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Flanders "County of Flanders"). It was not Edward's initial intention to engage the French army, but at [Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A9cy-en-Ponthieu "Crécy-en-Ponthieu"), just north of the [Somme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somme_/(river/) "Somme (river)"), he found favourable terrain and decided to fight a pursuing army led by Philip VI.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005316%E2%80%93318-111) On 26 August, the English army defeated a far larger French army in the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy").[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1996155%E2%80%93176-112) Shortly after this, on 17 October, an English army defeated and captured King David II of Scotland at the [Battle of Neville's Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Neville%27s_Cross "Battle of Neville's Cross").[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh199117-113) With his northern borders secured, Edward felt free to continue his major offensive against France, [laying siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Calais_/(1346/) "Siege of Calais (1346)") to the town of [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais"). The operation was the greatest English venture of the Hundred Years' War, involving an army of 32,000 men.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200026-114) The siege started on 4 September 1346, and lasted until the town surrendered on 3 August 1347.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1999537,_581-115)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Edward_III_counting_the_dead_on_the_battlefield_of_Cr%C3%A9cy.jpg/250px-Edward_III_counting_the_dead_on_the_battlefield_of_Cr%C3%A9cy.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_III_counting_the_dead_on_the_battlefield_of_Cr%C3%A9cy.jpg)

Edward III counting the dead on the [battlefield of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy")

After the fall of Calais, factors outside of Edward's control forced him to wind down the war effort. In 1348, the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death_in_England "Black Death in England") struck England with full force, killing a third or more of the country's population.[\[n\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-116) This loss of manpower led to a shortage of farm labour and a corresponding rise in wages. The great landowners struggled with the shortage of manpower and the resulting inflation in labour cost.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh1991109-117) To curb the rise in wages, the King and Parliament responded with the [Ordinance of Labourers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinance_of_Labourers "Ordinance of Labourers") in 1349, followed by the [Statute of Labourers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Labourers "Statute of Labourers") in 1351. These attempts to regulate wages could not succeed in the long run, but in the short term they were enforced with great vigour.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005547%E2%80%93548-118) All in all, the plague did not lead to a full-scale breakdown of government and society, and recovery was remarkably swift.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005553-119) This was to a large extent thanks to the competent leadership of royal administrators such as Treasurer [William Edington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Edington "William Edington") and Chief Justice [William de Shareshull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Shareshull "William de Shareshull").[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1986175%E2%80%93188-120)

It was not until the mid-1350s that military operations on the Continent were resumed on a large scale.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005550-121) In 1356, Edward's eldest son, [Edward, Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_the_Black_Prince "Edward the Black Prince"), won an important victory in the [Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers"). The greatly outnumbered English forces not only routed the French, but captured the French king John II and his youngest son, [Philip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_the_Bold "Philip the Bold").[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959139-122) After a succession of victories, the English held great possessions in France, the French king was in English custody, and the French central government had almost totally collapsed.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959139%E2%80%93140-123) There has been a historical debate as to whether Edward's claim to the French crown originally was genuine, or if it was simply a political ploy meant to put pressure on the French government.[\[o\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-124) Regardless of the original intent, the stated claim now seemed to be within reach. Yet a campaign in 1359, meant to complete the undertaking, was inconclusive.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005326-125) In 1360, therefore, Edward accepted the [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny"), whereby he renounced his claims to the French throne, but secured his extended French possessions in full sovereignty.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200034%E2%80%9337-126) Edward kept his subjects fully informed of political and military developments abroad by a large number of regular reports from himself and his captains to various outlets, including [convocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convocation "Convocation"), the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London") and the archbishops, that, while the scholar A. E. Prince acknowledged that taken singularly, these reports may not represent a cohesive [public relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_relations "Public relations") within government, they do perhaps indicate, as a whole, the existence of a "simple propaganda organization" with which the King boosted domestic morale.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrince1926417-127) These then ended up as part of popular chronicles, either verbatim or in part, whether newsletters or public letters.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry20037-128)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Gold_quarter_noble_of_Edward_III_%28YORYM_2015_140%29_reverse.jpg/250px-Gold_quarter_noble_of_Edward_III_%28YORYM_2015_140%29_reverse.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gold_quarter_noble_of_Edward_III_/(YORYM_2015_140/)_reverse.jpg)

Gold quarter [noble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_/(English_coin/) "Noble (English coin)") of Edward III, York Museums Trust

The middle years of Edward's reign were a period of significant legislative activity. Perhaps the best-known piece of legislation passed was the [Statute of Labourers of 1351](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Labourers_of_1351 "Statute of Labourers of 1351"), which addressed the labour shortage problem caused by the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death"). The statute fixed wages at their pre-plague level and checked peasant mobility by asserting that lords had the first claim on their men's services. In spite of concerted efforts to uphold the statute, it eventually failed due to intense competition among landowners for labour.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959335-129) The law has been described as an attempt "to legislate against the law of [supply and demand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supply_and_demand "Supply and demand")", which doomed it to certain failure.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHanawalt1989139-130) Nevertheless, the labour shortage had created a community of interest between the smaller landowners of the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons "House of Commons") and the greater landowners of the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords"). The resulting measures angered the peasants, leading to the [Peasants' Revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt "Peasants' Revolt") of 1381.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich198320-131)

The reign of Edward III coincided with the so-called [Babylonian Captivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy "Avignon Papacy") of the papacy at [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon"). During the wars with France, opposition emerged in England against perceived injustices by a papacy largely controlled by the French crown.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959272-132) Papal taxation of the English Church was suspected to be financing the nation's enemies, while the practice of provisions (the Pope's providing benefices for clerics) caused resentment in the English population. The statutes of [Provisors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Provisors "Statute of Provisors") and [Praemunire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praemunire "Praemunire"), of 1350 and 1353 respectively, aimed to amend this by banning papal benefices, as well as limiting the power of the papal court over English subjects.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959280%E2%80%93281-133) The statutes did not sever the ties between the king and the Pope, who were equally dependent upon each other.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2000120%E2%80%93121-134)

Other legislation of importance includes the [Treason Act 1351](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treason_Act_1351 "Treason Act 1351"). It was precisely the harmony of the reign that allowed a consensus on the definition of this controversial crime.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959257-135) Yet, the most significant legal reform was probably that concerning the [Justices of the Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justices_of_the_Peace "Justices of the Peace"). This institution began before the reign of Edward III but, by 1350, the justices had been given the power not only to investigate crimes and make arrests, but also to try cases, including those of [felony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felony "Felony").[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam192943%E2%80%9345-136) With this, an enduring fixture in the administration of local English justice had been established.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMussonOrmrod199950%E2%80%9354-137)

### Parliament and taxation

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_III_of_England&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Parliament and taxation")\]

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/King_Edward_III_half_groat_York_mint.jpg/330px-King_Edward_III_half_groat_York_mint.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Edward_III_half_groat_York_mint.jpg)

Half [groat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groat_/(coin/) "Groat (coin)") with portrait of King Edward III, York mint

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/The_Great_Seal_of_Edward_III.JPG/250px-The_Great_Seal_of_Edward_III.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Great_Seal_of_Edward_III.JPG)

The [Great Seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Seal_of_the_Realm "Great Seal of the Realm") of Edward III

[Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") as a representative institution was already well established by the time of Edward III, but the reign was nevertheless central to its development.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarriss200666-138) During this period, membership in the English [baronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron "Baron"), formerly a somewhat indistinct group, became restricted to those who received a personal [summons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereditary_peer#Writs_of_summons "Hereditary peer") to Parliament.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959186%E2%80%93187-139) This happened as Parliament gradually developed into a [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameral "Bicameral") institution, composed of a House of Lords and a House of Commons.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarriss200667-140) Yet it was not in the Lords, but in the Commons that the greatest changes took place, with the expanding political role of the Commons. Informative is the [Good Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Parliament "Good Parliament"), where the Commons for the first time – albeit with noble support – were responsible for precipitating a political crisis.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005288-141) In the process, both the procedure of [impeachment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impeachment_in_the_United_Kingdom "Impeachment in the United Kingdom") and the office of the [Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Speakers_of_the_House_of_Commons_of_England "List of Speakers of the House of Commons of England") were created.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFritzeRobison2002409-142) Even though the political gains were of only temporary duration, this parliament represented a watershed in English political history.

The political influence of the Commons originally lay in their right to grant taxes.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200052-143) The financial demands of the Hundred Years' War were enormous, and the King and his ministers tried different methods of covering the expenses. Edward had a steady income from [crown lands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_lands "Crown lands"), and could also take up substantial loans from Italian and domestic financiers.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown198980%E2%80%9384-144) To finance warfare, he had to resort to taxation of his subjects. Taxation took two primary forms: levy and customs. The levy was a grant of a proportion of all moveable property, normally a tenth for towns and a fifteenth for farmland. This could produce large sums of money, but each such levy had to be approved by Parliament, and the king had to prove the necessity.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown198970%E2%80%9371-145) The customs therefore provided a welcome supplement, as a steady and reliable source of income. An "ancient duty" on the export of wool had existed since 1275. [Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I "Edward I") had tried to introduce an additional duty on wool, but this unpopular _[maltolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maltolt "Maltolt")_, or "unjust exaction", was soon abandoned.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarriss197557,_69-146) Then, from 1336 onwards, a series of schemes aimed at increasing royal revenues from wool export were introduced. After some initial problems and discontent, it was agreed through the [Statute of the Staple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_the_Staple "Statute of the Staple") of 1353 that the new customs should be approved by Parliament, though in reality, they became permanent.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown198967%E2%80%9369,_226%E2%80%93228-147)

Through the steady taxation of Edward III's reign, Parliament – and in particular the Commons – gained political influence. A consensus emerged that in order for a tax to be just, the King had to prove its necessity, it had to be granted by the community of the realm, and it had to be to the benefit of that community.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarriss1975509-148) In addition to imposing taxes, Parliament would also present [petitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petition "Petition") for redress of grievances to the King, most often concerning misgovernment by royal officials.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005282%E2%80%93283-149) This way the system was beneficial for both parties. Through this process, the Commons, and the community they represented, became increasingly politically aware, and the foundation was laid for the particular English brand of constitutional monarchy.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarriss1975509%E2%80%93517-150) It became the norm for the king's ministers to argue his case before Parliament, the Commons to grant the king the tax he requested, and then the king's concessions to Parliament would be announced at its end.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaddicott2010108,_188-151)

The King occasionally attempted to avoid resorting to Parliament to raise taxes, such as in 1338 when he attempted a forced loan on wool. This soon collapsed – in the words of [E. B. Fryde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._B._Fryde "E. B. Fryde") it was a "lamentable failure"[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFryde1983260%E2%80%93261-152) – and once again, Edward had to return to Parliament. Edward also attempted to reinforce what he believed to be his ancient rights, such as the return of all [goods and chattels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_property "Personal property") of [felons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felons "Felons") to the Crown, and [scutage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scutage "Scutage"), as well as new proposals, such as that debts should be repaid to the Crown in one payment rather than incrementally. All these schemes collapsed, however, the latter because the lords claimed that such a method of taxation infringed upon their traditional rights.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFryde1983260%E2%80%93261-152) According to Fryde, "one of Edward's most onerous and wasteful liabilities" came in February 1339, when he effectively [pawned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pawned "Pawned") the [Great Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Jewels_of_the_United_Kingdom "Crown Jewels of the United Kingdom") of England to the [Archbishop of Trier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Trier "Archbishop of Trier"), for which the King promised repayment of £16,650.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFryde19831164%E2%80%931165-153) Edward met his creditors in [Ghent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghent "Ghent") in 1340, but, unable to immediately satisfy their demands, notes Bertie Wilkinson, "pretending that he wanted to take a walk, he secretly rode away".[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilkinson1995134-154)

### Chivalry and national identity

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_III_of_England&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Chivalry and national identity")\]

Furthermore, Edward bolstered the sense of community within this group by the creation of a new [order of chivalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_chivalry "Order of chivalry").[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt_George's_Windsor2023-155) In January 1344 a great feast was held in [Windsor Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor_Castle "Windsor Castle") to which large numbers were invited; not just the lords but the City of London also sent a contingent. The first night saw a feast at which all the attending ladies, with only two knights among them, dined, while the other men ate in their tents. This was followed by jousting over the next three days, where Edward – "not because of his kingly rank but because of his great exertions",[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarber200738-156) [Adam Murimuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Murimuth "Adam Murimuth") claims in his chronicle – was deemed champion. This was followed by the King's announcement of the founding of the [Round Table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_Table "Round Table") of [King Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Arthur "King Arthur"), to which "certain lords" took an oath. The first meeting of the new chapter was arranged for the following [Whitsun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitsun "Whitsun").[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarber200738%E2%80%9339-157)[\[p\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-159) Nothing, however, was to come of the project; as Murimuth comments, "this work was later stopped for various reasons".[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarber200739-160)

Instead, around four years later, Edward founded the [Order of the Garter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Garter "Order of the Garter"), probably in 1348.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt_George's_Windsor2023-155) The new order carried connotations from the legend by the circular shape of the garter.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck1985133-161) Edward's wartime experiences during the Crécy campaign (1346–7) seem to have been a determining factor in his abandonment of the Round Table project. It has been argued that the total warfare tactics employed by the English at [Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") in 1346 were contrary to Arthurian ideals and made Arthur a problematic paradigm for Edward, especially at the time of the institution of the Garter.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerard20122%E2%80%933-162) There are no formal references to King Arthur and the Round Table in the surviving early fifteenth century copies of the Statutes of the Garter, but the Garter Feast of 1358 did involve a round table game. Thus, there was some overlap between the projected Round Table fellowship and the actualized Order of the Garter.[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerard201689-163) [Polydore Vergil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydore_Vergil "Polydore Vergil") tells of how the young [Joan of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Kent "Joan of Kent") – allegedly the King's favourite at the time – accidentally dropped her [garter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garter "Garter") at a ball at Calais. Edward responded to the ensuing ridicule of the crowd by tying the garter around his own knee with the words _[honi soit qui mal y pense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honi_soit_qui_mal_y_pense "Honi soit qui mal y pense")_ (shame on him who thinks ill of it).[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959251%E2%80%93252-164)

This reinforcement of the [aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocracy "Aristocracy") and the emerging sense of an English national identity must be seen in conjunction with the war in France.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2000114-165) Just as the war with Scotland had done, the fear of a French invasion helped strengthen a sense of national unity and nationalise the aristocracy that had been largely Anglo-Norman since the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest"). Since the time of Edward I, popular myth suggested that the French planned to extinguish the English language, and as his grandfather had done, Edward III made the most of this scare.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005209%E2%80%93210-166) As a result, the English language experienced a strong revival during Edward III's reign; in 1362, a [Statute of Pleading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Pleading "Statute of Pleading") ordered English to be used in law courts,[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDodd201923-167)[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDudley2017270-168) and the year after, Parliament was for the first time opened in English.[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959524-169) At the same time, the vernacular saw a revival as a literary language, through the works of [William Langland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langland "William Langland"), [John Gower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gower "John Gower") and especially _[The Canterbury Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Canterbury_Tales "The Canterbury Tales")_ by [Geoffrey Chaucer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Chaucer "Geoffrey Chaucer").[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959526%E2%80%93532-170) Yet the extent of this [Anglicisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicisation "Anglicisation") must not be exaggerated. The statute of 1362 was in fact written in the French language and had little immediate effect, and Parliament was opened in that language as late as 1377.[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005556-171) The Order of the Garter, though a distinctly English institution, included also foreign members such as [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), and [Robert of Namur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_of_Namur_/(1323%E2%80%931391/) "Robert of Namur (1323–1391)").[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959253-172)[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005554-173)
