### Further campaigns in France and governance

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_III_of_England&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Further campaigns in France and governance")\]

While Edward's early reign had been energetic and successful, his later years were marked by inertia, military failure and political strife. The day-to-day affairs of the state had less appeal to Edward than military campaigning, so during the 1360s Edward increasingly relied on the help of his subordinates, in particular [William Wykeham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wykeham "William Wykeham").[\[q\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-174) A relative upstart, Wykeham was made [Keeper of the Privy Seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Privy_Seal "Lord Privy Seal") in 1363 and [Chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Chancellor "Lord Chancellor") in 1367, though due to political difficulties connected with his inexperience, the Parliament forced him to resign the chancellorship in 1371.[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200088%E2%80%9390-175) Compounding Edward's difficulties were the deaths of his most trusted men, some from the 1361–62 recurrence of the plague. [William Montagu, 1st Earl of Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Salisbury "William Montagu, 1st Earl of Salisbury"), Edward's companion in the 1330 coup, died as early as 1344. [William de Clinton, 1st Earl of Huntingdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Clinton,_1st_Earl_of_Huntingdon "William de Clinton, 1st Earl of Huntingdon"), who had also been with Edward at [Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottingham "Nottingham"), died in 1354. One of the earls created in 1337, [William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton"), died in 1360, and the next year [Henry of Grosmont, Duke of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Grosmont,_Duke_of_Lancaster "Henry of Grosmont, Duke of Lancaster"), perhaps the greatest of Edward's captains, succumbed to what was probably plague.[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler1969217%E2%80%93218-176) Their deaths left the majority of the magnates younger and more naturally aligned to the princes than to the King himself.[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2000127%E2%80%93128-177)

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Edward_III_Black_Prince_14thc.jpg/250px-Edward_III_Black_Prince_14thc.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_III_Black_Prince_14thc.jpg)

King Edward III grants Aquitaine to his son Edward the Black Prince. Initial letter "E" of miniature, 1390; [British Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Library "British Library"), London, [shelfmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelfmark "Shelfmark"): Cotton MS Nero D VI, f.31.

Increasingly, Edward began to rely on his sons for the leadership of military operations. The king's second son, [Lionel of Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_of_Antwerp "Lionel of Antwerp"), attempted to subdue by force the largely autonomous [Anglo-Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normans_in_Ireland "Normans in Ireland") lords in [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland"). The venture failed, and the only lasting mark he left was the suppressive [Statutes of Kilkenny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statutes_of_Kilkenny "Statutes of Kilkenny") in 1366.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959231-178) In France, meanwhile, the decade following the [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny") was one of relative tranquillity, but on 8 April 1364, John II died in captivity in England, after unsuccessfully trying to raise his own ransom at home.[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck198513-179) He was followed by the vigorous [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France"), who enlisted the help of the capable [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin"), [Constable of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constable_of_France "Constable of France")[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200035-180) In 1369, the French war started anew, and Edward's son [John of Gaunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Gaunt "John of Gaunt") was given the responsibility of a military campaign. The effort failed, and with the [Treaty of Bruges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Bruges_/(1375/) "Treaty of Bruges (1375)") in 1375, the great English possessions in France were reduced to only the coastal towns of [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais"), [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux "Bordeaux"), and [Bayonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayonne "Bayonne").[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959145-181)

[Alice Perrers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Perrers "Alice Perrers") was originally one of Philippa's household ladies, having been appointed by 1359.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2006223-182) Within five years, by which time she would have been 18, and after the death of her husband, she is speculated to have become the lover of the elderly King. She maintained an active business life outside her career in the royal household, particularly as a [moneylender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moneylender "Moneylender"), while also making the most out of her royal connections, accepted gifts from courtiers and those wishing to further their causes with the King. Edward presented her with gifts, including land, manors and jewels, and in 1371 these included those of the now-dead Philippa. Alice, in what may have been an attempt to keep her new estates after the King's death, tied them up in a series of [enfeoffments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feoffment "Feoffment"). This meant that legally they ceased to be royal gifts which could be [resumed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain#United_Kingdom "Eminent domain") to the Crown, but hers to receive from her feoffees when she chose.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiven-Wilson2004-183) These gifts included 50 manors in 25 counties and £20,000 in jewels.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell199831-184) The contemporary chronicler [Thomas Walsingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Walsingham "Thomas Walsingham") saw her as a low-born woman who, through her own ambition, made a fortune from the besotted King;[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2006225-185) and this was the popular view presented to the [Good Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Parliament "Good Parliament") of 1376, in which she was also accused of taking 2000 to 3000 [pounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avoirdupois "Avoirdupois") in gold and silver per annum from the [royal treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_treasury "Royal treasury").[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell199831-184) Another contemporary, the [Anonimalle Chronicler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Mary%27s_Abbey,_York "St Mary's Abbey, York"), complained that this was all "without any notable profit and in great damage to our lord the king",[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell199832-186) and urged that Alice be removed from the King's circle even though he was still living, albeit known to be dying.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell199832-186) Modern historians have credited her with more agency than merely using "womanly wiles" to get her own way, noting her head for business and the law.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell199833-187) Bothwell also notes that she probably recognised the future precariousness of her position after the King died – "which it was obvious to all in the 1370s was imminent"[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell199834-188) – and intended to use much of her wealth to provide for her two daughters, whose lives would be even more precarious in the following reign.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBothwell199835%E2%80%9336-189) She was correct in this expectation. Edward could not prevent her [banishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banishment "Banishment") during the Good Parliament, though she had returned to his inner circle later that year and remained there until his death. However, in 1378 (first year of [Richard II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_II "Richard II")'s reign) she was put on trial before Parliament. She was found guilty and sentenced to exile. Further, her property was forfeited to the Crown.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2008-190)

Military failure abroad, and the associated fiscal pressure of constant campaigns, led to political discontent in England.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolmes197566-191) Finance was a particular grievance; although it was rarely raised as an issue before 1371, after that time complaints about the royal household's expenditure were frequent.[\[r\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-193) The problems came to a head in the Parliament of 1376, the so-called [Good Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Parliament "Good Parliament"). The Parliament was called to grant taxation, but the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_England "House of Commons of England") took the opportunity to address specific grievances. In particular, criticism was directed at some of the King's closest advisors. [Lord Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Chamberlain "Lord Chamberlain") [William Latimer, 4th Baron Latimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Latimer,_4th_Baron_Latimer "William Latimer, 4th Baron Latimer"), and [Steward of the Household](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Steward "Lord Steward") [John Neville, 3rd Baron Neville de Raby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Neville,_3rd_Baron_Neville_de_Raby "John Neville, 3rd Baron Neville de Raby"), were dismissed from their positions.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolmes197566-191) Edward III's mistress, Alice Perrers, who was seen to hold far too much power over the ageing king, was banished from court.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200041,_43-194)[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959387%E2%80%93394-195)

Yet the real adversary of the Commons, supported by powerful men such as Wykeham and [Edmund Mortimer, 3rd Earl of March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Mortimer,_3rd_Earl_of_March "Edmund Mortimer, 3rd Earl of March"), was [John of Gaunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Gaunt "John of Gaunt"). Both the King and Edward of Woodstock were by this time incapacitated by illness, leaving Gaunt in virtual control of government.[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarriss2006440-196) Gaunt was forced to give in to the demands of Parliament, but at its [next convocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Parliament "Bad Parliament") in 1377, most of the achievements of the Good Parliament were reversed[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood1930623%E2%80%93625-197) and a [poll tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Poll_Tax "First Poll Tax") was instituted to pay for the war.

### Death and succession

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_III_of_England&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Death and succession")\]

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Edward-III-king-England.jpg/250px-Edward-III-king-England.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward-III-king-England.jpg)

Edward III's funerary monument in [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey")

Edward III did not have much to do with any of this; after around 1375 he played a limited role in the government of the realm. Around 29 September 1376, he fell ill with a large [abscess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abscess "Abscess"). After a brief period of recovery in February 1377, the King died of a stroke at Sheen on 21 June.[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200045-198)

Edward III was succeeded by his ten-year-old grandson, [King Richard II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Richard_II "King Richard II"), son of Edward of Woodstock, since Woodstock himself had died on 8 June 1376.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959392,_397-199) In 1376, Edward had signed [letters patent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letters_patent "Letters patent") on the order of succession to the crown, citing in second position his third son John of Gaunt, but ignoring [Philippa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa,_5th_Countess_of_Ulster "Philippa, 5th Countess of Ulster"), daughter of his second son [Lionel of Antwerp, Duke of Clarence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_of_Antwerp,_Duke_of_Clarence "Lionel of Antwerp, Duke of Clarence"). Philippa's exclusion contrasted with a decision by Edward I in 1290, which had recognized the right of women to inherit the crown and to pass it on to their descendants.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett1998585,_587-200) The order of succession determined in 1376 led the [House of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lancaster "House of Lancaster") to the throne in 1399 (Gaunt was [Duke of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Lancaster "Duke of Lancaster")), whereas the rule decided by Edward I would have favoured Philippa's descendants, among them the [House of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_York "House of York"), beginning with [Richard of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_of_York "Richard of York"), her great-grandson.[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett1998601%E2%80%93603-201) The large number of cousins that were created is sometimes argued to have laid the foundations for the [Wars of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses "Wars of the Roses") in the fifteenth century.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman2015568-202)

Edward III and his wife Philippa had seven sons and five daughters[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2022267%E2%80%93272-203) born over a 25-year period.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrme200352-204) This was considered a success by contemporaries and a sign of God's favour.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987398-205) Edward understood the importance of a "strong and united royal family", argues Ormrod.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987401-206) It allowed him, through their marriages, to make alliances within his own aristocracy and also with continental dynasties. However, the latter policy gradually fell apart with the gradual loss of England's European possessions towards the end of the century.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987400-60) For example, he organised the marriage of his sister [Eleanor of Woodstock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_of_Woodstock "Eleanor of Woodstock") to the [Count of Guelders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reginald_II,_Duke_of_Guelders "Reginald II, Duke of Guelders") as part of a [pro-Netherlandish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminology_of_the_Low_Countries "Terminology of the Low Countries"), anti-French policy in 1332. Yet when the coalition collapsed in 1340, the fact that he had only lost her in that particular marriage market was a positive.[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987402%E2%80%93404-207) From around this time, says Ormrod, "the Hundred Years' War became a family enterprise":[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987408-208) [Edward the Black Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_the_Black_Prince "Edward the Black Prince") commanded a force at Crécy, and ten years later his younger brothers Lionel, John and Edmund had joined the war.[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987408-208) However, while his sons were fighting in France, they could not be procreating the royal line; by 1358, only Lionel had married and provided Edward with a grandchild.[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987408%E2%80%93409-209) By the mid-1360s his family had furthered his continental policy, both diplomatically and militarily, sufficiently that he allowed his son Edward and his daughter [Isabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella,_Countess_of_Bedford "Isabella, Countess of Bedford") to do that rarest of things in the Middle Ages: marry for love. Neither the former's match with [Joan of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Kent "Joan of Kent") and the latter's to [Enguerrand VII de Coucy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enguerrand_VII_de_Coucy "Enguerrand VII de Coucy"), were particularly advantageous to the King; the first was a clandestine marriage, while de Courcy was a French hostage.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarber2013309,_314-210) Ormrod concludes that, by 1376:

> Edward III's greatest misfortune was that he lived long enough to witness the complete collapse of \[his\] elaborate dynastic plan. By 1377, the king's family had been depleted, his territories reduced, his diplomacy wrecked, and his own control of affairs nullified.[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987416-211)

A fourth son, Thomas of Windsor, is also sometimes posited as being born in 1347 and dying the following year. However, the historian [Kathryn Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathryn_Warner "Kathryn Warner") has suggested that, as William of Woodstock was also born and died the same year, and combined with the paucity of material evidence, it is likely that this Thomas is a composite. She argues that "the entire existence of 'Thomas of Windsor' in some modern books and websites appears to be based on the spurious story by two chroniclers that Philippa was heavily pregnant when she interceded for the Calais burghers in early August 1347".[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2022267%E2%80%93272-203) She also notes that for William, who also died young, there is much evidence for his existence, including "his funeral or tomb, or for the queen's purification after his birth, or for any kind of celebration held to mark the birth of another royal child".[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2022267%E2%80%93272-203) The [medievalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medievalist "Medievalist") [Nicholas Orme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Orme "Nicholas Orme") has noted that medieval chroniclers were particularly accurate when it came to recording royal births.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrme200352-204)

The [geneticist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneticist "Geneticist") [Adam Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Rutherford "Adam Rutherford") has calculated Edward had over 300 great-great-grandchildren and, therefore, over 20,000 descendants by 1600. Thus, by the 21st century, it is "virtually impossible" that a person with a predominantly British ancestry is not descended from Edward III, as they would have around 32,000 ancestors from 1600.[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERudgard2017-212)[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERutherford202084%E2%80%9385_+n-213) Conversely, Rutherford has calculated that statistically, the odds on a 20th-century British person not being descended from Edward III is 0.99532,768 = 4.64 × 10−72.[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERutherford202085_n-214)[\[s\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-215)

*   [Edward the Black Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_the_Black_Prince "Edward the Black Prince") (1330–1376), eldest son and [heir apparent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heir_apparent "Heir apparent"), born at [Woodstock Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodstock_Palace "Woodstock Palace"), Oxfordshire. He predeceased his father, having in 1361 married his cousin [Joan, Countess of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan,_Countess_of_Kent "Joan, Countess of Kent"), by whom he had issue: King [Richard II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Richard_II_of_England "King Richard II of England");[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarber2004b-216)
*   [Isabella of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella,_Countess_of_Bedford "Isabella, Countess of Bedford") (1332 – c. 1382), born at [Woodstock Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodstock_Palace "Woodstock Palace"), Oxfordshire, in 1365 married [Enguerrand VII de Coucy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enguerrand_VII_de_Coucy "Enguerrand VII de Coucy"), 1st [Earl of Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Bedford "Earl of Bedford"),[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2000110,_248-217) by whom she had issue;
*   [Joan of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_England_/(died_1348/) "Joan of England (died 1348)") (1333/4 – 1348), born in the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London"); she was betrothed to [Peter of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile") but died of the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") en route to Castile before the marriage could take place. Peter's two daughters from his union with [María de Padilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_de_Padilla "María de Padilla") married Joan's younger brothers John of Gaunt and Edmund of Langley;
*   William of Hatfield (1337–1337), second son, born at [Hatfield Manor House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatfield_Manor_House "Hatfield Manor House"), [Hatfield, South Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatfield,_South_Yorkshire "Hatfield, South Yorkshire"), died shortly after birth and was buried in York Minster;[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarner2022267%E2%80%93272-203)
*   [Lionel of Antwerp, 1st Duke of Clarence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_of_Antwerp,_1st_Duke_of_Clarence "Lionel of Antwerp, 1st Duke of Clarence") (1338–1368), third son (second surviving son), born at [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp") in the [Duchy of Brabant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brabant "Duchy of Brabant"), where his father was based.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2004b-218) In 1352 he married firstly [Elizabeth de Burgh, 4th Countess of Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_de_Burgh,_4th_Countess_of_Ulster "Elizabeth de Burgh, 4th Countess of Ulster"), without male issue, but his female issue was the senior royal ancestor of the Yorkist king Edward IV: [Philippa, 5th Countess of Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa,_5th_Countess_of_Ulster "Philippa, 5th Countess of Ulster"). Descent from Lionel was the basis of the Yorkist claim to the throne, not direct paternal descent from the 1st Duke of York, a more junior line. Secondly, in 1368, Lionel married [Violante Visconti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violante_Visconti "Violante Visconti"), without issue;[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWyatt2023179-219)
*   [John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Gaunt,_Duke_of_Lancaster "John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster") (1340–1399), Edward's third surviving son,[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiven-Wilson199643-220) was born at "Gaunt" ([Ghent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghent "Ghent")) in the [County of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Flanders "County of Flanders"), which city was an important buyer of English wool, then the foundation of English prosperity.[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman19922,_28%E2%80%9329-221) In 1359, he married firstly his third cousin, the great heiress [Blanche of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_of_Lancaster "Blanche of Lancaster"), descended from the 1st Earl of Lancaster, a younger son of King Henry III.[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman199233%E2%80%9334-222) By Blanche he had issue: Henry of Bolingbroke, who became King [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_England "Henry IV of England"), having seized the throne from his first cousin King Richard II.[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBevan199466-223)[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman199213%E2%80%9314-224) In 1371, he married secondly the [Infanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infanta "Infanta") [Constance of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constance_of_Castile,_Duchess_of_Lancaster "Constance of Castile, Duchess of Lancaster"),[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman199248-225) by whom he had issue. In 1396, he married thirdly, his mistress [Katherine Swynford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katherine_Swynford "Katherine Swynford"),[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman199250,_156-226) by whom he had illegitimate issue, later legitimised as the [House of Beaufort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Beaufort "House of Beaufort");[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodman1992157,_159-227)
*   [Edmund of Langley, 1st Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_of_Langley,_1st_Duke_of_York "Edmund of Langley, 1st Duke of York") (1341–1402), fifth son (fourth surviving son), born at [Kings Langley Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_Langley_Palace "Kings Langley Palace"), Hertfordshire. He married firstly [Isabella of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_Castile,_Duchess_of_York "Isabella of Castile, Duchess of York"), by whom he had issue, sister of [Constance of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constance_of_Castile,_Duchess_of_Lancaster "Constance of Castile, Duchess of Lancaster"), second wife of his elder brother John of Gaunt, 1st Duke of Lancaster. Secondly, in 1392 he married his second cousin [Joan Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Holland "Joan Holland"), without issue.[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck2004-228) His great-grandson (the 4th Duke of York) became King [Edward IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_IV_of_England "Edward IV of England") in 1461, having deposed his half-second cousin the Lancastrian King Henry VI;[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoss19743%E2%80%937-229)
*   Blanche (1342–1342), born in the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London"), died shortly after birth and was buried in Westminster Abbey;

Mark Ormrod has noted that in this period, politics was often dictated by the personality and character of the king. However, it was also understood that not only should a king rule well and wisely, but that he should be seen to do so. Ormrod argues that, while he did not begin his reign with these skills, unlike many of his fellow Plantagenet kings, he acquired them. His collection of chronicles indicates an interest in history, even to the extent that, on occasion, he consulted their authors.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200047-44)[\[t\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-239) He may have been particularly keen to emulate [Henry II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_II_of_England "Henry II of England") and [Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I "Edward I"), whose own martial prowess and success would have resonated with him.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200048-240) His tastes were conventional, Ormrod says,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200047-44) and J. R. Lander also has argued that this is reflected in his hobbies. Unlike his father's passion for manual work, including carpentry, thatching and rowing, Edward III "shared to the full the conventional tastes and pleasure of the aristocracy",[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTELander1973151-241) with his principal interest being architecture.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200048-240)[\[u\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-242) This conservativism is reflected in his religious views, which, expressed as they were through the patronage of [friaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friaries "Friaries") and visiting of [shrines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrine "Shrine"), demonstrate a conventional religion.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200048-240) This is also reflected in his [almsgiving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almsgiving "Almsgiving"). While ancestors such as Henry III had often been haphazard and exuberant in the amounts they gave and when they did so, Edward III maintained a regular 366 meals a week to be provided for the poor with another £25 to be distributed during the four main feasts.[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiven-Wilson198669-243)[\[v\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-244) However, alongside his conventionality ran a populist streak, and Ormrod has described him as a "natural showman", particularly in his alacrity to heal those suffering from [scrofula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrofula "Scrofula") by his [royal touch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_touch "Royal touch").[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200048-240)[\[w\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-247) In less than two years, between 1338 and 1340, he touched for scrofula in both England and while campaigning in France;[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrogan201537-248) another 355 occurred between November 1340 and the same month the following year.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200048-240) He was generous to the point of extravagance.[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiven-Wilson1986132-249) In an alternative view, [Norman Cantor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Cantor "Norman Cantor") has described Edward as an "avaricious and sadistic thug".[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTECantor200233-250)

From what is known of Edward's character, he could be impulsive and temperamental, as was seen by his actions against Stratford and the ministers in 1340/41.[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005289-251) Other escapades were not just impulsive but dangerous, such as in 1349, when he sailed to Calais with only a small bodyguard.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200048-240) At the same time, he was well known for his clemency; Mortimer's [grandson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_de_Mortimer,_2nd_Earl_of_March "Roger de Mortimer, 2nd Earl of March") was not only absolved, he came to play an important part in the French wars and was eventually made a Knight of the Garter.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack1959255-252) His favourite pursuit was the art of war and, in this, he conformed to the medieval notion of good kingship.[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod20009%E2%80%9310-253)[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005290%E2%80%93291-254) As a warrior he was so successful that one modern military historian has described him as the greatest general in English history.[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200234%E2%80%9345-255) He seems to have been unusually devoted to Queen Philippa. Much has been made of Edward's sexual licentiousness, but there is no evidence of any infidelity on his part before [Alice Perrers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Perrers "Alice Perrers") became his lover, and by that time the Queen was already terminally ill.[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2006400%E2%80%93401-256)[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980241-257) This devotion extended to the rest of the family as well; in contrast to many of his predecessors, Edward never experienced opposition from any of his five adult sons.[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2005290-258)

[![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/King_Edward_III_from_NPG.jpg/250px-King_Edward_III_from_NPG.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Edward_III_from_NPG.jpg)

Edward III as he was depicted in the late 16th century

Edward III, argues the scholar Michael A.R. Graves, left a "dual legacy". These were the large brood of children and grandchildren he left, and his claim to the French throne. In the first instance, his endowment of his sons as Dukes of Clarence, Lancaster and York allowed them to create their own dynasties which were both part of the royal family and the aristocracy, which, following [Henry Bolingbroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Bolingbroke "Henry Bolingbroke")'s usurpation of Edward's grandson, Richard II, "bedevilled" the [Lancastrian dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lancaster "House of Lancaster").[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraves20137-259) Secondly, while the resumption of Edward's claims and war in France was initially successful—contemporaries compared [Henry V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England")'s decisive victory at [Agincourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt "Battle of Agincourt") with Edward's at Crécy and Poitiers—when the tide turned against the English in France, the dynasty was also weakened.[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraves20137-259) Indeed, war in France was problematic for the [House of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_York "House of York") as well as Lancaster. [Edward IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_IV "Edward IV") was probably consciously following in his namesake's footsteps when he invaded France in 1475, even if the subsequent [Treaty of Picquigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Picquigny "Treaty of Picquigny") was wholly unintended.[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarpenter1997197-260) Edward IV's reign looked back on that of Edward III – with its martial and administrative progress – as something to model their own on, argues Morgan. Edward IV's own _Household Books_, summarise the approach as "we take to bylde upon a more perfit new house", and indeed many of their grants and warrants contain a final clause that whatever was under discussion should be as they were in Edward III's final year. Even the final destruction of the [Plantagenets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Plantagenet "House of Plantagenet") at [Bosworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bosworth "Battle of Bosworth") in 1485 failed to impinge on Edward III's posthumous image; he was also the most recent king [Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England") could lay claim of descent from.[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorgan1997869-261)

Edward III enjoyed unprecedented popularity in his own lifetime, and even the troubles of his later reign were never blamed directly on the King himself.[\[239\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200046,_88%E2%80%9389-262) His contemporary [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart") wrote in his _[Chronicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Froissart%27s_Chronicles "Froissart's Chronicles")_: "His like had not been seen since the days of King Arthur."[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200045-198) D. A. L. Morgan has drawn attention to the continuing popularity of Edward into the next century, observing that "by 1500 Edward III was well into his stride as the greatest King ever to have ruled England", quoting _The Great Chronicle of London_ on [Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England"), who if not for his [avarice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avarice "Avarice"), "mygth have been pereless of alle princis that regnyd ovyr England syne the tyme of Edwardthe thyrd".[\[240\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorgan1997858-263) This view persisted for a while but, with time, Edward's image changed. The [Whig historians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_historians "Whig historians") of a later age preferred constitutional reform to foreign conquest and accused Edward of ignoring his responsibilities to his own nation. [Bishop Stubbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_Stubbs "Bishop Stubbs"), in his _The Constitutional History of England_, states:

> Edward III was not a statesman, though he possessed some qualifications which might have made him a successful one. He was a warrior; ambitious, unscrupulous, selfish, extravagant and ostentatious. His obligations as a king sat very lightly on him. He felt himself bound by no special duty, either to maintain the theory of royal supremacy or to follow a policy which would benefit his people. Like [Richard I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_I "Richard I"), he valued England primarily as a source of supplies.[\[241\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStubbs1887393%E2%80%93394-264)

This view has been challenged through most of the 20th century, and Ormrod has observed that "no modern reader could seriously accept all these compliments at face value",[\[242\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200010-265) although also that in their efforts to counter the prevailing [hagiography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagiography "Hagiography"), early 20th-century historians were more critical:

> Edward III is now often seen as a rather second-rate ruler, stubborn and selfish in his foreign ambitions, weak and yielding in his domestic policies. He lacked the forcefulness of Henry II, the statesmanship of Edward I, the charisma of Henry V, or the application of Henry VII. He was prepared to accept short-term compromises and to ignore the wider implications Of his actions.[\[242\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200010-265)

Later scholarship, suggests Ormrod, "tended to be rather kinder".[\[243\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2004a-266) In a 1960 article, [May McKisack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_McKisack "May McKisack") points out the [teleological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teleology "Teleology") nature of Stubbs' judgement. A medieval king could not be expected to work towards some future ideal of a parliamentary monarchy as if it were good in itself; rather, his role was a pragmatic one – to maintain order and solve problems as they arose. At this, Edward excelled.[\[244\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKisack19604%E2%80%935-267) Edward had also been accused of endowing his younger sons too liberally and thereby promoting dynastic strife culminating in the [Wars of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses "Wars of the Roses"). This claim was rejected by [K. B. McFarlane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K._B._McFarlane "K. B. McFarlane"), who argued that this was not only the common policy of the age, but also the best.[\[245\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFarlane1981238-268) Later biographers of Edward such as Mark Ormrod and [Ian Mortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Mortimer_/(historian/) "Ian Mortimer (historian)") have followed this historiographical trend. The older negative view has not completely disappeared; Cantor has argued that Edward was a "destructive and merciless force".[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTECantor200233-250) Ormrod argues that in overturning the Stubbsian paradigm, historians may have gone too far in the opposite direction, not taking into account the problems he had to solve and the number of different factions he had to accommodate to get things done.[\[242\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod200010-265) [Chris Given-Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Given-Wilson "Chris Given-Wilson") and Michael Prestwich, in their introduction to the proceedings of the 1999 [Centre for Medieval Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Medieval_Studies "Centre for Medieval Studies") conference at the [University of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_York "University of York"), summarise modern consensus as being, effectively, that he was, overall, a strong king, a just king and a good warrior and strategist. This, they argue, is the most important point regarding modern scholarship on Edward III: not necessarily to overturn previous consensus, but to look at all aspects of a multi-faceted King and examine how he achieved this success.[\[246\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiven-WilsonPrestwich20011-269) Modern historians are also more distant than contemporaries in their view of the King's fecundity being a sign of success; more often, it is seen as a liability as each mouth had to be paid for, draining limited resources. Further, it may have led to later partisanship between the Crown and its cadet branches.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1987398-205)

Edward's grandson, the young Richard II, faced political and economic problems, many resulting from the Black Death, including the [Peasants' Revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt "Peasants' Revolt") that broke out across the south of England in 1381.[\[247\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERubin2006120%E2%80%93121-270)[\[248\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunn200273-271) Over the coming decades, Richard and groups of nobles vied for power and control of policy towards France until [Henry of Bolingbroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_England "Henry IV of England") seized the throne with the support of Parliament in 1399.[\[249\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERubin2006168%E2%80%93172-272)[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMyers197830%E2%80%9335-273) Ruling as Henry IV, he exercised power through a royal council and Parliament, while attempting to enforce political and religious conformity.[\[251\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERubin2006182%E2%80%93183,_186-274)[\[252\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMyers1978133-275) His son, [Henry V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England"), reinvigorated the war with France and came close to achieving strategic success shortly before his death in 1422.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERubin2006213%E2%80%93214,_220%E2%80%93223-276)[\[254\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMyers1978120%E2%80%93121-277) [Henry VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VI_of_England "Henry VI of England") became king at the age of only nine months and both the English political system and the military situation in France began to unravel.[\[255\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTERubin2006224%E2%80%93227-278)[\[256\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMyers1978122%E2%80%93125-279)

A sequence of bloody civil wars – later termed the [Wars of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses "Wars of the Roses") – erupted in 1455, spurred on by an economic crisis and a widespread perception of poor government.[\[257\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHicks20123%E2%80%938-280) The idea that Edward III was to blame for the later-15th century Wars of the Roses was prevalent as late as the 19th century, but came to be challenged in the 20th.[\[258\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarpenter199720,_32%E2%80%9333-281)[\[259\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollard198812-282)

Top Questions

*   When did Edward III become king of England?
    
*   What was England like during Edward III's reign?
    
*   What important wars or conflicts happened while Edward III was king?
    
*   How did Edward III help start the Hundred Years’ War?
    
*   How did Edward III influence English government and society?
    

**Edward III** (born November 13, 1312, [Windsor](https://www.britannica.com/place/Windsor-England), [Berkshire](https://www.britannica.com/place/Berkshire-county-England), England—died June 21, 1377, [Sheen](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Sheen), Surrey) was the [king](https://www.britannica.com/topic/king-monarch) of [England](https://www.britannica.com/place/England) from 1327 to 1377, who led England into the [Hundred Years’ War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Hundred-Years-War) with France. The descendants of his seven sons and five daughters contested the throne for generations, climaxing in the [Wars of the Roses](https://www.britannica.com/event/Wars-of-the-Roses) (1455–85).

Early years
-----------

The eldest son of [Edward II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-II-king-of-England) and [Isabella of France](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Isabella-of-France), Edward III was summoned to [Parliament](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Parliament) as earl of Chester (1320) and was made [duke](https://www.britannica.com/topic/duke) of Aquitaine (1325), but, contrary to tradition, he never received the title of [prince of Wales](https://www.britannica.com/topic/prince-of-Wales).

Edward III grew up amid struggles between his father and a number of barons who were attempting to limit the king’s power and to strengthen their own role in governing England. His mother, repelled by her husband’s [treatment](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/treatment) of the nobles and disaffected by the confiscation of her English estates by his supporters, played an important role in this conflict. In 1325 she left England to return to France to intervene in the dispute between her brother, [Charles IV](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-IV-king-of-France) of France, and her husband over the latter’s French possessions, [Guyenne](https://www.britannica.com/place/Guyenne), [Gascony](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gascony), and Ponthieu. She was successful; the land was secured for England on condition that the English king pay homage to Charles. This was performed on the king’s behalf by his young son.

The [heir apparent](https://www.britannica.com/topic/heir-apparent) was secure at his mother’s side. With [Roger Mortimer](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Roger-Mortimer-1st-Earl-of-March), an influential [baron](https://www.britannica.com/topic/baron) who had escaped to France in 1323 and had become her lover, Isabella now began preparations to invade England to [depose](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/depose) her husband. To raise funds for this enterprise, Edward III was betrothed to [Philippa](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philippa-of-Hainaut), daughter of William, count of Hainaut and Holland.

Within five months of their invasion of England, the queen and the nobles, who had much popular support, overpowered the king’s forces. Edward II, charged with incompetence and breaking his [coronation](https://www.britannica.com/topic/coronation-ceremony) oath, was forced to resign, and on January 29, 1327, Edward III, aged 14, was crowned king of England.

[![Image 1: Britain's Queen Elizabeth II smiles to the crowd from Buckingham Palace (London, England) balcony at the end of the Platinum Pageant in London on June 5, 2022 as part of Queen Elizabeth II's platinum jubilee celebrations. The curtain comes down on four days of momentous nationwide celebrations to honor Queen Elizabeth II's historic Platinum Jubilee with a day-long pageant lauding the 96 year old monarch's record seven decades on the throne. (British royalty)](https://cdn.britannica.com/06/235406-131-17CB8E3D/Queen-Elizabeth-II-Buckingham-Palace-Platinum-Jubilee-London-England-June-5-2022.jpg) Britannica Quiz Fit for a King (or Queen): the British Royalty Quiz](https://www.britannica.com/quiz/fit-for-a-king-or-queen-the-british-royalty-quiz)During the next four years Isabella and Mortimer governed in his name, though nominally his guardian was [Henry, earl of Lancaster](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Henry-1st-duke-of-Lancaster). In the summer of 1327 he took part in an abortive campaign against the Scots, which resulted in the [Treaty of Northampton](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Treaty-of-Northampton) (1328), making [Scotland](https://www.britannica.com/place/Scotland) an independent realm. Edward was deeply troubled by the settlement and signed it only after much persuasion by Isabella and Mortimer. He married Philippa at York on January 24, 1328. Soon afterward Edward made a successful effort to throw off his degrading dependence on his mother and Mortimer. While a council was being held at Nottingham, he entered the castle by night, through a subterranean passage, took Mortimer prisoner, and had him executed (November 1330). Edward had discreetly ignored his mother’s [liaison](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/liaison) with Mortimer and treated her with every respect, but her political influence was at an end.

Edward III now began to rule as well as to reign. Young, [ardent](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ardent), and active, he sought to remake England into the powerful nation it had been under [Edward I](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-I-king-of-England). He still resented the [concession](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/concession) of independence made to Scotland by the Treaty of Northampton. The death of [Robert I](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Robert-the-Bruce), the Bruce, king of Scotland, in 1329 gave him a chance of retrieving his position. The new king of Scots, his brother-in-law, [David II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/David-II), was a mere boy, and [Edward](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-king-of-Scotland) took advantage of his weakness to aid the Scottish barons who had been exiled by Bruce to place their leader, Edward Balliol, on the Scottish throne. David II fled to France, but Balliol was despised as a puppet of the English king, and David returned in 1341.

During the 1330s England gradually drifted into a state of hostility with [France](https://www.britannica.com/place/France), for which the most obvious reason was the [dispute](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/dispute) over English rule in Gascony. Contributory causes were France’s new king [Philip VI](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-VI)’s support of the Scots, Edward’s alliance with the Flemish cities—then on bad terms with their French overlord—and the revival in 1337 of Edward’s claim, first made in 1328, to the French crown. Edward twice attempted to invade France from the north (1339, 1340), but the only result of his campaigns was to reduce him to bankruptcy. In January 1340 he assumed the title of king of France. At first he may have done this to gratify the Flemings, whose [scruples](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/scruples) in fighting the French king disappeared when they persuaded themselves that Edward was the rightful king of France. But his pretensions to the French crown gradually became more important, and the persistence with which he and his successors urged them made stable peace impossible for more than a century. This was the struggle famous in history as the Hundred Years’ War. Until 1801 every English king also called himself king of France.

Edward was present in person at the great naval battle off the Flemish city of Sluis in June 1340, in which he all but destroyed the French navy. Despite this victory his resources were exhausted by his land campaign, and he was forced to make a truce (which was broken two years later) and return to England. During the years after 1342 he spent much time and money in rebuilding [Windsor Castle](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Windsor-Castle) and instituting the [Order of the Garter](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-Most-Noble-Order-of-the-Garter), which became Britain’s highest order of knighthood. A new phase of the French war began when Edward landed in [Normandy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Normandy) in July 1346, accompanied by his eldest son, [Prince Edward](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-the-Black-Prince), later known as the Black Prince (born 1330). At first the king showed some lack of strategic purpose, engaging in little more than a large-scale [plundering](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/plundering) raid to the gates of Paris. The campaign was made memorable by his decisive [victory over the French at Crécy](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Crecy) in Ponthieu (August 26), where he scattered the army with which Philip VI sought to cut off his retreat to the northeast. Edward laid siege to the French port of [Calais](https://www.britannica.com/place/Calais-France) in September 1346 and received its surrender in August 1347. Other victories in Gascony and [Brittany](https://www.britannica.com/place/Brittany-region-France), and the defeat and capture of David II at [Neville’s Cross](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Nevilles-Cross) near [Durham](https://www.britannica.com/place/Durham-England) (October 1346), gave further proof of Edward’s power, but Calais was to be his only lasting conquest. He ejected most of its French inhabitants, colonizing the town with Englishmen and establishing there a base from which to conduct further invasions of France. Nevertheless, in the midst of his successes, want of money forced him to make a new truce in September 1347.

Quick Facts

Byname:

Edward of Windsor

Died:

June 21, 1377, Sheen, Surrey (aged 64)

Edward returned to England in October 1347. He celebrated his [triumph](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/triumph) by a series of splendid tournaments. In 1348 he rejected an offer to become [Holy Roman](https://www.britannica.com/place/Holy-Roman-Empire) emperor. In the same year the [bubonic plague](https://www.britannica.com/science/bubonic-plague) known as the [Black Death](https://www.britannica.com/event/Black-Death) first appeared in England and raged until the end of 1349. Its horrors hardly checked the magnificent revels of Edward’s court, and neither the plague nor the truce stayed the slow course of the French war, though the fighting was indecisive and on a small scale. Edward’s martial exploits during the next years were those of a gallant knight rather than of a responsible general. Although the English [House of Commons](https://www.britannica.com/topic/House-of-Commons-British-government) was now weary of the war, efforts to make peace came to nothing, and large-scale operations began again in 1355, when Edward led an unsuccessful raid out of Calais. He harried the Lothians, part of southeastern Scotland, in the expedition famous as the Burned Candlemas (January and February 1356), and in the same year he received a formal surrender of the kingdom of Scotland from Balliol. His exploits were, however, eclipsed by those of his son Edward, whose [victory at Poitiers](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Poitiers-French-history-1356) (September 19, 1356), resulting in the capture of the French king, [John II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-II-king-of-France) (who had succeeded Philip VI in 1350), forced the French to accept a new truce. Edward entertained his captive magnificently but forced him by the [Treaty of London](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Treaties-of-London) (1359) to surrender so much territory that the agreement was [repudiated](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/repudiated) in France. In an effort to compel acceptance, Edward landed at Calais (October 28) and besieged [Reims](https://www.britannica.com/place/Reims), where he planned to be crowned king of France. The strenuous resistance of the citizens frustrated this scheme, and Edward marched into [Burgundy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Burgundy), eventually returning toward Paris. After this unsuccessful campaign, he was glad to conclude preliminaries of peace at Brittany (May 8, 1360). This treaty, less onerous to France than that of [London](https://www.britannica.com/place/London), took its final form in the [Treaty of Calais](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Treaty-of-Calais), ratified by both kings (October 1360). By it Edward [renounced](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/renounced) his claim to the French crown in return for the whole of [Aquitaine](https://www.britannica.com/place/Aquitaine), a rich area in southwestern France.

Introduction to English-language Wikipedia

This is a [general introduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:INFOPAGES "Wikipedia:INFOPAGES") for visitors to Wikipedia. For aspiring contributors, also see this [guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Contributing_to_Wikipedia "Wikipedia:Contributing to Wikipedia") and [tutorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Introduction "Help:Introduction"). For other uses, see [Wikipedia:Wikipedia (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Wikipedia_/(disambiguation/) "Wikipedia:Wikipedia (disambiguation)").

Imagine a world in which every single person on the planet is given free access to the sum of all human knowledge. That's what we're doing. — [Jimmy Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Wales "Jimmy Wales")

**[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia "Wikipedia")** is a [free online encyclopedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Free_encyclopedia "Wikipedia:Free encyclopedia") that anyone can edit, and [millions already have](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Wikipedians#Number_of_editors "Wikipedia:Wikipedians").

[Wikipedia's purpose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Purpose "Wikipedia:Purpose") is to benefit readers by presenting information on all branches of [knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge "Knowledge"). Hosted by the [Wikimedia Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Wikimedia_Foundation "Wikipedia:Wikimedia Foundation"), Wikipedia consists of [freely editable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Editing "Help:Editing") content, with articles that usually contain numerous links guiding readers to more information.

[Written collaboratively](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_writing "Collaborative writing") by volunteers known as [Wikipedians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia_community "Wikipedia community"), Wikipedia articles can be edited by anyone with [Internet access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_access "Internet access"), except in [limited cases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Protection_policy "Wikipedia:Protection policy") in which [editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Editing "Editing") is restricted to prevent [disruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Disruption "Wikipedia:Disruption") or [vandalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:VAND "Wikipedia:VAND"). Since its creation on [January 15, 2001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia_Day "Wikipedia Day"), it has grown into the world's [largest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Size_of_Wikipedia "Wikipedia:Size of Wikipedia") reference [website](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Website "Website"), attracting [over a billion visitors each month](https://stats.wikimedia.org/#/all-wikipedia-projects/reading/unique-devices "stats:"). Wikipedia currently has more than [sixty-six million articles](https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/List_of_Wikipedias#All_Wikipedias_ordered_by_number_of_articles "m:List of Wikipedias") in [more than 300 languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:SiteMatrix "Special:SiteMatrix"), including 7,109,957 articles in [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"), with 291,214 active contributors in the past month.

A short video explaining how Wikipedia works

Wikipedia's fundamental principles are summarized in its [five pillars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Five_pillars "Wikipedia:Five pillars"). While the [Wikipedia community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia_community "Wikipedia community") has developed many [policies and guidelines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Policies_and_guidelines "Wikipedia:Policies and guidelines"), new editors do not need to be familiar with them before they start contributing.

[Anyone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Who_writes_Wikipedia%3F "Wikipedia:Who writes Wikipedia?") can [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Editing "Help:Editing") Wikipedia's text, data, references, and images. The quality of content is more important than the expertise of who contributes it. Wikipedia's content must conform with its [policies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Editing_policy "Wikipedia:Editing policy"), including being [verifiable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiable "Wikipedia:Verifiable") by published [reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources"). Contributions based on [personal opinions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Neutral_point_of_view "Wikipedia:Neutral point of view"), beliefs, or personal experiences, [unreviewed research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Original_research "Wikipedia:Original research"), libellous material, and [copyright violations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Copyright_violations "Wikipedia:Copyright violations") are not allowed, and will not remain. Wikipedia's software makes it easy to reverse errors, and experienced [editors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia_editor "Wikipedia editor") [watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Watchlist "Wikipedia:Watchlist") and [patrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Recent_changes_patrol "Wikipedia:Recent changes patrol") bad edits.

[Wikipedia differs from printed references in important ways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:NOTPAPER "Wikipedia:NOTPAPER"). Anyone can instantly improve it, add quality information, remove misinformation, and fix errors and [vandalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vandalism "Wikipedia:Vandalism"). Since Wikipedia is continually updated, encyclopedic articles on major news events appear within minutes.

For over 24 years, editors have volunteered their time and talents to create history's most comprehensive encyclopedia while providing references and other resources to researchers worldwide (see [Researching with Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Researching_with_Wikipedia "Wikipedia:Researching with Wikipedia")). In summary, Wikipedia has tested the [wisdom of the crowd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisdom_of_the_crowd "Wisdom of the crowd") since 2001 and has found that it succeeds.

To start editing, simply click the Edit or Edit source button, or the pencil icon [![Image 5: Simple gray pencil icon](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Pencil_edit_icon.svg/40px-Pencil_edit_icon.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pencil_edit_icon.svg), at the top of any [non-protected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Protection_policy "Wikipedia:Protection policy") Wikipedia page or section.
