[![Image 1: jan5bretan](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/jan5bretan.jpg?w=122)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/jan5bretan.jpg)

_John IV de Montfort, Duke of Brittany_

After writing about [Yolande de Dreux](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/2016/10/30/yolande-and-the-hope-for-the-scottish-succession/) a few weeks back, I became intrigued with the story of her grandson, **John de Montfort**.

John was the only son of John, count of Montfort, and [Joan of Flanders](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/2019/08/12/book-corner-joanna-of-flanders-heroine-and-exile-by-julie-sarpy/). He was probably born in November or December of 1339. His great-grandmother was Beatrice of England, a daughter of Henry III, who was the mother of his grandfather, Arthur, duke of Brittany. John is first mention in 1341 when his childless uncle, John III, duke of Brittany, provided him with 20,000 livres from his patrimony. However, when the duke died on 30 April 1341, the duchy was thrown into turmoil. Civil war erupted when John’s father and uncle-by-marriage, Charles de Blois, both laid claim to the duchy.

John de Montfort the elder was the son of Arthur, duke of Brittany, by his 2nd wife, Yolande. Charles de Blois was married to Jeanne de Penthièvre, daughter of Arthur’s second son by his first wife; Guy of Brittany. The bitter conflict was to be absorbed into the much greater struggle, between France and England, that became known as the Hundred Years’ War. Edward III of England supported young John’s father, while Philip VI of France backed Charles de Blois.

In November 1341 John’s father was captured and it was up to his mother to assume the de Montfort cause. Edward III sent troops to secure various strongholds, but by late 1342, after an unproductive campaign, he had minimised his military involvement, leaving a lieutenant in charge as he headed back to England, accompanied by John, who was about 3 years old at the time, his mother and his sister, Joan.

John’s mother was imprisoned in Tickhill Castle, Yorkshire, supposedly after succumbing to a mental illness, though more likely for political reasons. As a result, John was raised in the household of the queen, Philippa of Hainault. Their fortunes revived briefly when John’s father arrived in England 1345, paying homage to Edward III at Easter, having broken his parole and escaped the duchy. He led a small force back to Brittany, but died suddenly in September of the same year, leaving 6-year-old John in the guardianship of Edward III.

[![Image 2: mary_plantagenet_of_brittany](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/mary_plantagenet_of_brittany.jpg?w=189)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/mary_plantagenet_of_brittany.jpg)

_Mary of England, John’s first wife_

Sir Thomas Dagworth captured Charles de Blois at Le Roche Derrien in June 1347, giving the English the opportunity to discuss the succession issue. It looked for a time, that Edward would sacrifice; in 1353 a treaty was actually drafted that was heavily in de Blois’ favour, depriving John of most of his rights. Luckily, for John, it was never implemented and de Blois was eventually released, in return for a huge ransom, in 1356.

Edward resolved now to back young John’s claims. Around 17-years-old, John experienced his first military campaign when he fought alongside Henry, duke of Lancaster, in the siege of Rennes, from October 1356 to July 1357, and later taking part in the Rheims campaign of 1359-60. In March, 1361, John married Edward III’s daughter, Mary, at Woodstock. The marriage would end in tragedy as Mary, still only 17, died of plague in September of the same year. Discussions throughout the early 1360s offered no lasting political solution and, now having attained his majority, John returned to Brittany in the summer of 1362.

Further discussions hosted by the Black Prince, including plans to partition the duchy, failed. However, when Charles de Blois was eventually defeated killed in battle at Auray on 29th September 1364 Jeanne de Penthièvre was forced to come to terms with John de Montfort and the Treaty of Guérande was signed on 12th April 1365. John was recognised as John IV duke of Brittany  by Charles V of France, to whom he performed homage for his duchy in December 1366.

Initially, as duke of Brittany, John’s ties to England continued to be strong, his financial debts and other obligations ensuring this. In 1366 he married [Joan Holland](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/2015/10/10/the-fascinating-marital-exploits-of-joan-the-fair-maid-of-kent/), step-daughter of Edward, the Black Prince. However, when a lull in the fighting ended in 1369 and France and England were at loggerheads once again, John was caught in a dilemma. As his overlord Charles V was expecting John to fight for France, while Edward III was his old ally and mentor and obviously felt deserving of his loyalty. His prevarications meant his Breton subjects grew restive and when John sided with Edward III, after receiving the earldom of Richmond in 1372 as a sweetener, they openly rebelled.

[![Image 3: joana_canterbury](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/joana_canterbury.jpg)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/joana_canterbury.jpg)

_Joan of Navarre, John’s 3rd wife_

By April 1373 John had lost everything; he fled to England as his duchy was overrun by French troops. And yet, worse was to follow. After participating in John of Gaunt’s _chevauchée_ from Calais to Bordeaux, John was tried for treason in the Paris _parlement_ in December 1378. In total, John spent 6 years in exile, living on his English estates and attending court and parliament; he was the 1st foreign prince to be made a Knight of the Garter, in 1374.

John was invited to Brittany in 1379 by his Breton subjects, who were beginning to become suspicious of Charles V’s intentions; realising that his attempts to bring Brittany into the French royal demesne would threaten her traditional privileges and independence. The Breton constable of France, Bertrand de Guesclin, deliberately failed to oppose the duke’s landing. After Charles V died in September 1380 a peace was negotiated with the aid of the count of Flanders and Louis, duke of Anjou, which was ratified in the 2nd Treaty of Guérande in April 1381.

A consequence of the treaty was that John de Montfort now opposed his former allies in England and Navarre. With Edward III dying in 1377, his young grandson was now King Richard II. The English still occupied Brest, and John was having difficulties in collecting revenues from his English estates. John’s wife, Duchess Joan, had been staying in England during the troubles but, after much wrangling, was finally returned to her husband in 1382, only to die in November 1384. Her death removed an important connection to the English court and Richard II, her half-brother.

The 1380s saw John consolidating his position in Brittany, making alliances with other French princes, such as the dukes of Berry and Burgundy and the king of Navarre. He developed the duchy’s institutions, encouraged trade, devised new taxes and exploited minting rights. On a cultural level,  John expanded his court and encouraged the arts by extensive patronage. He also encouraged loyalty to his family and dynasty, which was helped greatly by his marriage to Joan of Navarre in 1386 and the birth of his long-awaited heir in 1389.

[![Image 4: 330px-sceau_de_jean_v_-_duc_de_bretagne](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/330px-sceau_de_jean_v_-_duc_de_bretagne.png?w=295)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/330px-sceau_de_jean_v_-_duc_de_bretagne.png)

_John V, duke of Brittany_

As Anglo-French diplomatic relations thawed in the 1390s, John was able to make a marriage alliance with John of Gaunt, whereby one of his daughters would marry a son of Gaunt’s heir, the earl of Derby. John de Montfort attended the wedding of Richard II and Isabella of France in 1396 and Brest was returned to him in 1397.

Joan and John had an affectionate relationship, producing 8 children, 7 of whom survived to adulthood. John and a second son, Arthur, each became duke of Brittany; Arthur was also constable of France and succeeded his nephew, John’s son Peter, as duke. He died in 1458 and was succeeded by his nephew, Francis, son of his younger brother, Richard, count of Étampes, who had died in 1439. A fourth son, Gilles, died in 1412. Joan and John also had 3 daughters: Marie, countess of Alençon; Blanche, countess of Armagnac and Marguerite, vicomtess de Rohan.

John de Montfort paid one last visit to England in 1398, when he took formal possession of Richmond, attended a Garter ceremony at Windsor and spent some time on progress with Richard II before returning home. He died at Nantes on 1st November 1399, where he was buried. In 1402 his widow, now the wife of Henry IV of England, erected an English-made alabaster tomb over his grave; it was destroyed during the French Revolution. Joan acted as regent for her 10-year-old son, John, until her marriage to Henry; when she entrusted the regency and custody of her Breton children, to the Duke of Burgundy.

Brittany remained an independent duchy within France for another 100 years.

\*

Pictures courtesy of Wikipedia.

\*

Sources: Ian Mortimer _The Perfect King_; Marc Morris _Edward I: A Great and Terrible King_ by Marc Morris;  _Brewer’s British_ _Royalty_ by David Williamson; _The Mammoth Book of British kings & Queens_ by Mike Ashley; _Britain’s Royal Families_ by Alison Weir; _The Oxford Companion to British History_ edited by John Cannon_; The History Today Companion to British History_ Edited by Juliet Gardiner and Neil Wenborn_; The Story of Scotland_ by Nigel Tranter; _Scotland, History of a Nation_ by David Ross; _oxforddnb.com_; britannica.com; W.M. Ormrod _The Reign of Edward III_.

\*

My books
--------

**Signed, dedicated copies of all my books are available through my [online bookshop.](https://sharon-b-connolly.sumupstore.com/)**

#### **Out now: **_Scotland’s Medieval Queens_****

[![Image 5](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/smq-mine.jpg?w=636)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/smq-mine.jpg)

Scotland’s history is dramatic, violent and bloody. Being England’s northern neighbour has never been easy. Scotland’s queens have had to deal with war, murder, imprisonment, political rivalries and open betrayal. They have loved and lost, raised kings and queens, ruled and died for Scotland. From St Margaret, who became one of the patron saints of Scotland, to Elizabeth de Burgh and the dramatic story of the Scottish Wars of Independence, to the love story and tragedy of Joan Beaufort, to Margaret of Denmark and the dawn of the Renaissance, Scotland’s Medieval Queens have seen it all. This is the story of Scotland through their eyes.

**Available now from [Amazon](http://mybook.to/ScottishQueens) and [Pen and Sword Books](https://www.pen-and-sword.co.uk/Scotlands-Medieval-Queens-Hardback/p/51759)**

#### Also by Sharon Bennett Connolly:

[![Image 6](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/480217034_10234557967841333_4242594703446182069_n.jpg?w=636)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/480217034_10234557967841333_4242594703446182069_n.jpg)

**_[Heroines of the Tudor World](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/2024/06/15/publication-day-heroines-of-the-tudor-world/)_** tells the stories of the most remarkable women from European history in the time of the Tudor dynasty, 1485-1603. These are the women who ruled, the women who founded dynasties, the women who fought for religious freedom, their families and love. **_Heroines of the Tudor World_** is now available for pre-order from [Amberley Publishing](https://www.amberley-books.com/author-community-main-page/b/sharon-bennett-connolly/heroines-of-the-tudor-age.html) and [Amazon UK.](https://mybook.to/TudorHeroines) **_[Women of the Anarchy](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/2024/01/15/new-book-women-of-the-anarchy/)_** demonstrates how Empress Matilda and Matilda of Boulogne, unable to wield a sword themselves, were prime movers in this time of conflict and lawlessness. It shows how their strengths, weaknesses, and personal ambitions swung the fortunes of war one way – and then the other. Available from [Bookshop.org](https://uk.bookshop.org/p/books/women-of-the-anarchy-sharon-bennett-connolly/7425269?ean=9781445691718), [Amberley Publishing](https://www.amberley-books.com/author-community-main-page/b/sharon-bennett-connolly/women-of-the-anarchy.html) and [Amazon UK](https://mybook.to/WomenAnarchy). **_[King John’s Right-Hand Lady: The Story of Nicholaa de la Haye](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/king-johns-right-hand-lady/)_** is the story of a truly remarkable lady, the hereditary constable of Lincoln Castle and the first woman in England to be appointed sheriff in her own right. Available from all good bookshops [Pen & Sword Books](https://www.pen-and-sword.co.uk/King-Johns-Right-Hand-Lady-Hardback/p/23329), [bookshop.org](https://uk.bookshop.org/p/books/king-john-s-right-hand-lady-the-story-of-nicholaa-de-la-haye-sharon-bennett-connolly/7415550?ean=9781526756060) and [Amazon](https://mybook.to/Nicholaa).

[![Image 7](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ftby0azwaaeqc6o.jpg?w=835)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ftby0azwaaeqc6o.jpg)

**_[Defenders of the Norman Crown: The Rise and Fall of the Warenne Earls of Surrey](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/defenders-of-the-norman-crown/)_** tells the fascinating story of the Warenne dynasty, from its origins in Normandy, through the Conquest, Magna Carta, the wars and marriages that led to its ultimate demise in the reign of Edward III. Available from [Pen & Sword Books](https://www.pen-and-sword.co.uk/Defenders-of-the-Norman-Crown-Hardback/p/19041), [Amazon in the UK and US,](http://mybook.to/Warennes) and [Bookshop.org](https://uk.bookshop.org/shop/lindumbooks). **[Ladies of Magna Carta: Women of Influence in Thirteenth Century England](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/ladies-of-magna-carta/)** looks into the relationships of the various noble families of the 13th century, and how they were affected by the Barons’ Wars, Magna Carta and its aftermath; the bonds that were formed and those that were broken. It is now available in paperback and hardback from [Pen & Sword](https://www.pen-and-sword.co.uk/Ladies-of-Magna-Carta-Hardback/p/17766), [Amazon](http://mybook.to/LadiesofMagnaCarta), and [Bookshop.org](https://uk.bookshop.org/shop/lindumbooks). [**Heroines of the Medieval World**](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/heroines-of-the-medieval-world/) tells the stories of some of the most remarkable women from Medieval history, from Eleanor of Aquitaine to Julian of Norwich. Available now from [Amberley Publishing](https://www.amberley-books.com/heroines-of-the-medieval-world-9781445689449.html) and [Amazon,](http://mybook.to/Heroines) [and Bookshop.org](https://uk.bookshop.org/shop/lindumbooks). **[Silk and the Sword: The Women of the Norman Conquest](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/silk-and-the-sword-the-women-of-the-norman-conquest/)** traces the fortunes of the women who had a significant role to play in the momentous events of 1066. Available now from [Amazon](http://mybook.to/SilkandSword),  [Amberley Publishing,](https://www.amberley-books.com/silk-and-the-sword.html) and [Bookshop.org](https://uk.bookshop.org/shop/lindumbooks).

**_[Alternate Endings](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/2022/11/04/long-live-the-king/)_**: An anthology of historical fiction short stories including **_Long Live the King…_** which is my take what might have happened had King John not died in October 1216. Available in paperback and kindle from [Amazon](https://mybook.to/AltEndings).

#### Podcast:

[![Image 8](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/gbx-ue7w8aaofmd.jpg?w=1024)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/gbx-ue7w8aaofmd.jpg)

[![Image 1: Joanna of Flanders seeing English ships during the Siege of Hennebont](https://badassladiesofhistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/joan-of-flanders.jpg?w=207&h=300)](https://badassladiesofhistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/joan-of-flanders.jpg)

Joanna of Flanders seeing English ships during the Siege of Hennebont

Joanna of Flanders (c. 1295—c.1374 CE), also known as Jeanne la Flamme and Jeanne de Montfort, was a Bretton noblewoman who fought at the beginning of the Hundred Years War. She was the daughter of Louis I, Count of Nevers and Joan, Countess of Rethel. Her brother was Louis I, Count of Flanders. In 1329 she married John of Montfort, the Duke of Brittany and had two children by him, John and Joan. Unfortunately, due to some inconsistencies in the will of John III, the previous Duke of Brittany, there were discrepancies about who was the rightful Duke. The succession was split between the House of Montfort and the House of Blois. Philip IV, King of France, supported Charles de Blois’s claim, which he got through his wife, the niece and named heir of the previous Duke. When John IV did not agree, he was imprisoned by the King and de Blois.

At this, Joanna declared her son, who was still just a child, the leader of the Montfort faction. She raised an army and captured Redon. After this, she returned to Hennebont Castle to prepare it for an expected siege from Charles de Blois. To do so, she sent an emissary to Edward III of England, asking him for aid. As he had long considered himself as the rightful King of France, he agreed, knowing it would be wise to have so powerful an ally as the Duchy of Brittany.

During the Siege of Hennebont, Joanna took up arms and kept up the defenses. When she saw that de Blois had left his camp mostly unguarded, she quickly gathered 300 of her men. They rode out, burned supplies and destroyed tents. This earned Joanna the epithet, “Jeanne la Flamme”, or “Fiery Joan”. When the Blois army realized what was happening, they cut Joanna and her troops off from their retreat. Instead, they rode to Brest, where they gathered support. She secretly returned to Hennebont later.

As the people of Hennebont were starving, the Bishop of Leon tried to persuade Joanna to surrender to Charles de Blois. She refused, and was rewarded when she saw English ships out in the harbor courtesy of Edward III. Charles de Blois was forced to retreat for the moment. Knowing that he and his forces would return, Joanna sailed to England for more reinforcements. On the way back, they were intercepted by Spanish ships, as Louis of Spain had allied himself with Charles de Blois. In the accounts of the naval battles and warfare, Joanna fought fiercely with a glaive. The English and Joanna were victorious in this fight, and they sailed to Vannes. After taking the city, Joanna laid siege on Rennes. As neither side was victorious after a long siege, a truce was made in 1343. Joanna’s husband, John IV, was released. He died in 1345.

War broke out again, as John V, Joanna’s son, was still young and easily usurped. The English had allied themselves completely with the House of Montfort, and they captured Charles de Blois in 1347, in the name of Joanna. At that point, Joanna and her son had taken refuge in England. The war continued until 1364, when the House of Montfort was victorious, and John V was named the rightful Duke of Brittany. Unfortunately, Joanna had contracted a serious mental illness, and was in confinement in England. She never returned to France and died in 1374.

**Legacy:** She was celebrated in folklore and literature. She was a possible influence and inspiration for Jeanne d’Arc (which may not be true, as they were on opposing sides.) She was certainly an influence on the women’s movement during the Victorian Era.

> [Women Warriors — Meet Seven of History’s Most Amazing Female Commanders](https://militaryhistorynow.com/2013/05/15/women-warriors-meet-seven-of-historys-most-amazing-female-commanders/)

**Philip VI** (French: _Philippe_; 1293 – 22 August 1350), called **the Fortunate** (French: _le Fortuné_), **the Catholic** (_le Catholique_) and **of Valois** (_de Valois_), was the first [king of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_France "King of France") from the [House of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Valois "House of Valois"), reigning from 1328 until his death in 1350. Philip's reign was dominated by the consequences of [a succession dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession_to_the_French_throne#The_succession_in_1328 "Succession to the French throne"). When King [Charles IV of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IV_of_France "Charles IV of France") died in 1328, his [nearest male relative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximity_of_blood "Proximity of blood") was his sororal nephew, [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), but the French nobility preferred Charles's paternal cousin, Philip of Valois.

At first, Edward seemed to accept Philip's succession, but he pressed [his claim to the throne of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne") after a series of disagreements with Philip. The result was the beginning of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") in 1337.

After initial successes at sea, Philip's navy was annihilated at the [Battle of Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sluys "Battle of Sluys") in 1340, ensuring that the war would occur on the continent. The English took another decisive advantage at the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") (1346), while the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") struck France, further destabilising the country.

In 1349, Philip bought the [Dauphiné of Viennois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin%C3%A9_of_Viennois "Dauphiné of Viennois"), a county in the [Kingdom of Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Burgundy_/(Arles/) "Kingdom of Burgundy (Arles)") (Arles), under the suzerainty of the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), thus expanding the French influence beyond the river [Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rh%C3%B4ne "Rhône"). The acquisition was formalized by the treaty of [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romans-sur-Is%C3%A8re "Romans-sur-Isère"), concluded between Philip and [Humbert II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humbert_II_of_Viennois "Humbert II of Viennois"), dauphin of Viennois. The province was entrusted to Philip's grandson, prince [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") (future king Charles V).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiblerZinn201652,_290,_420-2)

Philip VI died in 1350 and was succeeded by his son [John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France").

Little is recorded about Philip's childhood and youth, in large part because he was of minor royal birth. Philip's father, [Charles, Count of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Count_of_Valois "Charles, Count of Valois"), was the younger brother of King [Philip IV of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_IV_of_France "Philip IV of France").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-3) Charles had striven throughout his life to gain the throne for himself but was never successful. He died in 1325, leaving his eldest son Philip as heir to the counties of [Anjou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Anjou "County of Anjou"), [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_/(province/) "Maine (province)"), and [Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_and_dukes_of_Valois "Counts and dukes of Valois").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Hallam366-4)

Accession to the throne
-----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Philip_VI_of_France&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Accession to the throne")\]

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Sacre_philippe_VI.jpg/250px-Sacre_philippe_VI.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sacre_philippe_VI.jpg)

Coronation of Philip VI

In 1328, Philip's cousin [Charles IV of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IV_of_France "Charles IV of France") died without a son, leaving his widow [Jeanne of Évreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_of_%C3%89vreux "Jeanne of Évreux") pregnant.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Hallam366-4) Philip was one of the two chief claimants to the throne of France. The other was King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), who was Charles's nephew and [closest male relative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximity_of_blood "Proximity of blood"), being the son of Charles's sister [Isabella of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_France "Isabella of France"). The Estates General had decided [12 years earlier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salic_law#The_succession_in_1316 "Salic law") that women could not inherit the throne of France. The question arose as to whether Isabella should have been able to transmit a claim that she herself did not possess.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption106-107-5) The assemblies of the French barons and prelates and the [University of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris") decided that males who derive their right to inheritance through their mother should be excluded according to [Salic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salic_law "Salic law"). As Philip was the eldest grandson of [Philip III of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_III_of_France "Philip III of France") through the male line, he became regent instead of Edward, who was a maternal grandson of [Philip IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_IV_of_France "Philip IV of France") and great-grandson of Philip III.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-6)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Hommage_d%E2%80%99%C3%89douard_III_d%E2%80%99Angleterre_%C3%A0_Philippe_de_Valois.png/250px-Hommage_d%E2%80%99%C3%89douard_III_d%E2%80%99Angleterre_%C3%A0_Philippe_de_Valois.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hommage_d%E2%80%99%C3%89douard_III_d%E2%80%99Angleterre_%C3%A0_Philippe_de_Valois.png)

Edward III of England pays homage to Philip VI of France in [Amiens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiens "Amiens"), from a 1370–75 manuscript of the _[Grandes Chroniques de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandes_Chroniques_de_France "Grandes Chroniques de France")_

During the period in which Queen Jeanne was waiting to deliver her child, Philip of Valois rose to the regency with support of the French magnates, following the pattern set up by his cousin, [Philip V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_France "Philip V of France"), who succeeded to the throne over his niece [Joan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_II_of_Navarre "Joan II of Navarre").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption106-107-5) Philip formally held the regency from 9 February until 1 April 1328. On 1 April, Jeanne of Évreux gave birth to a daughter named [Blanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_of_France,_Duchess_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Blanche of France, Duchess of Orléans"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-7) following which Philip was proclaimed king. He was crowned at the [Cathedral in Reims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre-Dame_de_Reims "Notre-Dame de Reims") on 29 May 1328.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-8) After his elevation to the throne, Philip sent the Abbot of [Fécamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9camp "Fécamp"), [Pierre Roger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), to summon Edward III of England to pay homage for the [duchy of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Aquitaine "Duchy of Aquitaine") and [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Gascony "Duchy of Gascony").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption109-110-9) After a subsequent second summons from Philip, Edward finally arrived at the [Cathedral of Amiens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiens_Cathedral "Amiens Cathedral") on 6 June 1329 and worded his vows in such a way to cause more disputes in later years.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption109-110-9)

The dynastic change had another consequence: Charles IV had also been [King of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Navarrese_monarchs "List of Navarrese monarchs"), but, unlike the [crown of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France"), the [crown of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Navarre "Kingdom of Navarre") was not subject to Salic law. Philip VI was neither an heir nor a descendant of [Joan I of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_I_of_Navarre "Joan I of Navarre"), whose inheritance (the kingdom of [Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navarre "Navarre"), as well as the counties of [Champagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne_/(province/) "Champagne (province)"), [Troyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troyes "Troyes"), [Meaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meaux "Meaux"), and [Brie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brie_/(region/) "Brie (region)")) had been in personal union with the crown of France for almost fifty years and had long been administered by the same royal machinery established by King Philip IV, the father of French bureaucracy. These counties were closely entrenched in the economic and administrative entity of the [crown lands of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_lands_of_France "Crown lands of France"), being located adjacent to [Île-de-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Ele-de-France "Île-de-France"). Philip, however, was not entitled to that inheritance; the rightful heiress was the surviving daughter of his cousin [King Louis X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_X_of_France "Louis X of France"), the future Joan II of Navarre, the [heir general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heir_general "Heir general") of Joan I of Navarre. Navarre thus passed to Joan II, with whom Philip struck a deal regarding the counties in Champagne: she received vast lands in [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy "Normandy") (adjacent to the [fief in Évreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_%C3%89vreux "Count of Évreux") that her husband [Philip III of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_III_of_Navarre "Philip III of Navarre") owned) as compensation, and he kept Champagne as part of the French crown lands.

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/The_Battle_of_Cassel_on_23rd_August_1328.png/250px-The_Battle_of_Cassel_on_23rd_August_1328.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Battle_of_Cassel_on_23rd_August_1328.png)

_[The Battle of Cassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Battle_of_Cassel "The Battle of Cassel")_ by [Hendrik Scheffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendrik_Scheffer "Hendrik Scheffer"), 1837

Philip's reign was plagued with crises, although it began with a military success in [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") at the [Battle of Cassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cassel_/(1328/) "Battle of Cassel (1328)") (August 1328), where Philip's forces re-seated [Louis I, Count of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I,_Count_of_Flanders "Louis I, Count of Flanders"), who had been unseated by [a popular revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasant_revolt_in_Flanders_1323%E2%80%9328 "Peasant revolt in Flanders 1323–28").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-DeVries102-10) Philip's wife, the able [Joan the Lame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_the_Lame_of_Burgundy "Joan the Lame of Burgundy"), gave the first of many demonstrations of her competence as regent in his absence.

Philip initially enjoyed relatively amicable relations with Edward III, and they planned a crusade together in 1332, which was never executed. However, the status of the [Duchy of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Aquitaine "Duchy of Aquitaine") remained a sore point, and tension increased. Philip provided refuge for [David II of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_II_of_Scotland "David II of Scotland") in 1334 and declared himself champion of his interests, which enraged Edward.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-11) By 1336, they were enemies, although not yet openly at war.

Philip successfully prevented an arrangement between the [Avignon papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_papacy "Avignon papacy") and [Holy Roman Emperor Louis IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor"), although in July 1337 Louis concluded an alliance with Edward III.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-12) The final breach with England came when Edward offered refuge to [Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois"), formerly one of Philip's trusted advisers,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption171-172-13) after Robert committed forgery to try to obtain an inheritance. As relations between Philip and Edward worsened, Robert's standing in England strengthened.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption171-172-13) On 26 December 1336, Philip officially demanded the extradition of Robert to France.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption171-172-13) On 24 May 1337, Philip declared that Edward had forfeited Aquitaine for disobedience and for sheltering the "king's mortal enemy", Robert of Artois.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-14) Thus began the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), complicated by Edward's renewed [claim to the throne of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne") in retaliation for the forfeiture of Aquitaine.

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Disguised_as_a_seller_of_fish_the_Flemish_leader_went_down_into_the_French_camp.jpg/250px-Disguised_as_a_seller_of_fish_the_Flemish_leader_went_down_into_the_French_camp.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Disguised_as_a_seller_of_fish_the_Flemish_leader_went_down_into_the_French_camp.jpg)

Flemish leader as fish seller went to search in French camp

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Philippe_VI_and_Jeanne_de_Bourgogne.jpg/250px-Philippe_VI_and_Jeanne_de_Bourgogne.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Philippe_VI_and_Jeanne_de_Bourgogne.jpg)

Philip VI and his first wife, Joan of Burgundy

Philip entered the Hundred Years' War in a position of comparative strength. [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_in_the_Middle_Ages "France in the Middle Ages") was richer and more populous than [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_in_the_Middle_Ages "England in the Middle Ages") and was at the height of its medieval glory. The opening stages of the war, accordingly, were largely successful for the French.

At sea, French privateers raided and burned towns and shipping all along the southern and southeastern coasts of England.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-15) The English made some retaliatory raids, including the burning of a fleet in the harbour of [Boulogne-sur-Mer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulogne-sur-Mer "Boulogne-sur-Mer"),[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption320-328-16) but the French largely had the upper hand. With his sea power established, Philip gave orders in 1339 to begin assembling a fleet off the [Zeeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeeland "Zeeland") coast at [Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sluys "Sluys"). In June 1340, however, in the bitterly fought [Battle of Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sluys "Battle of Sluys"), the English attacked the port and captured or destroyed the ships there, ending the threat of an invasion.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption320-328-16)

On land, Edward III largely concentrated upon [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") and the [Low Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries"), where he had gained allies through diplomacy and bribery. A raid in 1339 (the first _[chevauchée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevauch%C3%A9e "Chevauchée")_) into [Picardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picardy "Picardy") ended ignominiously when Philip wisely refused to give battle. Edward's slender finances would not permit him to play a waiting game, and he was forced to withdraw into Flanders and return to England to raise more money. In July 1340, Edward returned and mounted the [siege of Tournai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Tournai_/(1340/) "Siege of Tournai (1340)").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-17) By September 1340, Edward was in financial distress, hardly able to pay or feed his troops, and was open to dialogue.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption354-359-18) After being at [Bouvines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bouvines "Bouvines") for a week, Philip was finally persuaded to send [Joan of Valois, Countess of Hainaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Valois,_Countess_of_Hainaut "Joan of Valois, Countess of Hainaut"), to discuss terms to end the siege.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption354-359-18) On 23 September 1340, a nine-month truce was reached.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Sumption354-359-18)

So far, the war had gone quite well for Philip and the French. While often stereotyped as chivalry-besotted and incompetent, Philip and his men had in fact carried out a successful [Fabian strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_strategy "Fabian strategy") against the debt-plagued Edward and resisted the chivalric blandishments of single combat or a combat of two hundred knights that he offered. In 1341, the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession") allowed the English to place permanent garrisons in [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany"). However, Philip was still in a commanding position: during negotiations arbitrated by the pope in 1343, he refused Edward's offer to end the war in exchange for the [Duchy of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Aquitaine "Duchy of Aquitaine") in full sovereignty.

The next attack came in 1345, when the [Earl of Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Grosmont,_1st_Duke_of_Lancaster "Henry of Grosmont, 1st Duke of Lancaster") overran the [Agenais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agenais "Agenais") (lost twenty years before in the [War of Saint-Sardos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_Saint-Sardos "War of Saint-Sardos")) and took [Angoulême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angoul%C3%AAme "Angoulême"), while the forces in Brittany under Sir [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth") also made gains. The French responded in the spring of 1346 with a massive counterattack against [Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquitaine "Aquitaine"), where an army under [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France"), besieged Derby at [Aiguillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aiguillon,_Lot-et-Garonne "Aiguillon, Lot-et-Garonne"). On the advice of [Godfrey Harcourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Harcourt#The_Harcourts_and_the_Hundred_Years'_War "House of Harcourt") (like [Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois"), a banished French nobleman), Edward sailed for [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy "Normandy") instead of Aquitaine. As Harcourt predicted, the [Normans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normans "Normans") were ill-prepared for war, and many of the fighting men were at Aiguillon. Edward sacked and burned the country as he went, [taking Caen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Caen_/(1346/) "Battle of Caen (1346)") and advancing as far as [Poissy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poissy "Poissy") and then retreating before the army Philip had hastily assembled at Paris. Slipping across the [Somme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somme_/(river/) "Somme (river)"), Edward drew up to give battle at [Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A9cy-en-Ponthieu "Crécy-en-Ponthieu").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-19)

Close behind him, Philip had planned to halt for the night and reconnoitre the English position before giving battle the next day. However, his troops were disorderly, and the roads were jammed by the rear of the army coming up and the local peasantry, which furiously called for vengeance on the English. Finding them hopeless to control, he ordered a general attack as evening fell. Thus began the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy"). When it was done, the French army had been annihilated and a wounded Philip barely escaped capture. Fortune had turned against the French.

The English seized and held the advantage. Normandy called off the siege of Aiguillon and retreated northward, while Sir [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth") captured [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany") in Brittany. The English army pulled back from Crécy to mount the [siege of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Calais_/(1346%E2%80%931347/) "Siege of Calais (1346–1347)"); the town held out stubbornly, but the English were determined, and they easily supplied across the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel"). Philip led out a relieving army in July 1347, but unlike the [Siege of Tournai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Tournai_/(1340/) "Siege of Tournai (1340)"), it was now Edward who had the upper hand. With the plunder of his Norman expedition and the reforms he had executed in his tax system, he could hold to his siege lines and await an attack that Philip dared not deliver. It was Philip who marched away in August, and the city capitulated shortly thereafter.

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Funerailles_Philippe_VI.jpg/250px-Funerailles_Philippe_VI.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Funerailles_Philippe_VI.jpg)

King Philip's funerary procession, which was presided over by the [Archbishop of Reims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_de_Vienne_/(archbishop,_died_1351/) "Jean de Vienne (archbishop, died 1351)"), illustrated by [Loyset Liédet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyset_Li%C3%A9det "Loyset Liédet")

After the defeat at Crécy and loss of Calais, the [Estates of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates_General_/(France/) "Estates General (France)") refused to raise money for Philip, halting his plans to counter-attack by invading England. In 1348 the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") struck France and in the next few years killed one-third of the population, including Queen Joan. The resulting labour shortage caused inflation to soar, and the king attempted to [fix prices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_controls "Price controls"), further destabilising the country. His second marriage to his son's betrothed [Blanche of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_of_Navarre,_Queen_of_France "Blanche of Navarre, Queen of France") alienated his son and many nobles from the king.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-20)

Philip's last major achievement was the acquisition of the [Dauphiné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin%C3%A9 "Dauphiné") and the territory of [Montpellier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montpellier "Montpellier") in the [Languedoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languedoc "Languedoc") in 1349. At his death in 1350, France was very much a divided country filled with social unrest. Philip VI died at Coulombes Abbey, [Eure-et-Loir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eure-et-Loir "Eure-et-Loir"), on 22 August 1350[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-21) and is interred with his first wife, Joan of Burgundy, in [Saint Denis Basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Denis_Basilica "Saint Denis Basilica"), though his [viscera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscera "Viscera") were buried separately at the now demolished church of [Couvent des Jacobins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Couvent_des_Jacobins_de_la_rue_Saint-Jacques "Couvent des Jacobins de la rue Saint-Jacques") in Paris. He was succeeded by his first son by Joan of Burgundy, who became [John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France").

Marriages and children
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Philip_VI_of_France&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Marriages and children")\]

Philip married twice. In July 1313, he married [Joan the Lame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_the_Lame_of_Burgundy "Joan the Lame of Burgundy") (French: _Jeanne_), daughter of [Robert II, Duke of Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_II,_Duke_of_Burgundy "Robert II, Duke of Burgundy"),[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-22) and [Agnes of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_of_France,_Duchess_of_Burgundy "Agnes of France, Duchess of Burgundy"), the youngest daughter of [King Louis IX of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_IX_of_France "Louis IX of France"). She was thus Philip's first cousin once removed. The couple had the following children:

1.  [King John II of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") (26 April 1319 – 8 April 1364)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Keane17-23)
2.  Marie of France (1326 – 22 September 1333), who died aged only seven, but was already married to John of Brabant, the son and heir of [John III, Duke of Brabant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brabant "John III, Duke of Brabant"); no issue.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-24)
3.  Louis (born and died 17 January 1329).
4.  Louis (8 June 1330 – 23 June 1330)
5.  A son \[John?\] (born and died 2 October 1333).
6.  A son (28 May 1335), stillborn
7.  [Philip of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Philip, Duke of Orléans") (1 July 1336 – 1 September 1375), [Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Duke of Orléans")
8.  Joan (born and died November 1337)
9.  A son (born and died summer 1343)

After Joan died in 1349, Philip married [Blanche of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_of_Navarre,_Queen_of_France "Blanche of Navarre, Queen of France"),[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-25) daughter of Queen [Joan II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_II_of_Navarre "Joan II of Navarre") and [Philip III of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_III_of_Navarre "Philip III of Navarre"), on 11 January 1350. They had one daughter:

*   [Joan (Blanche) of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_France_/(1351%E2%80%931371/) "Joan of France (1351–1371)") (May 1351 – 16 September 1371),[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Keane17-23) who was intended to marry [John I of Aragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Aragon "John I of Aragon"), but who died during the journey.

By an unknown woman he had:

*   Jean d'Armagnac (died after 1350), a knight[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-:0-27)

By his mistress, Beatrice de la Berruère, he had another son:

*   Thomas de la Marche (1318–1361), bâtarde de France[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-28)

Philip is a character in _Les Rois maudits_ (_[The Accursed Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Accursed_Kings "The Accursed Kings")_), a series of French historical novels by [Maurice Druon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Druon "Maurice Druon"). He was portrayed by Benoît Brione in the 1972 French miniseries adaptation of the series, and by [Malik Zidi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malik_Zidi "Malik Zidi") in the 2005 adaptation.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France#cite_note-Rois_2005_AlloCin%C3%A9-29)

33.title: Charles de Blois
33.content:
He was born around 1319 in Blois, Kingdom of France, as the eldest son of Guy I de Châtillon, [Count of Blois](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EB%B0%9C%EB%A3%A8%EC%95%84%20%EB%B0%B1%EC%9E%91%20%EC%83%A4%EB%A5%BC "발루아 백작 샤를") , and Marguerite of Valois, the daughter of Charles, Count of Valois. He had brothers [Louis I](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EB%A3%A8%EC%9D%B4%201%EC%84%B8%20%EB%93%9C%20%EC%83%A4%ED%8B%B0%EC%98%B9 "Louis I of Châtillon") and Marie . Marguerite was the sister of King [Philip VI](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%ED%95%84%EB%A6%AC%ED%94%84%206%EC%84%B8 "Philip VI") of France , so she was Philip VI's nephew. On June 4, 1337, in Paris, he married Jeanne de Penthièvre, daughter of Guy de Penthièvre, son of Arthur II, Duke of Brittany , and niece of [Jean](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%94%20%EB%93%9C%20%ED%8C%A1%ED%8B%B0%EC%97%90%EB%B8%8C%EB%A5%B4 "Jeanne de Penthièvre")[III of Brittany, Duke of Brittany](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%A5%203%EC%84%B8%20%EB%93%9C%20%EB%B8%8C%EB%A5%B4%ED%83%80%EB%89%B4 "Jean III of Brittany") .

Jean III of Brittany was resentful of his half-brother [Jean de Montfort](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%A5%20%EB%93%9C%20%EB%AA%BD%ED%8F%AC%EB%A5%B4 "Jean de Montfort") 's long-standing conflict with him over the inheritance, so he identified his nephew Jeanne de Penthièvre as the successor to the dukedom from an early age and gave him a high-level education. However, on April 30, 1341, Emperor Zhang III, who was on his deathbed, died without clearly identifying his successor. On September 7, 1341, Philip VI recognized Jeanne de Penthièvre as the Duchess of Brittany at Complaint and Charles de Blois as the Duke of Brittany's guardian, and made the Breton nobles swear allegiance to Charles and Jeanne. I made it happen. However, Jean de Montfort argued that women were not eligible to inherit the dukedom based on the [Salic Law](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%82%B4%EB%A6%AC%EC%B9%B4%EB%B2%95 "salic law") , which the French royal family had introduced since [Philip V, and](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%ED%95%84%EB%A6%AC%ED%94%84%205%EC%84%B8 "Philip V") that she should assume the dukedom herself.

Jean de Montfort took advantage of the opportunity when Jeanne and Charles went to Paris to have an audience with Philip VI, and raised an army based on the support of nobles and commoners who wanted to be free from French interference, and attacked the most important places in Brittany, including Nantes, Rennes, Dinan, and Brest. We quickly conquered important cities and castles. In response, Charles de Blois declared that he would protect his wife's rights, and by September of that year, he recruited 5,000 French soldiers and 2,000 Genoese mercenaries and advanced on Nantes, where Jean de Montfort had made his base.

On October 14, 1341, Charles de Blois' army arrived at Chanteauso and began a siege. Jean de Montfort initially attempted to hold out in Nantes until English support arrived. However, as news spread that another French army sent by Philip VI was approaching behind Charles, more and more of his followers abandoned him and attempted to surrender to the enemy. Accordingly, Jean decided that he had no choice but to wait for the match now, and on October 16th he launched from Nantes and set out to relieve Chanteauseau.

At that time, Charles de Blois left the siege to the generals and stayed at the l'Humeau farm, 3 miles away from Chanteauso. Montfort's men stormed the place and almost overwhelmed Charles' bodyguards. However, they failed to capture Charles in time as he put up a barricade on the tower of the farmhouse and fought back. Meanwhile, the French army rushed to rescue Charles and a fierce battle broke out at Romo Farm. In the end, Jean, unable to overcome the inferiority of his troops, fled to Nantes, and many of his men were unable to resist the pursuit of the French cavalry and were killed or captured.

Charles de Blois then laid siege to Nantes, where Jean de Montfort had taken refuge. Jean de Montfort led his soldiers and militia to raid the enemy camp at the end of October 1341, but his mercenaries defected to the enemy during the battle, and while the militia was annihilated, he fled into the castle alone. Afterwards, Charles cut off the body's head and launched it into the castle through a catapult, and the city council, unable to bear it any longer, forced Jean to surrender. In the end, Jean could not hold out any longer and surrendered to Charles on November 2 in exchange for a guarantee of his personal safety. As soon as he opened the gates, Charles broke his promise, arrested him, and sent him to the Louvre prison. Afterwards, Charles conquered all of eastern Brittany during the winter of 1341 and most of western Brittany, including Rennes, in the spring of 1342.

However, Jean de Montfort's wife, [Jeanne de Flanders,](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%94%20%EB%93%9C%20%ED%94%8C%EB%9E%80%EB%8D%B0%EB%9F%B0 "Jeanne de Flanders") decided to fight to the end even in this gloomy situation, and fought [the Siege of Enbon](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%97%94%EB%B4%89%20%EA%B3%B5%EB%B0%A9%EC%A0%84 "Battle of Enbong") against Charles de Blois's offensive in May and June 1342. Soon after, when the English relief force led by [Walter Manny](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9B%94%ED%84%B0%20%EB%A7%A4%EB%8B%88 "Walter Manny") arrived, the French army gave up on the Aenbon invasion and withdrew. Afterwards, Charles de Blois, with the support of the French army, fought against the English army supporting Jeanne de Flanders, Jean de Montfort, and his son, Jean IV de Montfort.

On January 19, 1343, France and England signed the Truce of Lestroit. They agreed to observe a truce for three years, half of which was to be temporarily administered by the cardinals of Clement VI. Additionally, Jean de Montfort, who was imprisoned in the Louvre, was released on the condition that he could not leave France or return to Brittany. Meanwhile, it was agreed that Jeanne de Penthièvre would take over the Dukedom of Brittany. However, the Van people and the local clergy, loyal to Jean de Montfort, did not accept this agreement, and in September 1343, a few months after the treaty was signed, they drove out the cardinal and brought the English army into the city. In addition, [Olivier IV de Clisson](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%98%AC%EB%A6%AC%EB%B9%84%EC%97%90%204%EC%84%B8%20%EB%93%9C%20%ED%81%B4%EB%A6%AC%EC%86%A1 "Olivier IV de Clisson") , who was competing for control of Brittany, framed Philip VI for conspiring with England and had Olivier IV executed to eliminate his rival. Angered by this, Olivier IV's wife, [Jeanne de Belleville](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%94%20%EB%93%9C%20%EB%B2%A8%EB%B9%8C "Jeanne de Belleville") , and son [, Olivier V de Clisson](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%98%AC%EB%A6%AC%EB%B9%84%EC%97%90%205%EC%84%B8%20%EB%93%9C%20%ED%81%B4%EB%A6%AC%EC%86%A1 "Olivier V de Clisson") , engaged in piracy, attacking France for about nine months.

In March 1344, Charles de Blois claimed that the peace agreement had been broken, using the fact that the people of Van had driven out the cardinal and called the English army into the city as an excuse, and launched an offensive, subduing the cities that had joined the Montfort faction one by one. In March 1344, Charles besieged Quimper, captured it on May 1, and massacred about 1,400 to 2,000 civilians. English prisoners who had been dispatched to support Montfort's forces and were captured were held separately for ransom, but after being transported to Paris, they were charged with treason and executed. Jean de Montfort attempted to raise his power by secretly moving to Brittany, but when he received little response, he went into exile in England in March 1345.

This seemed to be the end of the Breton Civil War, but it resumed in the summer of 1346 when Edward III entrusted hundreds of elite soldiers to [William de Bohun](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9C%8C%EB%A6%AC%EC%97%84%20%EB%93%9C%20%EB%B3%B4%ED%9B%88 "william de bohun") , Earl of Northampton, and dispatched them to Brittany with Jean de Montfort. The English army attacked several villages and fortresses on the Brittany coast. Charles de Blois led about 1,000 soldiers north to repel them. On June 9, 1346, the English army led by William de Bohun defeated Charles de Blois at [the Battle of Saint-Paul-de-Léon](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%83%9D%ED%8F%B4%EB%93%9C%EB%A0%88%EC%98%B9%20%EC%A0%84%ED%88%AC "Battle of Saint-Paul-D-Leon") . Afterwards, Charles focused his efforts on rebuilding the army. Meanwhile, the English army set out to retake Quimper in July, but withdrew to Enbon after being repulsed by Charles.

At the time, the war situation was very favorable to Charles de Blois. [Jean de Montfort](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%A5%20%EB%93%9C%20%EB%AA%BD%ED%8F%AC%EB%A5%B4 "Jean de Montfort") died at Enbon on September 16, 1345, and [Jeanne de Flanders](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%94%20%EB%93%9C%20%ED%94%8C%EB%9E%80%EB%8D%B0%EB%9F%B0 "Jeanne de Flanders") , who played an active part in the Siege of Enbon, suffered from mental illness and was imprisoned in Tickhill Castle by Edward III, and their son, [Jean IV of Brittany, died](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%A5%204%EC%84%B8%20%EB%93%9C%20%EB%B8%8C%EB%A5%B4%ED%83%80%EB%89%B4 "Jean IV of Brittany") . He was just a 6-year-old boy. The majority of Brittany believed that the tide had fallen and served [Jeanne of Flanders](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%94%20%EB%93%9C%20%ED%94%8C%EB%9E%80%EB%8D%B0%EB%9F%B0 "Jeanne de Flanders") and Charles of Blois.

However , the French army led by Philip VI was completely defeated at [the Battle of Crecy](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%ED%81%AC%EB%A0%88%EC%8B%9C%20%EC%A0%84%ED%88%AC "battle of crecy") on August 26, 1346 . Public sentiment was once again shaken, and many nobles of Brittany made secret contact with the English army. In May 1347, Charles, who gathered 1,800 heavy soldiers, 600 archers, 2,000 crossbowmen, and a large number of peasant soldiers, decided to resume the offensive to calm the public sentiment in Brittany and drive the English army out of Brittany. His first target was La Roche-derien. He planned to lay siege to this place and immediately intercept and destroy the English relief force as soon as it reached the vicinity. The French army arrived at La Roche-der-Rien on May 20, surrounded the town, built three fortified camps on the north, east, and south, and bombarded it with nine catapults of various sizes. The largest catapult threw stones weighing up to 300 pounds, causing extensive damage, including partially destroying the town governor's house. However, Richard Tosham, the English governor of La Roche-derien, refused to surrender despite pressure from numerous people, including his wife.

[Thomas Dagworth](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%ED%86%A0%EB%A8%B8%EC%8A%A4%20%EB%8B%A4%EA%B7%B8%EC%9B%8C%EC%8A%A4 "Thomas Dagworth") , who heard the news that the village of La Roche-derien was in danger, gathered 300 horsemen and 400 archers at Carhaix, 50 miles southwest of La Roche-derrian, and marched toward La Roche-derrian, 6 In the middle of the month I rested at the abbey of Wegang, nine miles from the village. Afterwards, they decided to approach La Roche-derien along the east bank of the Jaudi River at night, and some troops marched along the road on the west bank of the Jaudi River and made noise to draw the enemy's attention towards it. .

In the early morning of June 20, when there was a noise along the road, Charles realized that the enemy was approaching and ordered his entire army to stand still and wait for the enemy to attack. Soon after, Dagworth's English army arrived at La Roche-derrian and attacked the camp to the east of the town. However, the French army, which had been waiting in advance, immediately counterattacked, and the English army had a hard time against the enemy, who responded calmly. Even Commander Dagworth was injured and became a prisoner.

If things had continued like this, the French army would have won, but as day dawned, Richard Tosham, who learned that our army had made a surprise attack on the enemy camp, left some of the troops guarding the castle walls and led the rest out of the village to attack the rear of Charles' French army. . The French army did not expect this, and many soldiers ran away in fear. The Breton-French troops of the other two camps, who did not leave the camp, suffered one after another from the English army's offensive and eventually collapsed. Dagworth was rescued, and Charles was captured with 17 wounds after a fierce fight.

In [the Battle of La Roche-derien,](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EB%9D%BC%20%EB%A1%9C%EC%8A%88%EB%8D%B0%EB%A6%AC%EC%95%99%20%EC%A0%84%ED%88%AC "Battle of La Roche-derien") French casualties amounted to 600. The casualties of the English army were not known, but were presumed to have been significant. Charles de Blois, who had been the commander of the French army in Brittany, was captured, treated, and then transported to England and imprisoned for several years. Likewise, both the Montfort faction and the Blois faction became disorganized as their commanders disappeared, and both France and England concentrated on other fronts such as Normandy-Flanders-Gascony, but did not pay much attention to this area. Therefore, the Breton civil war was reduced to a battle between small warlords and bandits.

On August 10, 1356, Charles de Blois was released from [the Tower of London](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EB%9F%B0%EB%8D%98%20%ED%83%91 "tower of london") after nine years and returned home after promising to pay a ransom of 700,000 gold florins. He decided to travel barefoot from La Roche-derien to the Cathedral of Treguier in winter to pay homage to the Breton saint, Ivo of Kermartin. When the people heard of his plan, they spread straw and blankets in the streets to prevent Charles from hurting his feet, but Charles immediately took a different path. As a result, Charles arrived at Treguier Cathedral, but his feet were so sore that he could not walk for 15 weeks. Afterwards, Charles resumed the war against the Montfort family, but neither England nor France had much interest in the Breton front, and neither the Montfort family nor Charles had the resources to mobilize troops, so they were unable to launch an active offensive to decide the winner.

In July 1363, Charles de Blois reached an agreement with [Jean IV of Brittany](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%A5%204%EC%84%B8%20%EB%93%9C%20%EB%B8%8C%EB%A5%B4%ED%83%80%EB%89%B4 "Jean IV of Brittany") at Besserell . According to this, Blois was to have the northeastern part, including the city of Nantes, and Montfort was to have the southern and western parts. He decided to request arbitration from King [John II](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9E%A5%202%EC%84%B8 "Chapter 2") of France and King [Edward III](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%97%90%EB%93%9C%EC%9B%8C%EB%93%9C%203%EC%84%B8 "Edward III") of England regarding the right to use the title of duke . However, Jeanne de Penthièvre refused the agreement, saying that she should become the full Duchess of Brittany, and the agreement was nullified. This became an opportunity for many nobles in Brittany, tired of the war, to withdraw their support for Blois.

On February 2, 1364, Charles de Blois and John IV of Brittany requested [Edward the Black Prince,](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%ED%9D%91%ED%83%9C%EC%9E%90%20%EC%97%90%EB%93%9C%EC%9B%8C%EB%93%9C "black prince edward") Duke of Aquitaine , to mediate the Breton civil war, but received no response. In July 1364, John IV of Brittany, who had recruited mercenaries from England, besieged Ore, one of the few port cities on the west coast of Brittany that supported the Blois family. Charles de Blois marched with [Bertrand du Guéclin](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EB%B2%A0%EB%A5%B4%ED%8A%B8%EB%9E%91%20%EB%92%A4%20%EA%B2%8C%ED%81%B4%EB%9E%AD "Bertrand du Guesclin") to defeat them .

On September 29, 1364, upon the arrival of Charles de Blois's army [northeast of Ore](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%98%A4%EB%A0%88%20%EC%A0%84%ED%88%AC "Battle of Ore") , the besiegers of John IV of Brittany formed battle formation next to a lake to the north of the town. The English army led by [John Chanders](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%A1%B4%20%EC%B1%88%EB%8D%94%EC%8A%A4 "John Chanders") occupied the right wing, John IV led the center, and another English army led by [Robert Knowles](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EB%A1%9C%EB%B2%84%ED%8A%B8%20%EB%86%80%EC%8A%A4 "Robert Knowles") occupied the left wing. And [Hugh Calvley](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%ED%9C%B4%20%EC%B9%BC%EB%B8%94%EB%A6%AC "Hugh Carbley") led the reserve unit. Charles de Blois's army also formed three ranks to oppose it. Charles himself commanded the right wing, Guéclin led the center, and Jean III, Count of Auxerre, led the left wing. It is not known who led the French reserve forces.

John IV and Charles attempted to negotiate by sending envoys before the battle. The two men were exhausted from the long civil war and hoped to end the war by dividing Brittany. However, the English generals had no intention of ending it so half-heartedly. They threatened to kill the envoys Charles had sent if he attempted to make further proposals. In particular, [Olivier V de Clisson,](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%98%AC%EB%A6%AC%EB%B9%84%EC%97%90%205%EC%84%B8%20%EB%93%9C%20%ED%81%B4%EB%A6%AC%EC%86%A1 "Olivier V de Clisson") who was allied with the English army, had no intention of forgiving Charles, his father's enemy. Guesquelin and other Blois supporters also showed intransigence, and negotiations eventually broke down. Many Bretons on both sides, who had hoped that the negotiations would go well and end peacefully, were disappointed and deserted.

Afterwards, both sides marched towards each other, and a firefight broke out between the English longbowmen and the French crossbowmen. Afterwards, men-at-arms and spearmen from both sides clashed head-on. Both sides were very desperate as they wanted to end the long and cruel war with this battle. After half a day of fierce hand-to-hand combat, John Chanders' English right-wing troops overwhelmed the Count of Auxerre's left-wing troops. The Count of Auxerre lost an eye and was taken prisoner, and his men fled to the central unit led by Guéclin. As a result, the formation of the central unit was disrupted, and Chanders did not miss this opportunity and intercepted the flank of the enemy's central unit.

Seeing that our troops were in danger, many of the right-wing troops under Charles fled, and the reserve troops in the rear also ran away. John IV and [Robert Knowles](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EB%A1%9C%EB%B2%84%ED%8A%B8%20%EB%86%80%EC%8A%A4 "Robert Knowles") , along with John Chanders, surrounded the central Guesquelin unit, and Hugh Calvley, who was leading the reserve unit, also jumped into the battlefield. In the end, the Blois army lost its will to fight and was routed, and Charles de Blois was killed. Guesclin fought desperately, but surrendered when he was completely surrounded. In this battle, 800 of the Breton-French allies of the Blois family were killed and 1,200 were taken prisoner. The damage suffered by the Montfort family's combined forces of Brittany and England is not known, but it would have been relatively small.

The day after the battle, Jean IV of Brittany sent a letter to King [Charles V](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%83%A4%EB%A5%BC%205%EC%84%B8 "Charles V") of France , requesting that he be recognized as the Duke of Brittany as he would remain loyal to France. Charles V decided to accept this and persuaded Jeanne de Penthievre to give up her intention to become the Duchess of Brittany. Joan had no choice but to accept, and on April 12, 1365, John IV signed the Treaty of Guérande, which stipulated that Joan would become a vassal of the King of France and be recognized as Duke of Brittany on the condition of paying a significant amount of compensation to Joan. Thus ended the War of Succession to the Duke of Brittany.

After Charles de Blois died, Breton residents frequently visited his tomb in Guingampo, and the Breton bishops who followed him promoted him as a martyr and gave lead statues of Charles to pilgrims who came to pray at his tomb. distributed. On February 1, 1368, men sent by John IV of Brittany destroyed a painting of Charles de Blois kneeling at the feet of Saint Francis of Assisi that hung in the chapel of the Cordelier Church in Dinan. However, on February 3, hundreds of believers who visited the chapel witnessed two streams of blood flowing from the remains of the painting around the chest and neck, and collected these remains as relics. Guillaume Paula, Bishop of Saint-Malo, ordered the chapel's guardian to restore the painting.

On September 15, 1368, Pope [Urban V](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%9A%B0%EB%A5%B4%EB%B0%94%EB%85%B8%205%EC%84%B8 "Urban 5") , at the strong request of John IV of Brittany, sent a letter to the Breton bishops condemning them for naming Charles a martyr without papal approval and forbidding them to erect his tomb. He threatened to [excommunicate](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%ED%8C%8C%EB%AC%B8 "stir") pilgrims . However, the pilgrims ignored this and continued to visit, and a worker named Rouran Taillard claimed that he was cured of gout after visiting Charles' tomb. [On](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%83%A4%EB%A5%BC%205%EC%84%B8 "Charles V") January 15 , 1371, the new Pope [Gregory](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EA%B7%B8%EB%A0%88%EA%B3%A0%EB%A6%AC%EC%98%A4%2011%EC%84%B8 "Gregory XI") John IV of Brittany strongly requested the Pope to stop the canonization investigation, but was ignored.

During the canonization investigation, the Franciscans of Perigueux reported in their Cum permissu Superioris that Charles had dedicated a chapel and that 11 people had made a pilgrimage to Charles's tomb and received grace. At this time, it is said that more than five Montfort supporters, including three Englishmen, also received grace. Antoine Hulze, the butler of John IV of Brittany, was cured of hemiplegia, and Comiton, an Englishman, was said to have had his legs cured. It is said that Jean-François slandered Charles de Blois, fell seriously ill and became mute, but was completely cured after apologizing to Charles.

After compiling these reports, Gregory XI decided to proceed with the process of canonizing Charles de Blois as a saint. However, the canonization process was postponed from time to time due to the Vatican's move to Rome and the subsequent [great schism in the Western Church,](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%84%9C%EB%B0%A9%EA%B5%90%ED%9A%8C%20%EB%8C%80%EB%B6%84%EC%97%B4 "Great Schism in the Western Church") and was never carried out. However, the French government regarded Charles de Blois as a de facto saint, and celebrated his feast day until the 19th century without the approval of the Vatican. Then, in 1894, the beatification process was resumed, and on December 14, 1904, Charles de Blois was [beatified](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%8B%9C%EB%B3%B5 "Beatification") as ' [Blessed](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EB%B3%B5%EC%9E%90 "Blessed") Charles of Blois . ' His feast day is September 30.

*       *   Jean I de Châtillon (1340 - 1404): Count of Penthièvre, Viscount of Limoges, Baron of Avogur, and Lord of Avenes.

    *   Marie de Blois (1345 – 1404): Countess of Guise and Baroness of Mayenne. She was the wife of [Louis I,](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EB%A3%A8%EC%9D%B4%201%EC%84%B8(%EC%95%99%EC%A3%BC) "Louis I (Anjou)") Duke of Anjou .

    *   Marguerite de Blois (? ~ after 1354): Wife of [Charles de la Cerda,](https://en.namu.wiki/w/%EC%83%A4%EB%A5%BC%20%EB%93%9C%20%EB%9D%BC%20%EC%84%B8%EB%A5%B4%EB%8B%A4 "Charles de la Cerda") Count of Angoulême.

31.content:
Top Questions

*   Who was Philip VI of France?
    
*   How did Philip VI become king of France?
    
*   When did Philip VI rule France?
    
*   Why was Philip VI's reign important in French history?
    
*   What major war started during Philip VI’s reign?
    
*   How did Philip VI's rule affect the future of France?
    

**Philip VI** (born 1293—died Aug. 22, 1350, near Paris) was the first French [king](https://www.britannica.com/topic/king-monarch) of the Valois [dynasty](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/dynasty). Reigning at the outbreak of the [Hundred Years’ War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Hundred-Years-War) (1337–1453), he had no means of imposing on his [country](https://www.britannica.com/topic/nation-state) the measures necessary for the maintenance of his monarchical power, though he continued the efforts of the 13th-century Capetians toward the centralization of the administration in [Paris](https://www.britannica.com/place/Paris). To raise taxes for war, he was obliged to make [concessions](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/concessions) to the nobility, the clergy, and the [bourgeoisie](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/bourgeoisie); hence his reign witnessed the important development of the political power of the estates. The bourgeoisie, profiting from the king’s power, proved grateful and loyal; among the clergy and nobility, however, a movement for reform of finances took root.

The elder son of [Charles of Valois](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-III-count-of-Valois), Philip was first cousin to the brothers [Louis X](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-X), [Philip V](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-V-king-of-France), and [Charles IV](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-IV-king-of-France), the last Capetian kings of the direct line. On the death of Charles IV in 1328, Philip, in the face of opposition from the partisans of the claim of [Edward III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-III-king-of-England) of England, assumed the regency until the end of the pregnancy of Charles IV’s widow. When the widow produced a daughter, who therefore could not succeed to the throne, Philip became king and was [crowned](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/crowned) at Reims in May 1328.

Quick Facts

French:

Philippe De Valois

Died:

Aug. 22, 1350, near Paris (aged 57)

After the outbreak of a revolt in [Flanders](https://www.britannica.com/place/Flanders-medieval-principality-and-historical-region-Europe) in August of that year, the count of Flanders appealed to Philip, whose knights butchered thousands of rebellious Flemings at the Battle of Cassel. When shortly thereafter Robert of Artois, who had helped Philip to win the crown, claimed the countship of Artois against a member of the royal family, Philip was forced to institute judicial proceedings against Robert, who became his bitter enemy. In 1334 Robert went to England and began to foment trouble between Edward III and Philip, hastening the deterioration of Anglo-French relations, which in 1337 led to the outbreak of the Hundred Years’ War. Military operations were at first restricted. In 1340, however, [France](https://www.britannica.com/place/France) suffered a grave defeat in the naval [Battle of Sluys](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Sluys). Meanwhile, the internal situation had worsened, as a result of [resentment](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/resentment) over the preponderant influence of the nominees of the powerful Duke of Burgundy in the king’s council. A serious crisis resulted in 1343 and forced Philip to summon to Paris the estates of the kingdom, which took some measures to appease [public opinion](https://www.britannica.com/topic/public-opinion) and to relieve the burdens of administration. France’s devastating defeat by the English at Crécy (1346) gave rise to another crisis. To conciliate opponents, the government was obliged to entrust finances to three abbots. A new meeting of the estates in November 1347 again forced the King to recast his council. The spread of the [Black Death](https://www.britannica.com/event/Black-Death) in 1348 and 1349, however, overshadowed all political questions. When Philip died, he left France divided by war and plague, although by purchase he had made some important additions to the territory of the kingdom.

[![Image 1: Napoleon Bonaparte. Napoleon in Coronation Robes or Napoleon I Emperor of France, 1804 by Baron Francois Gerard or Baron Francois-Pascal-Simon Gerard, from the Musee National, Chateau de Versailles.](https://cdn.britannica.com/95/115195-131-5A6187D9/Napoleon-His-Imperial-Robes-Francois-Gerard-Versailles-1805.jpg) Britannica Quiz Kings and Emperors (Part III) Quiz](https://www.britannica.com/quiz/kings-and-emperors-part-iii-quiz)
