External impact
In 2007, Wikipedia was deemed fit to be used as a major source by the UK Intellectual Property Office in a Formula One trademark case ruling.[217]
Over time, Wikipedia gained recognition amongst more traditional media as a "key source" for major new events, such as the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and related tsunami, the 2008 American Presidential election,[218] and 2007 Virginia Tech shooting. The latter article was accessed 750,000 times in two days, with newspapers published locally to the shootings adding that "Wikipedia has emerged as the clearinghouse for detailed information on the event."[219]
On 21 February 2007, Noam Cohen of the New York Times reported that some academics were banning the use of Wikipedia as a research tool.[220]
On 27 February 2007, an article in The Harvard Crimson newspaper reported that some professors at Harvard University included Wikipedia in their syllabi, but that there was a split in their perception of using Wikipedia.[221]
In July 2013, a large-scale study by four major universities identified the most disputed articles on Wikipedia, finding that Israel, Adolf Hitler, and God were more fiercely debated than any other subjects.[222]
Effect of biographical articles
Because Wikipedia biographies are often updated with new information comes, they are often used as a reference source on the lives of notable people. This has led to attempts to manipulate and falsify Wikipedia articles for promotional or defamatory purposes (Controversies) and has also led to novel uses of the biographical material provided.

In November 2005, the Seigenthaler controversy occurred when a hoaxer asserted on Wikipedia that journalist John Seigenthaler had been involved in the Kennedy assassination of 1963.
In December 2006, German comedian Atze Schröder sued Arne Klempert, secretary of Wikimedia Deutschland because he did not want his real name published in Wikipedia. Schröder later withdrew his complaint but wanted his attorney's costs to be paid by Klempert. A court decided that the artist had to cover those costs himself.[223]
On 16 February 2007, Turkish historian Taner Akçam was briefly detained upon arrival at Montréal–Pierre Elliott Trudeau International Airport because of false information on his Wikipedia biography claiming he was a terrorist.[224][225]
In November 2008, the German Left Party politician Lutz Heilmann claimed that some remarks in his Wikipedia article caused damage to his reputation. He succeeded in getting a court order to make Wikimedia Deutschland remove a key search portal. The result was a national outpouring of support for Wikipedia, more donations to Wikimedia Deutschland, and a rise in daily pageviews of the Lutz Heilmann article from a few dozen to half a million. Shortly after, Heilmann asked the court to withdraw the court order.[226]
In December 2008, Wikimedia Nederland, the Dutch chapter, won a preliminary injunction after an entrepreneur was linked in "his" article with the criminal Willem Holleeder and wanted the article deleted. The judge in Utrecht believed Wikimedia's assertion that it has no influence on the content of Dutch Wikipedia.[227]
In February 2009, when the German politician Karl Theodor Maria Nikolaus Johann Jacob Philipp Franz Joseph Sylvester Buhl-Freiherr von und zu Guttenberg became a federal minister on 10 February 2009, an unregistered user added an eleventh given name in the article on German Wikipedia: Wilhelm. Numerous newspapers adopted it. When wary Wikipedians tried to remove Wilhelm, the edit was reverted citing those newspapers. This case about Wikipedia reliability and journalists copying from Wikipedia was dubbed Falscher Wilhelm ("wrong Wilhelm").[228]
Early roles of Wales and Sanger

See also: Jimmy Wales § Co-founder status controversy, and Larry Sanger § Status as Wikipedia co-founder
Wales, along with others, came up with and funded the idea of an open-source, collaborative encyclopedia that would accept contributions from ordinary people.[19] Sanger played an important role in this as Nupedia's editor-in-chief and main employee.[229] In Sanger's introductory message to the Nupedia mailing list, he said that Jimmy Wales "contacted me and asked me to apply as editor-in-chief of Nupedia. [...] He had had the idea for Nupedia since at least last fall. He tells me that, when thinking about people (particularly philosophers) he knew who could manage this sort of long-term project, he thought I would be perfect for the job. This is indeed my dream job".[230]
Sanger suggested using a wiki to provide a complementary project for people "intimidated and bored" by Nupedia's elaborate processes,[27] and coined the portmanteau "Wikipedia" as the project name.[231][229] This was broadly seen as a way to unblock the growing community of Nupedians who found it hard to contribute.[229] Sanger continued to work on Nupedia while contributing to Wikipedia (including drafting policies such as "Ignore all rules"[232] and "Neutral point of view"[63]) and worked with an outreach lead to build up the community of both Nupedia and Wikipedia editors.[229] Upon departure in March 2002, Sanger emphasized the main issue was purely the cessation of funding for his role, which was not viable part-time,[21] and encouraged others to continue contributing to Wikipedia while noting that Nupedia could not survive without a full-time editor-in-chief.[21] Later that year he stopped contributing to either project, and by 2004 had become publicly critical of Wikipedia. In December 2004 he wrote an essay arguing that Wikipedia was suffering from anti-elitism.[233] In April 2005 he published a two-part memoir of his work on Nupedia and Wikipedia, highlighting his role in their creation and continuing belief that Nupedia deserved to be saved.[233] Later that year Wales began to push back on Sanger's characterization of his role in the project.[234][235][236] By 2006, after the launch of Citizendium, Sanger was harshly critical of Wikipedia, describing it as "broken beyond repair."[237]
In 2005, Wales described himself simply as the founder of Wikipedia;[234] however, according to Brian Bergstein of the Associated Press, "Sanger has long been cited as a co-founder."[229] Sanger and Wales were referred to as co-founders in various press releases, interviews, and news reports from 2001[238] and 2002.[239] Before January 2004, Wales did not dispute Sanger's status as co-founder.[240] In 2006, Wales said, "He used to work for me [...] I don't agree with calling him a co-founder, but he likes the title".[241] Starting in 2006, when Sanger wrote and was interviewed extensively about the launch of Citizendium, he emphasized his status as co-founder, and these earlier sources that described him as such.[229][238][242][243]

Controversies

Main articles: Criticism of Wikipedia, Litigation involving the Wikimedia Foundation, and Reliability of Wikipedia
In November 2005, the Seigenthaler controversy caused Brian Chase to resign from his employment, after his identity was ascertained by Daniel Brandt of Wikipedia Watch. Following this, the scientific journal Nature undertook a peer reviewed study to test articles in Wikipedia against their equivalents in Encyclopædia Britannica, and concluded they are comparable in terms of accuracy.[244][245] Britannica rejected their methodology and their conclusion.[246] Nature refused to release any form of apology, and instead asserted the reliability of its study and a rejection of the criticisms.[247]
During early-to-mid-2006, the congressional aides biography scandals were publicized, whereby political aides were caught trying to influence the Wikipedia biographies of several politicians. The aides removed undesirable information (including pejorative quotes and broken campaign promises), added favorable information or "glowing" tributes, or replaced the article in part or whole by staff-authored biographies. In July 2006, Joshua Gardner was exposed as a fake Duke of Cleveland with a Wikipedia page.[253]
In January 2007, English-language Wikipedians in Qatar were briefly blocked from editing, following a spate of vandalism, by an administrator who did not realize that the country's internet traffic is routed through a single IP address. Multiple media sources promptly declared that Wikipedia was banning Qatar from the site.[254]
On 23 January 2007, a Microsoft employee offered to pay Rick Jelliffe to review and change certain Wikipedia articles regarding an open-source document standard which was rival to a Microsoft format.[255]
In February 2007, The New Yorker magazine issued a rare editorial correction that a prominent English Wikipedia editor and administrator known as "Essjay", had invented a persona using fictitious credentials.[256][257] The editor, Ryan Jordan, became a Wikia employee in January 2007 and divulged his real name; this was noticed by Daniel Brandt of Wikipedia Watch, and communicated to the original article author (Essjay controversy).
Also in February 2007, Barbara Bauer, a literary agent, sued Wikimedia for defamation and causing harm to her business, the Barbara Bauer Literary Agency.[258] In Bauer v. Glatzer, Bauer claimed that information on Wikipedia critical of her abilities as a literary agent caused this harm. The Electronic Frontier Foundation defended Wikipedia[259] and moved to dismiss the case on 1 May 2008.[260] The case against the Wikimedia Foundation was dismissed on 1 July 2008.[261]
In June 2007, an anonymous user posted hoax information that, by coincidence, foreshadowed the Chris Benoit murder-suicide, hours before the bodies were found by investigators. The discovery of the edit attracted widespread media attention and was first covered in the sister site Wikinews.
In October 2007, in their obituaries of recently deceased TV theme composer Ronnie Hazlehurst, many British media organisations reported that he had co-written the S Club 7 song "Reach". In fact, he had not, and it was discovered that this information had been sourced from a hoax edit to Hazlehurst's Wikipedia article.[262]
On 14 July 2009, the National Portrait Gallery issued a cease-and-desist letter for alleged breach of copyright, against a Wikipedia editor who downloaded more than 3,000 high-resolution images from the NPG website, and placed them on Wikimedia Commons (National Portrait Gallery and Wikimedia Foundation copyright dispute).[263][264][265][266][267]
In April and May 2010, there was controversy over the hosting and display of sexual drawing and pornographic images including images of children on Wikipedia.[268][269][270] It led to the mass removal of pornographic content from Wikimedia Foundation sites.[271][272]
In November 2012, Lord Justice Leveson wrote in his report on British press standards, "The Independent was founded in 1986 by the journalists Andreas Whittam Smith, Stephen Glover and Brett Straub..." He had used the Wikipedia article for The Independent newspaper as his source, but an act of vandalism had replaced Matthew Symonds (a genuine co-founder) with Brett Straub (an unknown character).[273] The Economist said of the Leveson report, "Parts of it are a scissors-and-paste job culled from Wikipedia."[274]
In late 2013, commentators publicly shared observations of the reappearance of many of the pornographic images deleted from Wikipedia since 2010.[275]
Notable forks and derivatives
There are a large number of Wikipedia mirror and forks. Other sites also use the MediaWiki software and concept, popularized by Wikipedia. No list of them is maintained. Specialized foreign language forks using the Wikipedia concept include Enciclopedia Libre (Spanish), Wikiweise (German), WikiZnanie (Russian), Susning.nu (Swedish), and Baidu Baike (Chinese). Some of these (such as Enciclopedia Libre) use GFDL or compatible licenses as used by Wikipedia, leading to the exchange of material with their respective language Wikipedias. In 2006, Sanger founded Citizendium, based upon a modified version of MediaWiki.[276] The site said it aimed 'to improve on the Wikipedia model with "gentle expert oversight", among other things'.[66][277] In 2006, conservative activist and lawyer Andrew Schlafly founded Conservapedia, based on MediaWiki.

Publication on other media
The German Wikipedia was the first to be partly published also using other media (rather than online on the internet), including releases on CD in November 2004[278] and more extended versions on CDs or DVD in April 2005 and December 2006. In December 2005, the publisher Zenodot Verlagsgesellschaft mbH, a sister company of Directmedia, published a 139-page book explaining Wikipedia, its history and policies, which was accompanied by a 7.5 GB DVD containing 300,000 articles and 100,000 images from the German Wikipedia.[279] Originally, Directmedia also announced plans to print the German Wikipedia in its entirety, in 100 volumes of 800 pages each. The publication was due to begin in October 2006, and finish in 2010. In March 2006, however, this project was called off.[280]
In September 2008, Bertelsmann published a 1000 pages volume with a selection of popular German Wikipedia articles. Bertelsmann paid voluntarily 1 Euro per sold copy to Wikimedia Deutschland.[281] A free software project has also been launched to make a static version of English Wikipedia available for use on iPods. The "Encyclopodia" project was started around March 2006 and can currently be used on 1st to 4th-generation iPods.[282]

Lawsuits
In limited ways, the Wikimedia Foundation is protected by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. In the defamation action Bauer et al. v. Glatzer et al., it was held that Wikimedia had no case to answer because of this section.[294] A similar law in France caused a lawsuit to be dismissed in October 2007.[295] In 2013, a German appeals court or Oberlandesgericht (the Higher Regional Court of Stuttgart) ruled that Wikipedia is a "service provider" not a "content provider", and as such is immune from liability as long as it takes down content that is accused of being illegal.[296]

The **Ramparts of Vannes** are the [fortifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortification "Fortification") erected between the 3rd and 17th centuries to protect the city of [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes") in the [Morbihan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morbihan "Morbihan") department in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"). Founded by the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") at the end of the 1st century BC under the reign of [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus "Augustus"), the _[civitas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civitas "Civitas") [Venetorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veneti_/(Gaul/) "Veneti (Gaul)")_ was forced to protect itself behind a [castrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_fort "Roman fort") at the end of the 3rd century, during a major crisis shaking the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"). This first enclosure remained the city’s only protection for over a millennium. During the time of [Duke John IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV_of_Brittany "John IV of Brittany"), at the end of the 14th century, the city’s enclosure was rebuilt and extended southward to protect the new districts. The duke wanted to make Vannes not only a place of residence but also a stronghold he could rely on in case of conflict. The area of the city intra-muros was doubled, and the duke added his [Château de l’Hermine](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ch%C3%A2teau_de_l%E2%80%99Hermine&action=edit&redlink=1 "Château de l’Hermine (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_l%27Hermine_/(Vannes/) "fr:Château de l'Hermine (Vannes)")) to the new enclosure.

The [Wars of the League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion "French Wars of Religion") at the end of the 14th century forced the city to equip itself with several polygonal [bastions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion") (Gréguennic, Haute-Folie, Brozilay, Notre-Dame). The Garenne spur was the last defensive structure built in Vannes around 1630. From 1670, King [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV") sold parts of the ramparts piece by piece to finance his wars. The most significant event was, in 1697, the donation to the city of Vannes of the ruins of the Château de l’Hermine, which were then used for the redevelopment of the port and the maintenance of municipal buildings.

The urban developments of the 19th century led to the demolition of several segments of the northern and western walls. It was not until the partial destruction in 1886 of the Prison Gate, one of the oldest entrances to the old city, that Vannes residents attached to their heritage came together to form a heritage defense association in 1911. This led to the gradual establishment of protection for the ramparts as [historical monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_historique "Monument historique") between 1912 and 1958. For several decades, the city has been undertaking the restoration and enhancement of the parts of the ramparts it owns. A cornerstone of Vannes’ heritage and a quintessential tourist attraction, the Ramparts of Vannes are among the few urban fortifications still remaining in [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany").

At the end of the 3rd century, under the threat of [Germanic peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_peoples "Germanic peoples"), the [Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Roman_emperors "List of Roman emperors") [Probus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probus_/(emperor/) "Probus (emperor)") authorized [Darioritum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darioritum "Darioritum"), like all the cities of the [Saxon Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Shore "Saxon Shore"), to raise fortifications. The ancient town of Vannes thus surrounded itself with ramparts on the Mené hill and abandoned the Boismoreau hill, which formed the heart of the city.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:0-1) The choice of this location was due to its configuration: the Mené hill was at that time a rocky promontory surrounded by marshes.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) This first enclosure was roughly triangular and extended from the current rue du Méné, in the north, to the [Place des Lices](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Place_des_Lices&action=edit&redlink=1 "Place des Lices (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_des_Lices_/(Vannes/) "fr:Place des Lices (Vannes)")), in the south. More precisely, it was an “irregular hexagon comprising three large sides, of unequal lengths, connected to each other by three small sides, also of unequal lengths”.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-3) This first enclosure, with a perimeter of less than 1,000 metres (3,300 ft), encompassed approximately 5 hectares.[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-p%C3%A9ri-4)

Sources then dry up for the following centuries. What is certain is that a fortress is attested in the 10th century on the northern wall. Some sources mention the 5th or 6th centuries as a possible period for its construction, as it seems that [Eusebius of Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eusebius_of_Vannes&action=edit&redlink=1 "Eusebius of Vannes (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eus%C3%A8be_de_Vannes "fr:Eusèbe de Vannes")), semi-legendary king of Vannes, was already using this castle as a residence at the beginning of the 6th century.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) This fortress was named _Château de la Motte_. Its etymology is not settled: perhaps due to its dominant position over the city or due to significant earthworks during construction.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) The Château de la Motte later became the residence of the counts of Vannes, then of some of the [kings and dukes of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Breton_rulers "List of Breton rulers"), including [Macliau](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Macliau&action=edit&redlink=1 "Macliau (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macliau "fr:Macliau")), [Waroch II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waroch_II "Waroch II"), [Nominoë](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomino%C3%AB "Nominoë"), [John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Brittany "John I of Brittany"), and [Peter Mauclerc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_I_of_Brittany "Peter I of Brittany").

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Prise_de_Vannes_1342_%281845x2582%29.jpg/250px-Prise_de_Vannes_1342_%281845x2582%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prise_de_Vannes_1342_/(1845x2582/).jpg)

Capture of Vannes by Guillaume Fillastre (15th century).

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Litus_Saxonicum.png/250px-Litus_Saxonicum.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Litus_Saxonicum.png)

The Saxon Shore.

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Vannes_remparts_romains.JPG/250px-Vannes_remparts_romains.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vannes_remparts_romains.JPG)

The Roman section of the ramparts, north of the Joliette Tower.

The incessant wars of the duke with his neighbors during the XII weakened the ramparts. Thus, the city was besieged five times between 1156 and 1175, twice by [Henry Plantagenêt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_II_of_England "Henry II of England") (in 1168 and 1175).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:0-1) As a result, Duke [John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Brittany "John I of Brittany") decided to undertake the restoration of the ramparts starting in 1237. The [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake "Earthquake") of 1287 prompted his successor, [John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_Brittany "John II of Brittany"), to continue the work, which was completed in 1305. The Château de la Motte, too damaged by the earthquake, was then ceded to the bishop [Henri Tore](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henri_Tore&action=edit&redlink=1 "Henri Tore (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Tore "fr:Henri Tore")). He decided to rebuild it starting in 1288 to make it the episcopal manor of la Motte, the residence of the city’s bishops.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:0-1)

In 1342, during the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"), the city endured four more sieges, changing hands several times between the party of [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), supported by the French, and that of [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). The Vannes residents, who declared themselves in favor of John of Montfort in 1341, surrendered to the army of Charles of Blois at the beginning of 1342, but an English army, commanded by [Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois"), retook the city in August. A few days later, [Olivier de Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_V_de_Clisson "Olivier V de Clisson") recaptured the city for the French after another siege in which Robert d’Artois was mortally wounded. The city successfully resisted a final siege led by [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") in November.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5)

Access to the walled city during the High Middle Ages was through five gates: Saint-Patern, Saint-Salomon, Bali, Saint-Jean, and Mariolle.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-patrimoine-6)

### The Second Enclosure

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The Second Enclosure")\]

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Sceau_de_Jean_IV_-_Duc_de_Bretagne.png/250px-Sceau_de_Jean_IV_-_Duc_de_Bretagne.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sceau_de_Jean_IV_-_Duc_de_Bretagne.png)

Seal of Duke [John IV of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV_of_Brittany "John IV of Brittany").

After the war, [John IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV_of_Brittany "John IV of Brittany"), son of John of Montfort, designated Duke of Brittany by the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"), repaired and expanded the ramparts southward to encompass the city’s suburbs. The area of the [walled city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_city "Walled city") then increased from 5 to 13 hectares.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:3-7) Two gates and their [barbicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbican "Barbican"), Calmont and Gréguennic, were added to the enclosure; the city also acquired three towers around the mid-15th century: the Executioner’s Tower, the Powder Tower, and the Joliette Tower.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-patrimoine-6) The work was not fully completed until the reigns of [John V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V_of_Brittany "John V of Brittany") and [Francis II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II_of_Brittany "Francis II of Brittany").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2)

John IV added to this reinforcement of the city’s defenses the construction of his new residence, the Château de l’Hermine, built between 1380 and 1385. To do so, he exchanged the mill he owned at Pencastel ([Arzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arzon "Arzon")) for the one at Garenne, belonging to the [Abbey of Saint-Gildas de Rhuys](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Abbey_of_Saint-Gildas_de_Rhuys&action=edit&redlink=1 "Abbey of Saint-Gildas de Rhuys (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbaye_Saint-Gildas_de_Rhuys "fr:Abbaye Saint-Gildas de Rhuys")).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) As evidence of the growing importance of this new residence, births and marriages took place there at the end of the century and the beginning of the next: [John V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V_of_Brittany "John V of Brittany") was born there in 1389,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-8) and [Joan of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Navarre,_Queen_of_England "Joan of Navarre, Queen of England") married [Henry IV of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_England "Henry IV of England") by proxy there in 1402.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:0-1) It became the near-permanent residence of the subsequent dukes until [Francis II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II_of_Brittany "Francis II of Brittany"), who preferred staying in [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes"), where he had a new [château](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_des_ducs_de_Bretagne "Château des ducs de Bretagne") built. The Château de l’Hermine then became a place of refuge or detention, depending on the duke’s will and the status of his “guests”: a residence for [Charles of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Valois,_Duke_of_Berry "Charles of Valois, Duke of Berry") in his struggle against his brother [Louis XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XI "Louis XI") between 1466 and 1467, or for [Henry Tudor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England") in 1483–1484, and a prison for [Guillaume Chauvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Guillaume_Chauvin&action=edit&redlink=1 "Guillaume Chauvin (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Chauvin "fr:Guillaume Chauvin")), former chancellor of Brittany, between 1481 and 1484.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:0-1)

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Prise_de_Vannes_1342_%28Wavrin%29.png/250px-Prise_de_Vannes_1342_%28Wavrin%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prise_de_Vannes_1342_/(Wavrin/).png)

Second capture of Vannes by Jean de Wavrin (mid-15th century).

The [war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War "Breton War") reignited a few years later, and the city was besieged and captured five times between 1487 and 1490.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-9) The Breton defeat in this war marked the end of Breton independence, formalized nearly forty years later, on 4, with the request of the [Estates of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates_of_Brittany "Estates of Brittany"), at the Château de la Motte, to the King of France [Francis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_France "Francis I of France") for the [union of Brittany to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Union_of_Brittany_to_France&action=edit&redlink=1 "Union of Brittany to France (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_du_duch%C3%A9_de_Bretagne_%C3%A0_la_couronne_de_France "fr:Union du duché de Bretagne à la couronne de France"))[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-10)

This miniature by [Jean de Wavrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_de_Wavrin "Jean de Wavrin") depicts the second capture of Vannes in 1342 by John of Montfort and the English camp. The battle takes place in the city’s moats between the Powder Tower and the Prison Gate. Anachronistic since these elements were built after 1430 and the [Romanesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanesque_architecture "Romanesque architecture") tower of the [cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes_Cathedral "Vannes Cathedral") in the background was rebuilt only after 1450, this depiction is nevertheless faithful to the ramparts of the mid-15th century. The soldiers’ weapons ([swords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword "Sword") and [bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_/(weapon/) "Bow (weapon)")) are typical of the mid-14th century, while the arrow slits are adapted to [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery "Artillery") fire (mid-15th century).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2)

### Final reinforcements to partial dismantling

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Final reinforcements to partial dismantling")\]

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Philippe-emmanuel-de-mercoeur_%28d%C3%A9tail%29.png/250px-Philippe-emmanuel-de-mercoeur_%28d%C3%A9tail%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Philippe-emmanuel-de-mercoeur_/(d%C3%A9tail/).png)

[Philippe-Emmanuel de Lorraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe-Emmanuel_de_Lorraine "Philippe-Emmanuel de Lorraine"), Duke of Mercœur.

The integration of [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") into the [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") brought a certain calm, both economic and military. The utility of the ramparts became less certain, but the city continued to maintain them to some extent in the 17th century, although the demolition of the Château de l’Hermine was decided during this period.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5)

At the end of the 16th century, during the [Wars of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion "French Wars of Religion"), several strategic cities in Brittany adopted the principle of [bastioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion "Bastion") fortifications, a necessity due to improvements in [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery "Artillery"). Under the [Catholic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_League_/(France/) "Catholic League (France)"), Vannes sided with the [Duke of Mercœur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe-Emmanuel_de_Lorraine "Philippe-Emmanuel de Lorraine"), governor of Brittany and a Leaguer. During his stay in Vannes in 1592, he employed his engineers and architects to improve the city’s fortifications.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) The city then strengthened the ramparts with the bastions of Gréguennic, Brozillay, and Haute-Folie in the southeast of the enclosure.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-patrimoine-6) To the south, an opening was made for communication with the [port](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Port_de_Vannes&action=edit&redlink=1 "Port de Vannes (page does not exist)"). This was the Kaër-Calmont gate, which became the Saint-Vincent gate a few decades later. Between 1594 and 1598, Spanish troops were stationed in the city at the request of the Duke of Mercœur and the governor of Vannes, [René d’Arradon](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ren%C3%A9_d%E2%80%99Arradon&action=edit&redlink=1 "René d’Arradon (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_d%E2%80%99Arradon "fr:René d’Arradon")). The city’s coffers were empty, and the work remained unfinished by the end of the 16th century[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2)

After the failure of the League, Vannes suffered the repercussions of political instability and events along the Atlantic coast. Although the city no longer had a strategic role, its enclosure received final defensive improvements in the early decades of the 17th century. The bastions hastily erected under the League were improved between 1611 and 1619. Jean Bugeau rebuilt the Notre-Dame bastion in stone. The Haute-Folie bastion was rebuilt using [piles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pile_foundation "Pile foundation") by André Bugeau. The Saint-Salomon gate was also supposed to receive a bastion, but the project was abandoned.

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Plan_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9ral_de_la_prison_criminelle_de_Vannes_%281811%29.jpg/250px-Plan_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9ral_de_la_prison_criminelle_de_Vannes_%281811%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plan_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9ral_de_la_prison_criminelle_de_Vannes_/(1811/).jpg)

Plan of the criminal prison in 1811 (Prison Tower)

Between 1622 and 1624, Jean Bugeau was in charge of the construction of the bridge and the Kaër-Calmont (Ker-Calmont) gate. The work was completed in 1624, and the gate was renamed [Saint-Vincent Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Vincent_Gate "Saint-Vincent Gate") in homage to the preacher Saint [Vincent Ferrer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Ferrer "Vincent Ferrer"), who died in Vannes in 1419. The Garenne spur, intended to protect the passage of the Poterne gate, was built by the Vannes architect Antoine Angueneau between 1626 and 1628 after the withdrawal of the Nantes architect Jacques Corbineau.

Vannes experienced urban expansion in the second half of the 17th century, thanks to strong economic and religious growth and the establishment of the [Parliament of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Brittany "Parliament of Brittany") in the city between 1675 and 1689. To accommodate the steadily increasing population and facilitate movement within the intra-muros, the city undertook various developments. With the construction, between 1678 and 1688, of the Poterne and Saint-Jean gates by the architect François Cosnier, the city now had six gates.

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Vannes_-_Remparts_-_Tour_du_Conn%C3%A9table_-_Cath%C3%A9drale_%281900%29.png/250px-Vannes_-_Remparts_-_Tour_du_Conn%C3%A9table_-_Cath%C3%A9drale_%281900%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vannes_-_Remparts_-_Tour_du_Conn%C3%A9table_-_Cath%C3%A9drale_/(1900/).png)

Orchards at the foot of the ramparts around 1900.

The bishop [Charles de Rosmadec](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_de_Rosmadec&action=edit&redlink=1 "Charles de Rosmadec (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Rosmadec "fr:Charles de Rosmadec")) rebuilt the manor of la Motte starting in 1654,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) but in 1688, its dismantling was decided. In 1697, the remains of the Château de l’Hermine were donated to the city by the [King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_France "King of France") [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV"). These, along with the sections of the wall being demolished, served as a quarry for the restoration of municipal buildings.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) At the end of the 18th century, the city planned the destruction of parts of the ramparts to prevent the risk of collapse of the least well-maintained elements and to widen traffic routes. In 1784, the Notre-Dame gate and part of the bastion of the same name were demolished. During the Revolution, in 1791, the Saint-Salomon gate collapsed.

Julien Lagorce, a caterer, purchased the site of the former Château de l’Hermine to build a hotel in 1785.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) In 1791, the manor of la Motte was abandoned by the bishop of the time, [Sébastien-Michel Amelot](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=S%C3%A9bastien-Michel_Amelot&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sébastien-Michel Amelot (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A9bastien-Michel_Amelot "fr:Sébastien-Michel Amelot")). Nine years later, the Morbihan prefecture services moved in. However, poorly maintained, it continued to deteriorate. A section of the wall collapsed in 1860, prompting the departure of the prefectural services, which moved to the [current building](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Current_building&action=edit&redlink=1 "Current building (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%A9fecture_du_Morbihan "fr:Préfecture du Morbihan")) in 1865.

During the 19th century, the city implemented the embellishment plan drawn up in 1785–1787 by the engineer Maury. The development of [Place Gambetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Place_Gambetta&action=edit&redlink=1 "Place Gambetta (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_Gambetta_/(Vannes/) "fr:Place Gambetta (Vannes)")) concealed the ramparts on either side of the Saint-Vincent gate. Other sections of the walls were demolished to allow the creation of new streets. The rue Le Mintier de Lehélec was opened in the west in 1826–1827. The manor of la Motte was razed shortly afterward, along with the entire northern part of the walls, during the opening of rue Émile Billault (1862–1867).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) Part of the manor survived in the _Hôtel de France_ until its complete demolition in 1912.

The alignment of the port’s moats and the creation of rue Thiers between 1870 and 1900 led to the destruction of the ramparts between the Saint-François tower and the Haute-Folie bastion, including the Brozillay bastion. In 1886, the southern part of the Prison gate was demolished.

[![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Vannes_Remparts_Feteshisto2009.jpg/250px-Vannes_Remparts_Feteshisto2009.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vannes_Remparts_Feteshisto2009.jpg)

The ramparts garden during the [Vannes historical festivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vannes_historical_festivals&action=edit&redlink=1 "Vannes historical festivals (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%AAtes_historiques_de_Vannes "fr:Fêtes historiques de Vannes")) of 2009.

Protection and heritage
-----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Protection and heritage")\]

With nearly three-quarters of its ramparts preserved and despite the destruction of several segments in the 19th century, the urban enclosure of Vannes is one of the best-preserved in Brittany. The catalyst for raising awareness among the people of Vannes was, in 1911, the rumor of the complete destruction of the Prison Gate, which had already been partially demolished in 1886 to widen the street.

People from Vannes, attached to their heritage, came together to found, as early as 1911, _[Société des Amis de Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9_des_Amis_de_Vannes&action=edit&redlink=1 "Société des Amis de Vannes (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amis_de_Vannes "fr:Amis de Vannes"))_, an association dedicated to defending the city’s heritage. Its actions (starting with the launch of a public subscription, which raised 5,000 gold francs, donated to the Municipality at the time) enabled the city to purchase the gate and ensure its preservation.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-11)

[![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/H%C3%B4tel_Lagorce%2C_Jardin_du_Ch%C3%A2teau_de_l%E2%80%99Hermine%2C_Vannes-2212.jpg/250px-H%C3%B4tel_Lagorce%2C_Jardin_du_Ch%C3%A2teau_de_l%E2%80%99Hermine%2C_Vannes-2212.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:H%C3%B4tel_Lagorce,_Jardin_du_Ch%C3%A2teau_de_l%E2%80%99Hermine,_Vannes-2212.jpg)

The Marle and the garden of Hôtel Lagorce (known as Château de l’Hermine)

Thus, the listing in 1912 of the Prison Gate as a [historical monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_historique_/(France/) "Monument historique (France)") initiated a policy of protecting the ramparts. This was soon followed by the listing of the entirety of the city’s fortified heritage, with the process concluding in 1958 with the protection of the Gréguennic Bastion. As early as 1950, the mayor, Francis Decker, had the idea of creating a [French-style garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_formal_garden "French formal garden") to enhance the eastern part of the wall, which had previously been left fallow.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-12) The safeguarding and enhancement plan has, since 1982, served as a tool for protecting the safeguarded sector of the old town, a policy supported by the signing of the [French Towns and Lands of Art and History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Towns_and_Lands_of_Art_and_History "French Towns and Lands of Art and History") convention between the city and the Ministry of Culture.

The protection and enhancement of the ramparts take several forms, from numerous restoration projects to the hosting of exhibitions (Connétable Tower, maritime photography festival, etc.), as well as the establishment of the [Institut culturel de Bretagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Institut_culturel_de_Bretagne&action=edit&redlink=1 "Institut culturel de Bretagne (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_culturel_de_Bretagne "fr:Institut culturel de Bretagne")) and numerous associations in the Hôtel Lagorce (known as Château de l’Hermine), [fireworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireworks "Fireworks"), light projections, and the organization of events at the foot of the ramparts (book fair, historical festivals, [Festival d'Arvor](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Festival_d%27Arvor&action=edit&redlink=1 "Festival d'Arvor (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_d%27Arvor "fr:Festival d'Arvor")), Photo de Mer exhibition).
