The elements listed below are described in clockwise order starting from the Notre-Dame Bastion, located at the northwest of the first enclosure. Not all elements of the ramparts are owned by the city of Vannes and are not accessible during guided or free visits. The ramparts are not entirely visible from public thoroughfares. Many elements are integrated into the urban landscape. "_Using a rough estimate, it can be said that the ramparts of Vannes are destroyed for one-third, hidden for another third, and visible for the final third_".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:3-7)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-13) This estimate is rough and likely refers to the first enclosure. The city retains three-quarters of the second enclosure.

[![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Vannes_-_bastion_Notre-Dame.jpg/250px-Vannes_-_bastion_Notre-Dame.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vannes_-_bastion_Notre-Dame.jpg)

Splintered Notre-Dame bastion, visible on rue Burgault.

During the [Catholic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_League_/(France/) "Catholic League (France)"), at the end of the 16th century, a bastion was built to protect the Notre-Dame Gate.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-14) It was rebuilt between 1616 and 1618 by the architect Jean Bugeau. During the opening of Billault Street between 1865 and 1866, the northern flank of the bastion was destroyed. The southern flank, still visible, is equipped with two large firing embrasures. In 2014, the city acquired number 29 Émile Burgault Street, followed by number 27 in 2019, to demolish the buildings concealing part of the bastion, thereby enhancing its visibility and making it accessible to the public.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-15)

The section of the ramparts from the Notre-Dame Bastion to Saint-Salomon Street, as well as the section adjacent to the bastion on Émile-Burgault Street, have been listed as [historical monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_historique_/(France/) "Monument historique (France)") since 26 and 27, respectively.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-16)

[![Image 15](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Vannes_-_porte_Saint-Jean.jpg/250px-Vannes_-_porte_Saint-Jean.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vannes_-_porte_Saint-Jean.jpg)

The Saint-Jean Gate, seen from the intramuros.

The Saint-Jean Gate takes its name from the nearby chapel of the same name, located close to the [Saint-Pierre Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes_Cathedral "Vannes Cathedral"), which was demolished in 1856.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-17) Closed before 1358, it was reopened in 1688 by the Vannes architect François Cosnier.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) It was known by the names _Porte du Mené_, _Porte du Bourreau_ (due to its proximity to the Executioner’s Tower), _Porte du Nord_, and _Porte de l’Âne_. The upper part of the gate features a stone plaque installed by the Amis de Vannes in 1911 or 1912, following a long-standing wish of the [Estates of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates_of_Brittany "Estates of Brittany") to place above this gate the [coat of arms of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_France "Coat of arms of France"), surrounded by the coats of arms of the [Duke of Chaulnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Chaulnes "Duke of Chaulnes"), Governor of [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany"), Lavardin de Beaumanoir, lieutenant general in [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes"), the Count of [Lannion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lannion "Lannion"), Governor of Vannes, and finally, those of the city of Vannes.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-18)

The section of the ramparts from the Prison Gate to the Saint-Jean Gate, as well as the Saint-Jean Gate itself, have been listed as [historical monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_historique_/(France/) "Monument historique (France)") since 26.

#### Executioner’s Tower

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Executioner’s Tower")\]

[![Image 16](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Tour_du_Bourreau_%28Vannes%29.jpg/250px-Tour_du_Bourreau_%28Vannes%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tour_du_Bourreau_/(Vannes/).jpg)

The Executioner’s Tower around 1900.

[![Image 17](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Tour_du_Bourreau_des_remparts_de_Vannes_en_2012.jpg/250px-Tour_du_Bourreau_des_remparts_de_Vannes_en_2012.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tour_du_Bourreau_des_remparts_de_Vannes_en_2012.jpg)

The Executioner’s Tower in 2012, seen from the Saint-Jean Gate.

This tower, equipped with [Breton machicolations with arches on corbels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machicolation "Machicolation"), formerly known as the _Tour des Filles_ because it served as a prison for women, was modified after the construction of the second enclosure. Built on foundations dating from the 14th century, the tower was completed in the mid-15th century. The name Executioner’s Tower comes from its use as housing for the city’s sworn executioner.

The Executioner’s Tower, or Tour des Filles, and the portion of the old ramparts extending eastward have been listed as [historical monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_historique_/(France/) "Monument historique (France)") since 29.

#### Prison Gate and tower

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Prison Gate and tower")\]

[![Image 18](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Porte_Prison%2C_Vannes-2252.jpg/250px-Porte_Prison%2C_Vannes-2252.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Porte_Prison,_Vannes-2252.jpg)

The Prison Gate in 2007

The gate, built in dressed granite, features a round tower flanked by a rectangular building. It is characterized by a cart gate under a [pointed arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointed_arch "Pointed arch") and a pedestrian passage, diverted in a chicane.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-19)

A fortified gate at the northeast of the city’s ramparts, the Prison Gate is one of the oldest entrances to the walled city. Built in the 13th century under the reign of Duke [John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "John II, Duke of Brittany"), it was named the Saint-Patern Gate, after the district it served. In the second half of the 14th century, under Duke [John IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), the gate was equipped with a tilting [drawbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drawbridge "Drawbridge"), a [postern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postern "Postern") for pedestrian passage, and a large, lowered discharge arch. His successor, [John V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V,_Duke_of_Brittany "John V, Duke of Brittany"), continued the work, which included rebuilding the upper parts with [Breton machicolations with pointed arches on corbels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machicolation "Machicolation"), constructing a [barbican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbican "Barbican"), and adding cannon ports. The fortified gate was operated by a double [drawbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drawbridge "Drawbridge") system, one for the cart gate and one for the pedestrian passage.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-20) In the 15th century, a now-deteriorated coat of arms (defaced during the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution")), likely bearing the arms of Brittany, was inserted between the drawbridge grooves. During the French Revolution, suspects and convicts were imprisoned there, including refractory clergy and priests, such as the [Blessed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatification "Beatification") [Pierre-René Rogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Ren%C3%A9_Rogue "Pierre-René Rogue"), and royalists, such as the leadership of the [émigrés who landed at Quiberon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiberon_Expedition "Quiberon Expedition") in 1795. The gate then took the name Prison Gate. Following the construction of a new prison, the gate and towers were sold to a private individual in 1825. The second half of the 19th century saw the alienation of the structure to private owners who often lacked the means to maintain it. The southern tower was demolished in 1886 (except for part of its ground floor and the outer facing of its lower level) to make way for a revenue building.

The Prison Gate and its adjacent tower, threatened with destruction, led to the founding of the Amis de Vannes, which had them listed as historical monuments on 2 and prompted the city to purchase them on 25 June 1912. The base of the left tower flanking the Prison Gate has been listed since 24, with this part acquired by the city on 30. It has since undergone several restoration campaigns. Between September 2010 and early 2012, works including "_the restoration of exterior masonry, interior facings, joinery, sculptures above the cart gate, as well as selective repairs to openings and waterproofing of the curtain walls and remains of the southern tower_" were carried out.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-21)

[![Image 19](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Vannes_Tour-Joliette.JPG/250px-Vannes_Tour-Joliette.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vannes_Tour-Joliette.JPG)

The Joliette Tower.

[![Image 20](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Powder_Tower_of_Vannes_by_night_-_by_G.Le_Mouel.JPG/250px-Powder_Tower_of_Vannes_by_night_-_by_G.Le_Mouel.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Powder_Tower_of_Vannes_by_night_-_by_G.Le_Mouel.JPG)

The Powder Magazine Tower at night.

The Joliette Tower was rebuilt in the second half of the 15th century, replacing an older tower constructed at the end of the 12th century. Part of the northern curtain wall adjacent to it rests on the original Gallo-Roman wall. Embrasures were added to the tower to accommodate [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery "Artillery") pieces: two archer-cannon ports at the lower level, served by a long straight staircase.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2)

The section of the ramparts, including the Joliette Tower, has been listed as a historical monument since 16.

Like the Joliette Tower, the Poudrière Tower was rebuilt in the second half of the 15th century on the foundations of an earlier 12th-century tower. This tower, equipped with artillery [casemates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casemates "Casemates") (two cannon ports served by a straight staircase and a return), was used at the end of the Middle Ages as a storage for [gunpowder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpowder "Gunpowder"), earning it the name _Poudrière_. The section of the curtain wall between the Joliette and Powder Magazine Towers is the only part permanently accessible to the public, with entry via Vierges Street.

The Poudrière Tower and its adjacent rampart sections have been listed as historical monuments since 26.

[![Image 21](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Vannes_-_Tour_du_Conn%C3%A9table_-_Vue_Sud.jpg/250px-Vannes_-_Tour_du_Conn%C3%A9table_-_Vue_Sud.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vannes_-_Tour_du_Conn%C3%A9table_-_Vue_Sud.jpg)

The Connétable Tower seen from the south.

This large tower is located on the flank of the city’s ramparts facing the Garenne plateau. The Connétable Tower was erected in the mid-15th century, during the expansion of the intra-muros area of Vannes. Situated near the Château de l’Hermine, this tower may have been part of its defenses. Although the tower has [artillery casemates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casemate "Casemate") in the lower chamber, its primary function was as the residence of the connétable, the commander of the [duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke "Duke")’s armies. The name _Connétable Tower_ thus derives from its role as the residence for the city’s connétable or possibly because it housed [Arthur III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur III, Duke of Brittany"), [Connétable de Richemont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conn%C3%A9table_de_France "Connétable de France"). The tower, standing 20 metres (66 ft) tall, is built on five levels and is flanked by two staircases. The two main rooms are illuminated by large openings, including two stone-mullioned windows facing south. The pointed roof is topped by a chimney. The tower was likely part of an unrealized residential project, as evidenced by the presence of unfinished masonry on the intra-muros side toward the Place des Lices.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-22) A [postage stamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postage_stamp "Postage stamp") depicting the illuminated ramparts and the Connétable Tower was issued on 26 with a [first day of issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_day_of_issue "First day of issue") cancellation on the 24th in the city.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-23) The Connétable Tower and adjacent rampart sections have been listed as [historical monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_historique_/(France/) "Monument historique (France)") since 28.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-24)

[![Image 22](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Eperon_de_la_Garenne_%28Echauguette%29-_2010.jpg/250px-Eperon_de_la_Garenne_%28Echauguette%29-_2010.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eperon_de_la_Garenne_/(Echauguette/)-_2010.jpg)

The sentry turret of the Garenne Spur.

Vannes decided to reinforce its enclosure one final time in 1625 with the construction of a bastion between the Connétable Tower and the ruins of the Château de l’Hermine. A project was proposed by Jacques Corbineau, an architect from [Laval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laval,_Mayenne "Laval, Mayenne"), but it was the architect Antoine Augereau who completed the work between 1626 and 1628. The Garenne Spur is located just north of the Poterne Gate. Shaped like an ace of spades, it features a large [casemate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casemate "Casemate") opening to the north. Two firing embrasures allowed artillery to enfilade the entire curtain wall of the Connétable Tower. At its base are the old wash houses and some stone houses.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-25)

The Garenne Spur has been inscribed as a historical monument since 10.

[![Image 23](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Porte_Poterne_%28Vannes%29_-_2010_-_by_G.Le_Mouel.JPG/250px-Porte_Poterne_%28Vannes%29_-_2010_-_by_G.Le_Mouel.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Porte_Poterne_/(Vannes/)_-_2010_-_by_G.Le_Mouel.JPG)

The Poterne Gate and its bridge.

Access to this fortified gate is via a small stone bridge that serves as a sluice for the Vannes river, the [Marle River](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marle_River&action=edit&redlink=1 "Marle River (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marle_/(fleuve/) "fr:Marle (fleuve)")). The gate was opened between 1678 and 1680 by Cosnier, during the city’s embellishment period.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) In the 18th century, its arch was broken to widen the passage. A small niche above the gate houses a copy of a 17th-century [polychrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polychrome "Polychrome") wooden statue of the Virgin. The original is kept in the [Musée de la Cohue](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_de_la_Cohue&action=edit&redlink=1 "Musée de la Cohue (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_des_Beaux-Arts_La_Cohue_de_Vannes "fr:Musée des Beaux-Arts La Cohue de Vannes")).[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-26) The Poterne Gate, terrace, and portion of the ramparts have been listed as historical monuments since 28.

[![Image 24](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/H%C3%B4tel_Lagorce%2C_Jardin_du_Ch%C3%A2teau_de_l%E2%80%99Hermine%2C_Vannes-2214.jpg/250px-H%C3%B4tel_Lagorce%2C_Jardin_du_Ch%C3%A2teau_de_l%E2%80%99Hermine%2C_Vannes-2214.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:H%C3%B4tel_Lagorce,_Jardin_du_Ch%C3%A2teau_de_l%E2%80%99Hermine,_Vannes-2214.jpg)

The Hôtel Lagorce.

The Hôtel Lagorce is one of the rampart elements not part of the fortified systemThe fortified system was completed with the construction of the Garenne Spur in 1628. This private mansion, integrated between two curtain walls, was built on the ruins of the former fortress of Duke [John IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). Gradually abandoned, the château was used as a quarry starting in the 18th century. Its foundations were leased in 1785. The city community granted the land containing the château ruins on 18, with the [leasehold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leasehold "Leasehold") deed signed on 14. to Julien Lagorce, a Vannes caterer who built a private mansion in place of the former ducal residence. Financially ruined, Lagorce sold the mansion in 1802 to M. Castellot, a merchant from [Lorient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorient "Lorient"). The Hôtel Lagorce, later known as Castellot and then Jollivet-Castellot, was sold again to a Vannes entrepreneur who, after restoring and raising it in 1854, transferred it in 1874 to the State to house the General Staff of the artillery school.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-27) The east wing of the mansion underwent renovations to be converted into classrooms. The partition walls were removed, and metal beams were installed to reinforce the building’s structure. In 1960, the mansion became the headquarters of the Public Treasury administration until 1974, when the city of Vannes acquired it to establish the Morbihan law school. Since 2003, it has been the headquarters of the Institut culturel de Bretagne and houses the offices of several associations. Until 2010, it also housed the library of the [Société polymathique du Morbihan](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9_polymathique_du_Morbihan&action=edit&redlink=1 "Société polymathique du Morbihan (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9_polymathique_du_Morbihan "fr:Société polymathique du Morbihan")). In 2006, the ground floor rooms were fully modernized to host exhibitions. The memory of the former ducal fortress remains strong, and the Hôtel Lagorce is today better known as the Château de l’Hermine.

#### Calmont Gate and tower

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Calmont Gate and tower")\]

[![Image 25](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Porte_Calmont_%28Vannes%29_-_2010.jpg/250px-Porte_Calmont_%28Vannes%29_-_2010.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Porte_Calmont_/(Vannes/)_-_2010.jpg)

Calmont Gate, its two passages, and the wooden bridge in 2010

This fortified gate and the partially demolished tower flanking it date from the 14th to 15th centuries. It owes its name to the fact that this gate allows passage between the walled city and the Calmont district, located southeast of the city center. The double passage (cart and pedestrian) was controlled by [drawbridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drawbridge "Drawbridge") with arrows and protected by [machicolations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machicolations "Machicolations"), now gone. The third level of the tower was razed and had the same characteristics as the Trumpet Tower: the upper chamber, located under a pointed roof, was surrounded by a covered walkway resting on machicolation corbels.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-28) To the right of the gate, at the top of the curtain wall, corbels can be seen that supported a [guardhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardhouse "Guardhouse") built in an overhang above the moat.

[![Image 26](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Tour_Calmont_%28Vannes%29_-_2010.jpg/250px-Tour_Calmont_%28Vannes%29_-_2010.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tour_Calmont_/(Vannes/)_-_2010.jpg)

Calmont Tower

Under the cart gate, a recess is noticeable, which housed a concealed door. Hypotheses suggest this opening was either an escape route or a dock for small boats. At the base of the tower is the entrance to the underground canal of the Marle, which passes under Place Gambetta to the port.

After the opening of the Saint-Vincent Gate, completed in 1624, the Calmont Gate was closed. In 1681, a structure was built opposite the gate to support a sluice controlling the flow of the Marle toward the port. In the 18th century, a Vannes family turned the northern curtain wall into a small promenade leading to a pavilion located against the Hôtel Lagorce. During the gate’s restoration in 1992, the chief architect of historical monuments authorized the installation of a [fixed bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_bridge "Fixed bridge") made of wood supported by a metal structure to restore passage between the intra-muros and a small shaded square with views of the Hôtel Lagorce and the ramparts’ gardens.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-29) In 2008, the outer facing of the curtain wall between the Calmont Tower and the Hôtel Lagorce was restored.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) In 2010–2011, waterproofing works on the curtain wall’s ground were carried out. In 2018, the poor condition of the wooden footbridge leading to Bertrand-Frélaut Square caused the temporary closure of the Calmont Gate. Works to completely restore the footbridge were carried out in early 2019. The wooden guardrails were replaced with wrought iron. Alongside the footbridge restoration, further restoration work was undertaken, including repointing the base of the gate’s parapet, paving the Trumpet Tower alley, and removing a step under the gate to make the passage between Bertrand-Frélaut Square and Saint-Vincent Street accessible to people with reduced mobility.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-30)

The Calmont Gate has been listed as a historical monument since 29.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-31)

[![Image 27](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Tour_Trompette_%28fin_XIX%C3%A8me_si%C3%A8cle%29.jpg/250px-Tour_Trompette_%28fin_XIX%C3%A8me_si%C3%A8cle%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tour_Trompette_/(fin_XIX%C3%A8me_si%C3%A8cle/).jpg)

The Trumpet Tower in 1885.

This tower was named after the [herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herald "Herald"), the city’s trumpeter, who used it as a residence. It appears to date from the 14th century for its base and the second half of the 15th century for its upper levels.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-32) "_The row of corbels forming machicolations supports the crenelated parapet on which the covered walkway’s roof rests_".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) It was set on fire by the Spanish in 1597,[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-33) a troop of 3,000 men sent by their king to assist [Philippe-Emmanuel de Lorraine, Duke of Mercœur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Emmanuel,_Duke_of_Merc%C5%93ur "Philippe Emmanuel, Duke of Mercœur"), governor of Brittany, during the [Catholic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_League_/(France/) "Catholic League (France)") episode. This event earned it the nickname _Burnt Tower_.

The Trumpet Tower has been inscribed as a historical monument since 23.

[![Image 28](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Vannes_Porte_St-Vincent.JPG/250px-Vannes_Porte_St-Vincent.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vannes_Porte_St-Vincent.JPG)

The Saint-Vincent Gate.

At the end of the 16th century, an opening was made in the southern ramparts for communication with the port: the Kaër-Calmont GateNamed after the suburbs it served: Kaër to the southwest and Calmont to the southeast.. Between 1620 and 1624, Jean Bugeau was tasked with constructing the bridge and the Kaër-Calmont (or Ker-Calmont) Gate. Upon completion, the gate was renamed Saint-Vincent Gate in homage to the preacher Saint [Vincent Ferrer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Ferrer "Vincent Ferrer"), who died in Vannes in 1419. The gate replaced fortifications from the 14th to 16th centuries, of which a bastion remains behind the left side of the square: the Gréguennic Bastion. It is a classical structure with columns and niches in full arch.

Successive [tides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide "Tide") of the [gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Morbihan "Gulf of Morbihan") damaged the gate’s base, and its structure showed severe deterioration by the early 18th century. The gate was repaired for the first time in 1727. A reconstruction project was initiated in 1738, but the architect Jannesson’s plans were not executed. The gate was entirely rebuilt in 1747 by the engineer Duchemin, who retained the facade designed by Bugeau but removed the roof and upper chamber.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-34)

In the central niche, a statue from 1891 of Saint Vincent Ferrer recalls the importance of this preacher in Vannes’ history. The city’s arms were carved in granite at the same time. The original statue of the saint, installed in 1624 and crafted in [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") by the Vannes painter Guillaume Lemarchand,[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-35) was replaced during the French Revolution by that of a [sans-culotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sans-culotte "Sans-culotte") and has since disappeared. A legend claims that when the saint’s statue lowers its hand, the city will be submerged by water.

The Saint-Vincent Gate is a "_dressed granite gate structured with three bays framed by columns and three levels. At the lower level, the cart gate is flanked by two narrow bays, one blind and the other with a pedestrian door. Two niches open at the second level in the lateral bays, framing the city’s arms. The third level consists of a central niche framed by volutes._".

In late 2014, maintenance and restoration work on the gate, both extra- and intra-muros, was carried out, along with the restoration of the Saint Vincent statue.

The Saint-Vincent Gate has been listed as a historical monument since 11.

#### Gréguennic Gate and bastion

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Gréguennic Gate and bastion")\]

[![Image 29](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Bastion_de_Gr%C3%A9guennic_%28Vannes%29_-_2010.jpg/250px-Bastion_de_Gr%C3%A9guennic_%28Vannes%29_-_2010.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastion_de_Gr%C3%A9guennic_/(Vannes/)_-_2010.jpg)

Interior of the Gréguennic Bastion during the 2010 Photo de Mer exhibition

Texts from the 14th to 15th centuries mention a fortified gate, the Gréguennic Gate, dating from the period of the enclosure’s southern expansion. The Gréguennic Gate, along with the Calmont Gate, is one of the two gates opened in the south following the extension of the enclosure. The gate provides access to the port and “_consists of two towers projecting from the wall_”.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) Only the ground floor of the eastern tower and the adjacent curtain wall of the western tower are equipped with arrow slits.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) Originally, the gate was protected by a simple [portcullis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portcullis "Portcullis") with a counterweight. A [barbican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbican "Barbican"), “_served by a [fixed bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_bridge "Fixed bridge") on the city side and a [drawbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drawbridge "Drawbridge") with arrows on the sea side_”, was added to reinforce the gate in the early 15th century.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) At the end of the 16th century, the enclosure was strengthened by the addition of bastions such as the Gréguennic Bastion, whose construction was initiated under the governance of [Duke of Mercœur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe-Emmanuel_de_Lorraine "Philippe-Emmanuel de Lorraine"). The barbican disappeared, and although almost entirely preserved, the gate lost its role as an entrance to the walled city.

[![Image 30](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Bastion_de_Gr%C3%A9guennic_%28Vannes%29_-_Tour_est.jpg/250px-Bastion_de_Gr%C3%A9guennic_%28Vannes%29_-_Tour_est.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bastion_de_Gr%C3%A9guennic_/(Vannes/)_-_Tour_est.jpg)

Eastern tower of the Gréguennic Gate

The site’s renovation starting in 1992 cleared this four-sided bastion, completed in 1593,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) and built to defend the moat and the port. The old towers and the Gréguennic Gate were largely preserved. The tower has two firing embrasures. Five casemates are arranged in a battery within the thickness of the western wall, along a narrow corridor.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) Each casemate, except the central one which has two, is pierced with a single firing embrasure and a vent hole for evacuating cannon smoke. Only the southwest side lacks a firing embrasure. Cannons placed on the walkway reinforced the firing plan of the ground floor.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2)

Access to the bastion is via the former gate, which must have been significant given its multiple expansions, closures, or heightenings before being replaced by the Saint-Vincent Gate in the 17th century.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-36) Today, the bastion is entirely concealed by the layout of Place Gambetta and the intra-muros. The installation of a glazed floor in the covered passageThe Gréguennic Bastion is accessed via a covered passage located on the ground floor of a residential building on the intra-muros side. between Place de la Poissonnerie and the bastion allows observation of remnants of the old structures.

The Gréguennic Bastion has been inscribed as a historical monument since 7.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-37)

#### Haute-Folie Bastion

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Haute-Folie Bastion")\]

[![Image 31](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Plan_d%27alignements_des_bastions_sud-ouest_de_Vannes_2nd_18%C3%A8me.png/250px-Plan_d%27alignements_des_bastions_sud-ouest_de_Vannes_2nd_18%C3%A8me.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plan_d%27alignements_des_bastions_sud-ouest_de_Vannes_2nd_18%C3%A8me.png)

Alignment plan of the southwest bastions of Vannes’ ramparts - 18th-century drawing.

Built during the troubled period of the [French Wars of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion "French Wars of Religion"), the Haute-Folie Bastion was originally made of earth and turf and equipped with a drawbridge. The bastion was completed by André Bugeau in 1618 “_following the principle of masonry on piles driven into the mud_”.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:1-2) In the 18th century, like its neighbors, it took the name of its occupant and became the Gaumont Bastion. It is now concealed by the buildings on Thiers and Carnot Streets to the west and Place de la Poissonnerie to the east.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) The Haute-Folie Bastion has been inscribed as a historical monument since 7.

#### Saint-François Tower

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Saint-François Tower")\]

[![Image 32](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Plan_de_rue_projet%C3%A9e_%28Ouest_remparts_de_Vannes%29_1785.jpg/250px-Plan_de_rue_projet%C3%A9e_%28Ouest_remparts_de_Vannes%29_1785.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plan_de_rue_projet%C3%A9e_/(Ouest_remparts_de_Vannes/)_1785.jpg)

Plan of the proposed street passing through the Cordeliers convent

This tower was built in the late 14th century during the southern extension of the enclosure. It takes its name from the [Franciscan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscan_Order "Franciscan Order") (or [Cordeliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordeliers "Cordeliers")) convent, founded by [John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I,_Duke_of_Brittany "John I, Duke of Brittany") in 1260. The only convent located within the city walls due to its early establishment south of the first enclosure, it bordered the eastern part of the ramparts, of which the tower is a component.

The adjacent plan depicts the project to create a street passing through the Cordeliers convent. Drawn in 1785 by Detaille de Keroyand, a [civil engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_engineer "Civil engineer"), it shows part of the western walls and moats, the Brozillay Bastion, the Saint-François Tower, and the Saint-Salomon Gate. The Le Mintier de Lehélec Street was only created between 1826 and 1827. During the alignment of the port’s moats between 1870 and 1900, part of the Saint-François Tower and the curtain wall up to the Haute-Folie Bastion were destroyed, leaving only its base.

The Saint-François Tower (including adjacent ramparts and part of the so-called Saracen walls) has been inscribed as a historical monument since 7.

Disappeared elements
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Disappeared elements")\]

#### Notre-Dame Gate and tower

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Notre-Dame Gate and tower")\]

Located near the Château de la Motte, the gate was one of the fortifications of the first seat of the counts of Vannes. A statue of Notre-Dame was placed at the top of this gate, with a small roof or canopy surmounting it, hence its original name, _Porte du Bali_.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-38) This old gate was renovated during the 15th century and equipped with a tower. The construction of the Notre-Dame Bastion at the end of the 16th century led to the creation of a new gate to the west of the older one and the absorption of the nearest tower into the bastion. Until its destruction in 1784, the new gate was also called _Porte Neuve_. The gate was located west of the current Émile Burgault Street, opposite the town hall.

All that remains of this gate is a [sentry turret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentry_turret "Sentry turret") overlooking Émile Burgault Street.

#### Château de la Motte

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Château de la Motte")\]

[![Image 33](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_la_Motte.jpg/250px-Ch%C3%A2teau_de_la_Motte.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ch%C3%A2teau_de_la_Motte.jpg)

Plan of the episcopal manor of La Motte in the 18th century.

The oldest known residence of power in the city, the Château de la Motte was adjacent to the Notre-Dame Tower in the northern part of the enclosure, on the highest point of the city. This castle was built around the 5th or 6th century and is believed to have been the residence of King Eusebius at the beginning of the 6th century,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) although some sources suggest a later construction date (9th or 10th century). Before the castle was ruined by the Normans in the early 10th century, this fortress was the residence of the counts of Vannes. Restored by the dukes, it was temporarily inhabited by Peter Mauclerc and John I. Damaged by the earthquake that struck Vannes in 1287, Duke John II, who preferred the [Château de Suscinio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Suscinio "Château de Suscinio"), ceded La Motte to Henri Tore, the bishop of the city. The structure was rebuilt starting in 1288. The castle then became the episcopal manor of La Motte.

In 1532, the episcopal manor hosted the congregation and assembly of the Estates of Brittany in the presence of King [Francis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_France "Francis I of France"). It was in the great hall of the manor that the request for the union of Brittany with France was deliberated: the [Lettre de Vannes](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Lettre_de_Vannes "wikisource:Lettre de Vannes").

[![Image 34](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Vannes_-_clich%C3%A9_1860.png/250px-Vannes_-_clich%C3%A9_1860.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vannes_-_clich%C3%A9_1860.png)

Photograph of Vannes prior to 1860 - The La Motte manor is the tallest structure.

The manor was rebuilt again at the initiative of Monseigneur Charles de Rosmadec in 1654. The work lasted 18 months (1.5 a). Further works were carried out by [Louis Cazet](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louis_Cazet&action=edit&redlink=1 "Louis Cazet (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Cazet "fr:Louis Cazet")), and his successor, François d’Argouges, acquired the northern moats, known as du Mené, in 1688, converting them into a large garden. Sébastien-Michel Amelot was the last bishop to reside there, abandoning La Motte in 1791 due to his refusal to swear allegiance to the [Civil Constitution of the Clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Constitution_of_the_Clergy "Civil Constitution of the Clergy").

After the Revolution, Vannes was chosen as the capital of the new Morbihan department. The department’s directorate was established there in 1793. The first prefect, Henri Giraud Duplessis, settled at La Motte in March 1800. The castle remained the prefecture’s seat for 60 years (1,900 Ms). On 11, a retaining wall collapsed, killing two people. The Ministry of the Interior sent an architect from the civil buildings council, who concluded that repairs were impossible, and the structure was reinforced with iron to prevent total collapse. The manor and its dependencies were sold in 1866 for 110,000 francs.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5) The castle was partially demolished in 1867, allowing the construction of a new road to the [station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes_railway_station "Vannes railway station"): Billault Street. The Hôtel de France, demolished in 1912,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-39) retained two facade windows on each floor.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:2-5)

#### Château de l’Hermine

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Château de l’Hermine")\]

The Château de l’Hermine is a defensive and residential building commissioned by Duke [John IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), who sought to benefit from the more central position of Vannes in his [duchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"). The fortress was accompanied by extensive dependencies where he created a park, with the grounds extending from the Garenne to the [Étang au Duc](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%C3%89tang_au_Duc&action=edit&redlink=1 "Étang au Duc (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tang_au_Duc_/(Vannes/) "fr:Étang au Duc (Vannes)")). According to the [Froissart's _Chronicles_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Froissart%27s_Chronicles "Froissart's Chronicles"), it is “_very beautiful and very strong_”,[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-40) and for [Bertrand d’Argentré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_d%E2%80%99Argentr%C3%A9 "Bertrand d’Argentré") in his _Histoire de Bretagne_, dated 1582, “_it is a small building for a prince, consisting of a single residential structure and many small towers, with two large towers on the outside_”.

The construction of this building took place between 1380 and 1385, with the work continuing until the mid-15th century. The duke’s household services were located in the bailey: the mint workshop, the oven house, the [tennis court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_court "Tennis court"), and the ducal stables.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-:0-1) The extent of this was revealed by excavations conducted at the end of the 20th century. The construction of the Lices mill, the chamber of accounts, and the Lices chapel between 1420 and 1425 completed the complex.

The integration of the duchy into France in 1532 left it without maintenance. Given to the city by [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV") in 1697, it then became the site of a quarry used for the restoration of municipal buildings and the development of the port.

#### Saint-Vincent Bridge

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramparts_of_Vannes&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Saint-Vincent Bridge")\]

[![Image 35](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Pont_Saint-Vincent_%28Vannes%29.jpg/250px-Pont_Saint-Vincent_%28Vannes%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pont_Saint-Vincent_/(Vannes/).jpg)

The Saint-Vincent Bridge and its sluice in the 18th century

Little is known about the existence of a passage between the Kaër land to the west and Calmont to the east before the opening of the Saint-Vincent Gate. A document mentioning the repair of a bridge in 1598 is the first evidence of a passage between the two banks of the port.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramparts_of_Vannes#cite_note-41) The bridge is not strictly part of the fortifications but is an essential urban element facilitating access between the city and the port.

The bridge had to be modified following the construction of the Billy quay in 1697. In 1787, the city embellishment project designed by the engineer Maury planned the creation of a square between the gate and the port’s end, but the French Revolution halted it. The project was revived by the municipal council in 1835, and the city architect Philippe Brunet-Debaines was tasked with its realization. Marius Charier took over the project after Brunet-Debaines’ death in 1838. In 1843, the construction of the square, the buildings on the former mudflats on either side of the bridge, and the underground Marle canal were completed. The Place du Morbihan (later Place Gambetta) replaced the Saint-Vincent Bridge. In 1976, during the square’s refurbishment, the remaining arches were broken open; roadworks in 2005 revealed the presence of one last intact arch.

[![Image 36](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Coupe_bastion_de_Brozillay_-_Vannes_an_III.png/250px-Coupe_bastion_de_Brozillay_-_Vannes_an_III.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coupe_bastion_de_Brozillay_-_Vannes_an_III.png)

Brozillay Bastion - drawing from 28 Germinal Year III (17).

Opened during the expansion works at the end of the 14th century, the Michelet Gate was located northwest of the Gréguennic Gate. It disappeared during the construction of the Haute-Folie Bastion at the end of the 16th century.

The Brozillay Bastion, or _Ker Bastion_, the third bastion built during the [Catholic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_League_/(France/) "Catholic League (France)"), had the same technical characteristics as the Gréguennic Bastion. Built in [masonry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masonry "Masonry"), it is a “_hollow bastion equipped with a low battery and spaced [casemates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casemates "Casemates") along the [curtain wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtain_wall_/(fortification/) "Curtain wall (fortification)"). \[...\] At each corner of the structure, a [sentry turret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentry_turret "Sentry turret") on [machicolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machicolation "Machicolation") corbels serves as a lookout post_”.

In the 18th century, like its neighbors, it took the name of its owner and became the Bavalan Bastion, behind the hotel of the same name. Between 1870 and 1900, during the opening of Thiers Street, the curtain walls from the Saint-François Tower to the Haute-Folie Bastion, including the Brozillay Bastion, were destroyed.

Caught under a rain of arrows from Welsh archers, the army of Charles suffered many losses.
