| Hundred Years' War 1345–1347 | | --- | | Part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") | | [![Image 1: A colourful medieval image of a town under attack](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Prise_caen_1346.jpg/330px-Prise_caen_1346.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prise_caen_1346.jpg) The English assault on Caen, from [Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart")'s [_Chronicles_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Froissart%27s_Chronicles "Froissart's Chronicles") | |
DateJune 1345 – 28 September 1347
Location

France and northern England

ResultEnglish victory
| | Belligerents | | [Kingdom of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") | [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") | | Commanders and leaders | | * King [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III "Edward III") * [Henry, Earl of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Grosmont,_1st_Duke_of_Lancaster "Henry of Grosmont, 1st Duke of Lancaster") | King [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") ([WIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wounded_in_action "Wounded in action")) [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John,_Duke_of_Normandy "John, Duke of Normandy") | | Casualties and losses | | Unknown, light | Unknown, heavy | English [offensives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offensive_/(military/) "Offensive (military)") in 1345–1347, during the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), resulted in repeated defeats of the French, the loss or devastation of much French territory and the capture by the English of the port of [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais"). The war had broken out in 1337 and flared up in 1340 when the king of England, [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), [laid claim to the French crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne") and [campaigned in northern France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournaisis_campaign_of_1340 "Tournaisis campaign of 1340"). There was then a lull in the major hostilities, although much small-scale fighting continued. Edward determined early in 1345 to renew full-scale war and personally led the main English army to northern France. Edward delayed its disembarkation, and his fleet was scattered by a storm, ruining this offensive. He also despatched a small force to [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") in south-west France under [Henry, Earl of Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Grosmont,_Duke_of_Lancaster "Henry of Grosmont, Duke of Lancaster"), which was spectacularly successful. The following spring a large French army, led by the heir to the French throne, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France"), [counter-attacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterattack "Counterattack") Derby's forces. Edward responded by landing an army of 10,000 men in northern [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Normandy "Duchy of Normandy"). The English devastated much of Normandy and [stormed and sacked Caen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Caen_/(1346/) "Battle of Caen (1346)"), slaughtering the population. They cut a swath along the left bank of the [Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine "Seine") to within 20 miles (32 km) of Paris. The English army then turned north and inflicted a heavy defeat on a French army led by their king, [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), at the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") on 26 August 1346. They promptly exploited this by laying [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besiege "Besiege") to Calais. The period from Derby's victory outside Bergerac in late August 1345 to the start of the siege of Calais on 4 September 1346 became known as Edward III's _annus mirabilis_ (year of marvels). After an eleven-month siege, which stretched both countries' financial and military resources to the limit, the town fell. Shortly afterwards, the [Truce of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Calais "Truce of Calais") was agreed; it ran for nine months to 7 July 1348, but was extended repeatedly until it was formally set aside in 1355. The war eventually ended in 1453 with the English expelled from all French territory except Calais, which served as an English [entrepôt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrep%C3%B4t "Entrepôt") into northern France until 1558. [![Image 2: a head and shoulders drawing of Edward III, in armour and bearing a sword](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Edward_III_%2818th_century%29.jpg/250px-Edward_III_%2818th_century%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_III_/(18th_century/).jpg) [![Image 3: A Medieval image of Philip VI seated, wearing a blue robe](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Philippe_VI_de_Valois_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Philippe_VI_de_Valois_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Philippe_VI_de_Valois_/(cropped/).jpg) Since the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest") of 1066, English monarchs had held titles and lands within France by inheritance. Their possession made them [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the kings of France. The status of the English king's French [fiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") was a major source of conflict between the two monarchies throughout the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"). French monarchs systematically sought to check the growth of English power, stripping away lands as the opportunity arose.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007394-1) Over the centuries, English holdings in France had varied in size, but by 1337 only [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") in south western France and [Ponthieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponthieu "Ponthieu") in northern France were left.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris19948-2) The Gascons preferred their relationship with a distant English king who left them alone to one with a French king who would interfere in their affairs.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrowcroftCannon2015389-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTELacey2008122-4) Following a series of disagreements between [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") (r. 1328–1350) and [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") (r. 1327–1377), on 24 May 1337 Philip's [Great Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_du_Roi "Conseil du Roi") in Paris agreed that Gascony and Ponthieu should be taken back into Philip's hands on the grounds that Edward was in breach of his obligations as a vassal. This marked the start of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), which was to last 116 years.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990184-5) Although Gascony was the cause of the war, Edward was able to spare few resources for it, and whenever an English army campaigned on the continent during the first eight years of the war it operated in northern France.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200495-6) In 1340, Edward laid formal claim to the [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France"), as the closest male relative of Philip's predecessor, [Charles IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IV_of_France "Charles IV of France").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006d158-7) He then led an inconclusive and vastly expensive campaign against [Tournai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournai "Tournai"), after which there was a relative lull in the fighting, formalised in the [Truce of Espléchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") the same year.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006e161-8) Edward determined early in 1345 to renew full-scale war and to attack France on three fronts: [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton"), would lead a small force to [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany"), a slightly larger force would proceed to Gascony under the command of [Henry, Earl of Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Grosmont,_Duke_of_Lancaster "Henry of Grosmont, Duke of Lancaster"), and the main force would accompany Edward to either northern France or [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Flanders "County of Flanders").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuizot1870s-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990453-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007314-11) The previous [Seneschal of Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneschal_of_Gascony "Seneschal of Gascony"), [Nicholas de la Beche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_de_la_Beche "Nicholas de la Beche"), was replaced by the more senior [Ralph, Earl of Stafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_de_Stafford,_1st_Earl_of_Stafford "Ralph de Stafford, 1st Earl of Stafford"), who sailed for Gascony in February with an advance force.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGribit201663-12) French intelligence had uncovered the English plan for [offensives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offensive_/(military/) "Offensive (military)") in the three [theatres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theater_/(warfare/) "Theater (warfare)"), but France did not have the money to raise a major army in each. The French anticipated, correctly, that the English planned to make their main effort in northern France. Thus they directed what resources they had there, planning to assemble their main army at [Arras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arras "Arras") on 22 July. South-western France was encouraged to rely on its own resources, but as the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"), signed in early 1343, was still in effect, the local lords were reluctant to spend money and little was done.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990455%E2%80%93457-13) Edward's main army sailed on 29 June. They anchored off [Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sluys "Sluys") in Flanders until 22 July, while Edward attended to diplomatic affairs.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuizot1870s-9)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTELucas1929519%E2%80%93524-14) When they subsequently sailed, probably intending to land in [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Normandy "Duchy of Normandy"), they were scattered by a storm and found their way to English ports over the following week. After more than five weeks on board ship, the men and horses had to be disembarked. There was a further week's delay while the King and his [council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curia_regis "Curia regis") debated what to do, by which time it proved impossible to take any action with this force before winter.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007315-15) Aware of this, Philip despatched reinforcements to Brittany and Gascony. [Peter, Duke of Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_I,_Duke_of_Bourbon "Peter I, Duke of Bourbon") was appointed commander-in-chief of the south-west front on 8 August.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990461%E2%80%93463-16) [![Image 4: A map of south-west France in 1345 showing the main movements of troops between August and November](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Map_of_Gascon_campaign_of_1345.svg/330px-Map_of_Gascon_campaign_of_1345.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Gascon_campaign_of_1345.svg) The main troop movements in south-west France between August and November 1345 Red arrows – Derby's advance to Bergerac and Périgueux Orange arrow – Derby's withdrawal Blue arrows – Louis of Poitiers' advance to Périgueux and Auberoche Pink arrow – Derby's return to Auberoche Green arrow – Derby's move back to Gascony and La Réole Derby's force embarked at [Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton "Southampton") at the end of May 1345. Bad weather forced his fleet of 151 ships to shelter in [Falmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmouth,_Cornwall "Falmouth, Cornwall") for several weeks en route, finally departing on 23 July.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200494-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler1961131%E2%80%93132-18) The Gascons, primed by Stafford to expect Derby's arrival in late May and sensing the French weakness, took the field without him. The Gascons captured the large, weakly garrisoned castles of Montravel and Monbreton on the [Dordogne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dordogne_/(river/) "Dordogne (river)") in early June; both were taken by surprise and their seizure broke the tenuous Truce of Malestroit.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990457-19) Stafford carried out a short march north to [besiege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege "Siege") [Blaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blaye "Blaye"). He left the Gascons to prosecute this and proceeded to Langon, south of Bordeaux, to set up a second siege.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGribit201661,_113-20) The French issued an urgent call to arms.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990457-19) Meanwhile, small independent parties of Gascons raided across the region. Local French groups joined them, and several minor nobles threw in their lot with the Anglo-Gascons. They had some successes, but their main effect was to tie down most of the French garrisons in the region and to cause them to call for reinforcements – to no avail. The few French troops not garrisoning fortifications immobilised themselves with sieges of English-controlled fortifications: [Casseneuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casseneuil "Casseneuil") in the [Agenais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agenais "Agenais"); Monchamp near [Condom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condom,_Gers "Condom, Gers"); and [Montcuq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montcuq "Montcuq"), a strong but strategically insignificant castle south of [Bergerac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergerac,_Dordogne "Bergerac, Dordogne").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200496-21) Large areas were left effectively undefended.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990457%E2%80%93458-22) On 9 August Derby arrived in Bordeaux with 500 [men-at-arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man-at-arms "Man-at-arms"), 1,500 English and Welsh [archers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow "English longbow"), 500 of them mounted on ponies to increase their mobility,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200495-6) and ancillary and support troops, such as a team of 24 [miners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_/(military/) "Mining (military)").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler1961178-23) The majority were veterans of earlier campaigns.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGribit201659-24) After two weeks of further recruiting and consolidation of his forces Derby decided on a change of strategy. Rather than continue a war of sieges he determined to strike directly at the French before they could concentrate their forces.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200497-25) The French in the region were under the command of [Bertrand de l'Isle-Jourdain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_I_of_L%27Isle-Jourdain "Bertrand I of L'Isle-Jourdain"),[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200489-26) who was assembling his forces at the communications centre and strategically important town of Bergerac. This was 60 miles (97 kilometres) east of Bordeaux and controlled an important bridge over the Dordogne River.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200496-21) Derby moved rapidly and took the French army by surprise in late August 1345, [ambushing its cavalry component outside Bergerac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bergerac "Battle of Bergerac") and then driving its panicking infantry back to the town.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2004100%E2%80%93101-27) French casualties were heavy, with many killed and a large number captured, including their commander. The surviving French rallied around [John, Count of Armagnac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I,_Count_of_Armagnac "John I, Count of Armagnac"), and retreated north to [Périgueux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A9rigueux "Périgueux"), the provincial capital.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990466-28) Within days of the battle, Bergerac fell to an Anglo-Gascon assault and was subsequently [sacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looting "Looting").[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999104%E2%80%93105-29) After consolidating and reorganising for two weeks Derby left a large garrison in the town and moved north to Périgueux,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998189-30) taking several strong points on the way.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler1961196-31) During September, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France"), the son and heir of Philip VI, gathered an army reportedly numbering more than 20,000 men and manoeuvred in the area. In early October a very large detachment drove off Derby's force, which withdrew towards Bordeaux. Further reinforced, the French started besieging the English-held strong points.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990467%E2%80%93468-32) A French force of 7,000, commanded by [Louis of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_of_Poitiers_/(French_Noble/) "Louis of Poitiers (French Noble)"), besieged the castle of Auberoche, 9 mi (14 km) east of Périgueux.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006a-33) After a night march Derby [attacked the French camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auberoche "Battle of Auberoche") on 21 October while they were at dinner, taking them by surprise and causing heavy initial casualties. The French rallied and there was a protracted hand-to-hand struggle, which ended when the commander of the small English garrison in the castle [sortied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sortie "Sortie") and fell upon the rear of the French. They broke and fled. French casualties are described by modern historians as "appalling",[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990469-34) "extremely high",[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998189-30) "staggering",[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999112-35) and "heavy".[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006a-33) Many French nobles were taken prisoner; lower ranking men were, as was customary,[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing2002269%E2%80%93270-36) killed on the spot. The French commander, [Louis of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I_de_Poitiers,_Count_of_Valentinois "Louis I de Poitiers, Count of Valentinois"), died of his wounds. Surviving prisoners included l'Isle-Jourdain, the second in command, two counts, seven viscounts, three barons, the seneschals of [Clermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clermont-Ferrand "Clermont-Ferrand") and [Toulouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse "Toulouse"), a nephew of the [Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI") and so many [knights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights "Knights") that they were not counted.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990469-34) The four-month campaign has been described as "the first successful land campaign of ... the Hundred Years' War",[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGribit20161-37) which had commenced more than eight years earlier. Modern historians have praised the generalship demonstrated by Derby in this campaign: "superb and innovative tactician";[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2004107,_n._61-38) "ris\[ing\] to the level of genius";[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2004106-39) "brilliant in the extreme";[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999117-40) "stunning";[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGribit201622-41) "brilliant".[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOman1998126-42) A chronicler writing fifty years after the event described him as "one of the best warriors in the world".[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200489-26) For the 1346 [campaigning season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Season#Military_campaigning_seasons "Season") Duke John was again placed in charge of all French forces in south-west France. In March a French army of between 15,000 and 20,000,[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner20063-43) enormously superior to any force the Anglo-Gascons could field,[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990485%E2%80%93486-44) marched on the Anglo-Gascon-held town of [Aiguillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aiguillon,_Lot-et-Garonne "Aiguillon, Lot-et-Garonne") and besieged it on 1 April.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner20063-43) On 2 April an _[arrière-ban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arri%C3%A8re-ban "Arrière-ban")_, a formal call to arms for all able-bodied males, was announced for southern France.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner20063-43)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990485-45) French national financial, logistical and manpower efforts were focused on this offensive.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990484-46) [![Image 5: A map of south-east England and north-east France showing the route of the English army](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Map_of_the_route_of_Edward_III%27s_chevauch%C3%A9e_of_1346.svg/330px-Map_of_the_route_of_Edward_III%27s_chevauch%C3%A9e_of_1346.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_the_route_of_Edward_III%27s_chevauch%C3%A9e_of_1346.svg) The route of the English army During the first six months of 1346 Edward again gathered a large army in England. The French were aware of this, but given the extreme difficulty of disembarking an army other than at a port, the English no longer having access to a port in Flanders, but with friendly ports in [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") and Gascony, they assumed Edward would sail for one of the latter; probably Gascony, in order to relieve Aiguillon.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler1961234-47) To guard against any possibility of an English landing in northern France, Philip VI relied on his powerful navy.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990494-48) This reliance was misplaced as his navy was late assembling and in any event would have been unable to effectively patrol the whole Channel.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990494-48) Edward's army embarked in the largest fleet ever assembled by the English to that date,[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-49) 747 ships.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTELambert2011247-50) The French were unable to prevent Edward successfully crossing the Channel and landing at [St. Vaast la Hogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vaast_la_Hogue "St. Vaast la Hogue") on 12 July,[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOman1998131-51) 20 mi (32 km) from [Cherbourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherbourg "Cherbourg") in northern Normandy. The English army was approximately 10,000 strong[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999138-52)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand198915-53) and it achieved complete strategic surprise.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004103-54) Philip recalled his main army, under Duke John, from Gascony. After a furious argument with his advisers, and according to some accounts his father's messenger, John refused to move until his honour was satisfied by the fall of the Aiguillon.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999150-55) Edward's aim was to conduct a _[chevauchée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevauch%C3%A9e "Chevauchée")_, a large-scale raid, across French territory to reduce his opponent's morale and wealth by razing his towns and stealing the populace's portable wealth.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers199492-56) His army marched south through the [Cotentin peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotentin_peninsula "Cotentin peninsula"), cutting a wide swath of destruction through some of the richest lands in France and burning every town they passed.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton2007b71-57)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2000252,_257-58) The English fleet paralleled the army's route and landing parties devastated the country for up to 5 mi (8 km) inland, taking vast amounts of loot; after their crews filled their holds, many ships deserted.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990507-59) The fleet also captured or burnt more than 100 French ships; 61 of these had been converted into military vessels.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004103-54) [Caen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caen "Caen"), the cultural, political, religious and financial centre of north-west Normandy, was [stormed on 26 July](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Caen_/(1346/) "Battle of Caen (1346)"). Much of the population was massacred, there was an orgy of drunken rape[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2008-60)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod1990275-61) and the city was sacked for five days.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990508-62) On 29 July Philip called an _arrière-ban_ for northern France at [Rouen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouen "Rouen").[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999150-55) The English army marched out of Caen towards the River [Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine "Seine") on 1 August, arriving on the 7th.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990508%E2%80%93510-63) Philip again sent orders to John insisting he abandon the siege of Aiguillon and march his army north. Meanwhile the English devastated the country to the suburbs of Rouen before leaving a swath of destruction, rapine and slaughter along the left bank of the Seine to [Poissy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poissy "Poissy"), 20 mi (32 km) from Paris, which they reached on 12 August.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999150-55)[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990514%E2%80%93515-64) On 14 August John attempted to arrange a local truce at Aiguillon. Lancaster, as Derby was now known,[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-66) well aware of the situation in the north and in the French camps around Aiguillon, refused. On 20 August, after five months of siege, the French abandoned the operation and marched away in considerable haste and disorder.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2010-67) On 16 August the English army outside Paris had turned north, they then became trapped in territory which the French had denuded of food. They escaped by fighting their way across the [Somme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somme_/(river/) "Somme (river)") against a French blocking force in the [Battle of Blanchetaque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Blanchetaque "Battle of Blanchetaque") on 24 August.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200231%E2%80%9339-68)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHardy201064%E2%80%9365-69)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999156%E2%80%93160-70) [![Image 6: A colourful medieval image of a battle between French and English forces](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Battle_of_crecy_froissart.jpg/250px-Battle_of_crecy_froissart.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_crecy_froissart.jpg) Two days later, on 26 August 1346, fighting on ground of their own choosing, the English offered battle to the French at the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy").[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998166%E2%80%93175-71) The French army was very large for the period, several times larger than the English force.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998164-72) The French unfurled their sacred battle banner, the _[oriflamme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriflamme "Oriflamme")_, indicating that no prisoners would be taken.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998166-73) There was an initial archery exchange, which the English won, [routing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rout "Rout") the Italian [crossbowmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbowmen "Crossbowmen") opposing them.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998168%E2%80%93169-74) The French then launched cavalry charges by their mounted knights at the English men-at-arms, who had dismounted for the battle. These charges were disordered because of their impromptu nature, by having to force their way through the fleeing Italians, by the muddy ground, by having to charge uphill, and by [pits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_denial_weapon "Area denial weapon") dug by the English.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19997-75) The attacks were further broken up by fire from the English archers, which caused heavy casualties.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1998240-76) By the time the French charges reached the English infantry they had lost much of their impetus.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998170%E2%80%93171-77) A contemporary described the [hand-to-hand combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand-to-hand_combat "Hand-to-hand combat") which ensued as "murderous, without pity, cruel, and very horrible".[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998171-78) The French charges continued into the night, all with the same result: fierce fighting followed by a French repulse. Philip himself was caught up in the fighting, had two horses killed from underneath him, and received an arrow in the jaw.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1998238-79) The _oriflamme_ was captured after its [bearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard-bearer "Standard-bearer") was killed. The French broke and fled; the English, exhausted, slept where they had fought.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998171-78) The French losses were very heavy and were recorded at the time as 1,200 knights and over 15,000 others killed.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998173%E2%80%93174-80) The highest contemporary estimate of English fatalities was 300.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton2007191-81) The scale of the English victory is described by the modern historian Andrew Ayton as "unprecedented" and "a devastating military humiliation" for the French.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton20077,_20-82) The modern historian [Jonathan Sumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Sumption,_Lord_Sumption "Jonathan Sumption, Lord Sumption") considers it "a political catastrophe for the French Crown".[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990532-83) The battle was reported to the [English Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") on 13 September in glowing terms as a sign of [divine favour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_providence "Divine providence") and as a justification for the huge cost of the war to date.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton200733-84) After resting for two days and burying the dead, the English marched north. They continued to devastate the land, and set several towns on fire, including [Wissant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wissant "Wissant"), the normal port of disembarkation for English shipping to northern France.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990532-83) Outside the burning town Edward held a council, which decided to capture Calais. This was an ideal [entrepôt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrep%C3%B4t "Entrepôt") from an English point of view, possessing a secure harbour and established port facilities, and being in the part of France closest to the [ports of south-east England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinque_Ports "Cinque Ports"). It was also close to the border of Flanders, which was nominally part of France, but in rebellion, allied to the English and willing to send troops to assist Edward.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOman1998148-85)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990532,_534-86) The English arrived outside the town on 4 September and besieged it.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999207-87) Calais was strongly fortified, surrounded by extensive marshes, adequately garrisoned and provisioned, and could be reinforced and supplied by sea.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne1999208-88)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990535,_557-89)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2000249-90) The day after the siege commenced, English ships arrived off-shore and resupplied, re-equipped and reinforced the English army.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarari1999387-91)[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990537-92) Over time a major victualling operation drew on sources throughout England and Wales to supply the besiegers, as well as overland from nearby Flanders. Parliament grudgingly agreed to fund the siege. Edward declared it a matter of honour and avowed his intent to remain until the town fell. The period from Derby's victory outside Bergerac in late August 1345 and the start of the siege of Calais on 4 September became known as Edward III's _annus mirabilis_ (year of marvels).[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTELambert2011247-50)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990537%E2%80%93538,_557-93) Philip vacillated: on the day the siege of Calais began he disbanded most of his army, to save money and convinced Edward had finished his chevauchée and would proceed to Flanders and ship his army home. On or shortly after 7 September, Duke John made contact with Philip, having just disbanded his own army. On 9 September Philip announced the army would reassemble at [Compiègne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compi%C3%A8gne "Compiègne") on 1 October, an impossibly short interval, and then march to the relief of Calais.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990539-94) [![Image 7: A map of Lancaster's route in 1346](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Map_of_route_of_Lancaster%27s_chevauch%C3%A9e_of_1346.svg/250px-Map_of_route_of_Lancaster%27s_chevauch%C3%A9e_of_1346.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_route_of_Lancaster%27s_chevauch%C3%A9e_of_1346.svg) Map of route of Lancaster's chevauchée of 1346 Among other consequences, this equivocation allowed Lancaster in the south west to launch offensives into [Quercy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quercy "Quercy") and the [Bazadais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bazas "Bazas"); and himself lead a chevauchée 160 mi (260 km) north through [Saintonge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saintonge_/(region/) "Saintonge (region)"), [Aunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aunis "Aunis") and [Poitou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Poitou "County of Poitou"), capturing numerous towns, castles and smaller fortified places and storming the rich city of [Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poitiers "Poitiers"). These offensives completely disrupted the French defences and shifted the focus of the fighting from the heart of Gascony to 60 mi (97 km) or more beyond its borders.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarari1999385%E2%80%93386-95)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler196967%E2%80%9371-96)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990541%E2%80%93550-97) Few French troops had arrived at Compiègne by 1 October and as Philip and his court waited for the numbers to swell, news of Lancaster's conquests came in. Believing Lancaster was heading for Paris, the French changed the assembly point for any men not already committed to Compiègne to Orléans, and reinforced them with some of those already mustered, to block this. After Lancaster turned south to head back to Gascony, those Frenchmen already at or heading towards Orléans were redirected to Compiègne; French planning collapsed into chaos.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990554-98) Even though only 3,000 men-at-arms had assembled at Compiègne, the French treasurer was unable to pay them. Philip cancelled all offensive arrangements on 27 October and dispersed his army.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990554%E2%80%93555-99) Recriminations were rife: officials at all levels of the [_Chambre des Comptes_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Auditors_/(France/) "Court of Auditors (France)") (the French treasury) were dismissed and all financial affairs were put into the hands of a committee of three senior abbots. The King's council bent their efforts to blaming each other for the kingdom's misfortunes. Duke John fell out with his father and refused to attend court for several months.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990555%E2%80%93556-100) ### Battle of Neville's Cross \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War,_1345%E2%80%931347&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: Battle of Neville's Cross")\] Philip had been calling on the Scots to fulfil their obligation under the terms of the [Auld Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auld_Alliance "Auld Alliance") and invade England since June 1346. The Scottish King, [David II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_David_II "King David II"), convinced that English force was focused entirely on France, obliged on 7 October.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPenman2004157%E2%80%93180-101)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicholson1974111-102) He was taken by surprise by the appearance of a smaller English force raised exclusively from the northern English counties. A battle was fought at [Neville's Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Neville%27s_Cross "Battle of Neville's Cross") outside [Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_England "Durham, England") on 17 October. It ended with the rout of the Scots, the capture of their King and the death or capture of most of their leadership.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006c228%E2%80%93229-103) Strategically the battle freed English forces for the war against France, and the English border counties were able to guard against the remaining Scottish threat from their own resources.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1999145%E2%80%93148-104)[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-105) [![Image 8: A colourful Medieval depiction of a fortification being assaulted](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Siege_of_a_city%2C_medieval_miniature.jpg/330px-Siege_of_a_city%2C_medieval_miniature.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Siege_of_a_city,_medieval_miniature.jpg) A medieval town under siege During the winter the French made great efforts to strengthen their naval resources. These included French and [mercenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary "Mercenary") Italian galleys and French merchant ships, many adapted for military use. During March and April 1347, more than 1,000 [long tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_ton "Long ton") (1,000 [t](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonne "Tonne")) of supplies were run into Calais without opposition.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990559%E2%80%93560-106) Philip attempted to take the field in late April, but the French ability to assemble their army in a timely fashion had not improved since the autumn and by July it had still not fully mustered.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990560-107) In April and May the French tried and failed to cut the English supply route to Flanders while the English tried and failed to capture [Saint-Omer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Omer "Saint-Omer") and [Lille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille "Lille").[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990565,_567-108) In late April the English established a fortification which enabled them to command the entrance to the harbour.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990568-109) In May, June and July the French attempted to force convoys through, unsuccessfully.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990576%E2%80%93577-110) On 25 June the commander of the Calais garrison wrote to Philip saying their food was exhausted and suggesting they may have to resort to cannibalism.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990577-111) Despite increasing financial difficulties, the English steadily reinforced their army through 1347, reaching a peak strength of 32,000.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-105)[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-113) A force of 20,000 Flemish allies gathered less than a day's march from Calais.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990578-112) These forces were supported by 24,000 sailors, in a total of 853 ships.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTELambert2011247-50)[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-115) On 17 July Philip led the French army north to within view of the town, 6 mi (10 km) away. Their army was between 15,000 and 20,000 strong. The English position clearly being unassailable, Philip hesitated. On the night of 1 August the French withdrew.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990578%E2%80%93580-116)[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOman1998153%E2%80%93154-117) On 3 August 1347 Calais surrendered and the entire French population was expelled. A vast amount of [booty](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/booty "wikt:booty") was found within the town. Edward repopulated Calais with English, and a few Flemings.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990580%E2%80%93583-118) Calais was vital to England's effort against the French for the rest of the war and served as an English entrepôt into northern France for more than two hundred years.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006a72-119)[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006b74-120) It allowed the accumulation of supplies and [materiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materiel "Materiel") prior to a campaign. A ring of substantial fortifications defending the approaches to Calais were rapidly constructed, marking the boundary of an area known as the [Pale of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pale_of_Calais "Pale of Calais").[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006a72-119)[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199919%E2%80%9321,_23-121) As soon as Calais capitulated, Edward paid off much of his army and released his Flemish allies.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton2007c195-122) Philip in turn stood down the French army. Edward promptly launched strong raids up to 30 mi (48 km) into French territory.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990583-123) Philip attempted to recall his army but experienced serious difficulties. His treasury was exhausted and taxes for the war had to be collected in many places at sword point. Despite these exigencies, ready cash was not forthcoming.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990584-124) The French army had little stomach for further conflict, and Philip was reduced to threatening to confiscate the estates of nobles who refused to muster.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990584-124) He set back the date for his army to assemble by a month.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990584-124) Edward also had difficulties in raising money, partly because he had not anticipated a return to large-scale conflict and so had an empty treasury; he employed draconian measures to raise money, which were extremely unpopular.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199021,_189-125) The English also suffered two military setbacks: a large raid was routed by the French garrison of Saint-Omer; and a supply convoy en route to Calais was captured by French raiders from Boulogne.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990584-124) Two [cardinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_/(Catholic_Church/) "Cardinal (Catholic Church)") acting as papal [emissaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomat "Diplomat") found the two kings to be willing to listen to their proposals. On 28 September 1347 a truce, known as the [Truce of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Calais "Truce of Calais"), was formally agreed.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990585-126) The truce is considered to have most favoured the English. For its duration the English were confirmed in possession of their extensive territorial conquests in France and Scotland; the Flemish were confirmed in their [de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto "De facto") independence; and Philip was prevented from punishing those French nobles who had conspired, or even fought, against him.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990585-126) It ran for nine months to 7 July 1348, but was extended repeatedly over the years.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006b74%E2%80%9375-127) In 1355 the truce was formally set aside[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006b74%E2%80%9375-127) and full-scale war resumed. In 1360 the Edwardian phase of the war ended with the [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny").[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1994102-128) By this treaty vast areas of France were ceded to England, including the [Pale of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pale_of_Calais "Pale of Calais").[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1999135%E2%80%93136,_447-129) In 1369 large-scale fighting broke out again and the Hundred Years' War did not [end until 1453](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War,_1415%E2%80%931453 "Hundred Years' War, 1415–1453"), by which time England had lost all its territory in France other than Calais.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200246,_91-130) Calais was finally lost following the [1558 siege of the town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Calais_/(1558/) "Siege of Calais (1558)").[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War,_1345%E2%80%931347#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJaques2007184-131) Notes, citations and sources ---------------------------- **Charles of Blois-Châtillon** (1319 – 29 September 1364), nicknamed "the Saint", was the legalist \[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Brittany "Duke of Brittany") from 1341 until his death, via his marriage to [Joan, Duchess of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") and Countess of Penthièvre, holding the title against the claims of [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). The cause of his possible [canonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonization "Canonization") was the subject of a good deal of political maneuvering on the part of his cousin, [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France"), who endorsed it, and his rival, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), who opposed it. The cause fell dormant after [Pope Gregory XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Gregory_XI "Pope Gregory XI") left [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon") in 1376, but was revived in 1894. Charles of Blois was [beatified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatified "Beatified") in 1904.

Charles was born in [Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blois "Blois"), the son of [Guy de Châtillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_I_of_Blois-Ch%C3%A2tillon "Guy I of Blois-Châtillon"), [count of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Blois "Count of Blois"), by [Margaret of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_of_Valois,_Countess_of_Blois "Margaret of Valois, Countess of Blois"), a sister of King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). A devout [ascetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asceticism "Asceticism") from an early age, he showed interest in religious books but was forbidden from reading them by his father, as they did not seem appropriate to his position as a [knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight "Knight").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016289-1) As he grew older, Charles took piety to the extreme of mortifying his own flesh.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016290-2) It is said that he placed pebbles in his shoes, slept on straw instead of a bed, confessed every night in fear of sleeping in a state of sin, and wore a [cilice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cilice "Cilice") (hairshirt) under his armor in battle. He was nevertheless an accomplished military leader, who inspired loyalty by his religious fervour.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016289-1)

On 4 June 1337 in Paris, he married [Joan the Lame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joanna_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joanna of Penthièvre"), heiress and niece of [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1993174-3)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016289-1)

### Breton War of Succession

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Breton War of Succession")\]

Together, Charles and his wife, Joan of Penthièvre, fought the House of Montfort in the [Breton War of Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") (1341–1364), with the support of the crown of France.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016289-1) Despite his piety, Charles did not hesitate in ordering the massacre of 1,400 civilians after the siege of [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper "Quimper") as well as the massacre of thousands after the siege of [Guerande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerande "Guerande").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1999434-4) After initial successes, Charles was taken prisoner by the English in 1347.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016289-1) His official captor was [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988265-5)

He stayed nine years as prisoner in the [Kingdom of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"). During that time, he used to visit English graveyards, where he prayed and recited [Psalm 130](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_130 "Psalm 130"), much to the chagrin of his own squire. When Charles asked the squire to take part in the prayer, the younger man refused, saying that the men who were buried at the English graveyards had killed his parents and friends and burned their houses.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016289-1)

Charles was released against a ransom of about half a million [écus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cu "Écu") in 1356.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAutrand2000441-6) Upon returning to France, he decided to travel barefoot in winter from [La Roche-Derrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Roche-Derrien "La Roche-Derrien") to [Tréguier Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%A9guier_Cathedral "Tréguier Cathedral") out of devotion to Saint [Ivo of Kermartin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivo_of_Kermartin "Ivo of Kermartin"). When the common people heard of his plan, they placed straw and blankets on the street, but Charles promptly took another way. His feet became so sore that he could not walk for 15 weeks.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016289-1) He then resumed the war against the Montforts.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAutrand2000441-6)

Charles was eventually killed in combat during the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") in 1364, which with the second treaty of Guerande in 1381 determined the end of the [Breton War of Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") as a victory for the Montforts.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAutrand2000441-6)

By his marriage to Joan the Lame, Countess of Penthièvre, he had five children:

*   [John I, Count of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I,_Count_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "John I, Count of Penthièvre") (1340–1404)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-7) and [Viscount of Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscount_of_Limoges "Viscount of Limoges").
*   Guy
*   Henry (d. 1400)
*   [Marie of Blois, Duchess of Anjou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_of_Blois,_Duchess_of_Anjou "Marie of Blois, Duchess of Anjou") (1345–1404), Lady of [Guise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guise "Guise"), married in 1360 to [Louis I, Duke of Anjou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I,_Duke_of_Anjou "Louis I, Duke of Anjou")[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruel1905198-8)
*   Margaret of Blois, Countess of Angoulême, married in 1351 to [Charles de la Cerda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_la_Cerda "Charles de la Cerda") (d. 1354), the [Count of Angoulême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Angoul%C3%AAme "Count of Angoulême") and Constable of France.

According to [Froissart's Chronicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Froissart%27s_Chronicles "Froissart's Chronicles"), Charles also had an illegitimate child, John of Blois, who died in the Battle of Auray. However, considering Charles' extreme piety, historian [Johan Huizinga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Huizinga "Johan Huizinga") questioned whether Charles actually had a child born outside marriage and that [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart") could have been mistaken in identifying John as Charles' son.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016290-2)

Charles was buried at [Guingamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guingamp "Guingamp"), where the Franciscans actively promoted his unapproved cult as saint and martyr. Such variety of _ex votos_ bedecked his tomb, that in 1368 [Duke John IV of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") persuaded [Pope Urban V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Urban_V "Pope Urban V") to issue a bull directing the Breton bishops to stop this.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones2000221-9) But the bishops failed to enforce it.

Nonetheless, his family successfully lobbied for his canonization as a [Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint "Saint") of the Roman Catholic church for his devotion to religion.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuizinga2016290-2) Bending to pressure from [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France"), Pope Urban authorized a commission to study the matter. Urban died December 1370 to be succeeded by [Pope Gregory XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Gregory_XI "Pope Gregory XI"). The commission held its first meeting in Angers in September 1371, and forwarded its report to Avignon the following January. Gregory appointed three cardinals to review the matter. The Pope returned to Italy in September 1376, arriving in Rome in November 1377; he died the following March. Gregory was succeeded in Avignon by [Clement VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antipope_Clement_VII "Antipope Clement VII"), but the documents were probably in Rome with [Pope Urban VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Urban_VI "Pope Urban VI").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones2000228-10) There appears to be no record of further activity regarding Charles' cause for canonization at this time. In 1454, Charles' grandson urged his relatives to continue to advocate for his recognition.

The process was re-opened in 1894, and on 14 December 1904, Charles de Châtillon was beatified as _Blessed Charles of Blois_. His feast Day is 30 September.
